docs.title: Declarative dynamic programming (puremacro.dp)
docs.text:
puremacro.dp does for dynamic programs what a Dynare .mod file does for DSGE models: you declare the model as equations and the library writes the solver call. States, shocks, choices, the reward, constraints and an optional market-clearing condition are strings in Dynare expression syntax, parsed by the same parser as .mod files. Model.solve() compiles them to the puremacro.vfi engines, so you never write a return-function closure, broadcast grids by hand or pass positional parameter lists.

You can also write the declarations in a Dynare-style DP .mod file and call dp.solve_mod("household.mod"). It uses these same solvers and returns the same solution object; it is Puremacro DP syntax, not a Dynare DSGE file.

solve(method=...) engine what it handles "vfi" (default without a drift) VFIProblem, FiniteHorizonProblem any discrete-time model on grids; several states "egm" vfi.solve_egm, one EGM step per age one asset with budget c + a(+1) = R*a + y(z); life cycles; a discrete choice with or without taste shocks; Krusell-Smith "hjb" (default with a drift) vfi.solve_hjb_achdou continuous time: one state whose drift is linear in one control

With prices(...) and clear(...) the household solve sits inside a root-find for the market-clearing price. With aggregate_state(...) it sits inside the Krusell and Smith (1998) forecast-rule loop.

docs.title: An Aiyagari economy
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from puremacro import dp

m = dp.Model("aiyagari")
m.parameters(beta=0.96, gamma=1.0, alpha=0.36, delta=0.08)
m.prices(r=(0.005, 0.0396))                       # bracket for the root-find
m.exogenous("z", dp.AR1(rho=0.9, sigma=0.2, n=5)) # Tauchen; method="rouwenhorst"
m.state("a", np.linspace(1e-4, 80.0, 150))
m.local("w = (1 - alpha)*(alpha/(r + delta))^(alpha/(1 - alpha))")
m.local("c = w*exp(z) + (1 + r)*a - a(+1)")
m.reward("crra(c, gamma)")
m.subject_to("c > 0")
m.aggregate(K="a", L="exp(z)")
m.clear("K - L*(alpha/(r + delta))^(1/(1 - alpha))")

sol = m.solve("egm")
print(sol.prices["r"], sol.aggregates["K"])       # about 0.0305 and 7.49
print(sol.summary())

a is today's value of a state and a(+1) its value next period. An identifier that is not a state, a shock or the discrete choice resolves, in order, to a local, a parameter, a price, an aggregate (only inside clear) and age (only in finite-horizon models). crra(c, gamma) is (c^(1-gamma) - 1)/(1 - gamma), and log(c) at gamma = 1. Any other felicity can be written out as an expression: EGM takes its marginal utility from the symbolic derivative and inverts it numerically.

The same model solves by discrete VFI with m.solve() (r about 0.0303 on this grid, in about 8 s against about 1 s for EGM). The two differ because VFI puts a(+1) on grid nodes and EGM does not.

One-asset EGM verifies that the declared budget is affine in current and next assets after expanding local expressions. Matching that form at grid nodes is insufficient for continuous policies. Products of asset-dependent terms, asset-dependent denominators, nonlinear powers and functions of assets are rejected, even when they happen to match on the grid. Multiplication and division by asset-independent terms and custom functions of exogenous income remain supported. The coefficient on next assets must be -1, checked separately from income scale at each calibration, age and discrete choice.

Explicit constraints must be a zero bound on consumption (c > 0, 0 < c, or their non-strict forms); local aliases are accepted. Numerical checks also require the reward's feasible domain to be exactly positive consumption. The grid supplies the borrowing limit. Use VFI for other resource equations or constraints; EGM rejects extra constraints even if they are redundant at every declared grid node.

docs.title: Reading a solution
docs.text:
DPSolution holds the solution whatever the engine:

  • sol.V, sol.distribution: arrays of shape (n_states, n_shocks), with a leading age axis in a life cycle;
  • sol.policy(expr): any model expression at the optimal choice, e.g. sol.policy("c") or sol.policy("a(+1)");
  • sol.mean(expr): its population mean under the stationary distribution, one value per age in a life cycle;
  • sol.prices, sol.aggregates, sol.equilibrium, sol.grids, sol.P;
  • sol.elapsed: wall-clock solve time in seconds (float);
  • sol.to_microframe(columns=None, *, age=None): converts the stationary or life-cycle grid-node distribution (sol.dist > 0) into a MicroFrame with SurveyDesign.weights_only("weight") (unit="node"), attaching state, shock, policy, value, and local columns;
  • sol.raw: the underlying engine's result.
c = sol.policy("c")                 # (150, 5)
print(sol.mean("c"), sol.mean("a")) # mean consumption and assets

When max_iter runs out. The outcome depends on the engine. The one-asset "vfi" and "egm" engines (discrete-choice EGM included) return no converged field, so they raise RuntimeError("... did not converge ...") and hand back no partial solution. The two-asset EGM solver and the "hjb" solver emit a RuntimeWarning and return the last iterate with sol.raw.converged = False; the Krusell-Smith loop does the same at max_outer (sol.equilibrium.converged). Check the flag before using the policy: dp_sequence_jacobian and dp_nonlinear_transition refuse an unconverged two-asset household with RuntimeError.

docs.title: Life cycles
docs.text:
horizon(T, survival=..., terminal=..., newborns=...) makes the problem finite. age (0 to T-1) can appear in any equation, so income profiles, retirement and age-varying returns are written in place. A relational expression such as (age < T_ret) is 1 when it holds and 0 otherwise.

T = 60
lc = dp.Model("life cycle")
lc.parameters(beta=0.96, gamma=2.0, r=0.03, T_ret=45)
lc.exogenous("z", dp.AR1(rho=0.95, sigma=0.1, n=5))
lc.state("a", np.linspace(0.0, 30.0, 120))
lc.local("y = (age < T_ret)*exp(z + 0.04*age - 0.0008*age^2) + (age >= T_ret)*0.6")
lc.local("c = (1 + r)*a + y - a(+1)")
lc.reward("crra(c, gamma)")
lc.subject_to("c > 0")
lc.horizon(T, survival=np.full(T, 0.99))

life = lc.solve("egm")
assets = life.mean("a")             # mean assets by age; they peak at retirement
print(int(assets.argmax()))         # 45

Each cohort has mass one in life.distribution, and survival is not applied there: it only discounts the future. life.population_shares() gives each age's share of the population with survival applied, and the statistics that pool ages use it (see Panels and inequality). Newborns start at the lowest grid point with shocks drawn from their stationary distribution unless newborns= says otherwise.

docs.title: Discrete choices and taste shocks
docs.text:
discrete("h", values) adds a discrete choice made together with a(+1). Under method="egm" each option is inverted by the Euler equation and an upper envelope keeps the optimal segments (Iskhakov, Jørgensen, Rust and Schjerning 2017). The borrowing-limit and top-of-grid corners are admitted only where their Kuhn-Tucker condition holds. taste_shocks(scale) adds type-I extreme value shocks: values become log-sums, choices logit probabilities, and mean("h") is a participation rate.

w = dp.Model("work or not")
w.parameters(beta=0.95, gamma=2.0, r=0.03, chi=0.5, b=0.3, sig=0.05)
w.exogenous("z", dp.AR1(rho=0.9, sigma=0.2, n=5))
w.state("a", np.linspace(0.0, 60.0, 200))
w.discrete("h", [0.0, 1.0])
w.local("c = (1 + r)*a + h*exp(z) + (1 - h)*b - a(+1)")
w.reward("crra(c, gamma) - chi*h")
w.subject_to("c > 0")
w.taste_shocks("sig")
w.aggregate(H="h", A="a")

work = w.solve("egm")
print(work.aggregates["H"])         # participation rate, about 0.63

The reward and income may depend on the option; the return on assets may not. Aggregates over a discrete choice converge slowly in the number of grid points under either method, because the distribution's mass sits on grid nodes: check them on a finer grid before reporting them.

docs.title: Continuous time
docs.text:
Declare a control, a drift for the state and a discount_rate, with dp.Jump (a Poisson generator) for the shocks. The compiler checks that the drift is linear in the control with slope -1 and derives u' and its inverse from the reward. Prices and clear work as in discrete time, with aggregates integrated against the Kolmogorov forward density.

ct = dp.Model("continuous-time Aiyagari")
ct.parameters(rho=0.05, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.33, delta=0.05)
ct.prices(r=(0.005, 0.048))
ct.exogenous("e", dp.Jump([0.2, 1.0], [[-0.1, 0.1], [0.1, -0.1]]))
ct.state("a", np.linspace(0.0, 30.0, 100))
ct.local("w = (1 - alpha)*(alpha/(r + delta))^(alpha/(1 - alpha))")
ct.control("c")
ct.drift("a", "r*a + w*e - c")
ct.discount_rate("rho")
ct.reward("crra(c, gamma)")
ct.aggregate(K="a", L="e")
ct.clear("K - L*(alpha/(r + delta))^(1/(1 - alpha))")

hjb = ct.solve()                    # method="hjb" because the model has a drift
print(hjb.prices["r"])              # about 0.0200

Several Jump shocks combine as their product chain. sol.distribution is the mass at each node (the density times the quadrature weights).

docs.title: Aggregate risk: Krusell and Smith
docs.text:
aggregate_shock("Z", process) and aggregate_state("K", grid, mean="a") turn the model into the Krusell and Smith (1998) fixed point: households forecast K with a log-linear rule, the economy is simulated, and the rule is re-estimated until it stops moving. Prices and technology are model equations, so any firm and any household reward work.

ks = dp.Model("krusell-smith")
ks.parameters(beta=0.99, gamma=1.0, alpha=0.36, delta=0.025, L=0.9)
ks.exogenous("e", dp.Markov([0.5, 1.1], [[0.6, 0.4], [0.2, 0.8]]))
ks.aggregate_shock("Z", dp.Markov([0.99, 1.01], [[0.875, 0.125], [0.125, 0.875]]))
ks.state("a", np.linspace(0.0, 150.0, 100))
ks.aggregate_state("K", np.linspace(25.0, 45.0, 5), mean="a")
ks.local("r = alpha*Z*(K/L)^(alpha - 1) - delta", "w = (1 - alpha)*Z*(K/L)^alpha")
ks.local("c = (1 + r)*a + w*e - a(+1)")
ks.reward("crra(c, gamma)")
ks.subject_to("c > 0")

agg = ks.solve("egm", ks=dict(T=1000, burn_in=200, max_outer=60))
rule = agg.equilibrium                 # log K' = b0 + b1 log K, one rule per Z
print(rule.b1, rule.r_squared, rule.converged)   # b1 about 0.96; converges in 8 rounds

L is the mean of the idiosyncratic chain e (its stationary distribution is (1/3, 2/3)). A long simulation (T in the thousands) gives tighter forecast coefficients than this quick run.

Use method="egm" here. Discrete VFI puts next-period assets on grid nodes, and on a coarse grid simulated capital then never moves: the forecast regression returns b1 = 0 with R² = 1 and passes the tolerance. Both this loop and vfi.krusell_smith raise a RuntimeWarning in that case and when they stop at max_outer without converging. Read rule.converged and rule.r_squared before using the forecast rule.

docs.title: Panels and inequality
docs.text:
Inequality statistics are computed exactly from sol.distribution, with no simulation: each grid node is a mass point with its stationary mass. sol.gini(expr) is the standard weighted Gini, 1 - sum_i w_i (L_i + L_{i-1}) on the Lorenz curve, the same function as MicroFrame.gini. Negative values are allowed (the Gini can then exceed 1) and it is NaN when the total is not positive. sol.top_share(expr, p), sol.quantile(expr, q) and sol.lorenz(expr) complete the picture.

print(sol.gini("a"), sol.top_share("a", 0.10))   # about 0.62 and 0.41
print(sol.quantile("a", 0.5))                    # median wealth, about 3.76
curve = sol.lorenz("a")                          # columns pop_share, value_share

sol.simulate(n_agents=10_000, periods=None, *, seed=0, init=None, burn_in=0, record=None) draws individual histories under the solved policy and returns a dp.Panel. periods=None and init=None take per-horizon defaults: 200 periods and "stationary" in an infinite horizon, the T ages of the horizon and "newborn" in a life cycle. In an infinite horizon each agent starts in a (state, shock) cell drawn from sol.distribution, so the panel is in the stationary distribution from the first period; init={"a": 0.1} starts everyone at a given state instead, and burn_in drops the first periods. VFI states stay on grid nodes, EGM interpolates the policy between them. A discrete choice is simulated too: the argmax option without taste shocks, a logit draw with them, recorded as the option's value. The panel records the states, the shocks and the controls (record= takes any model expression, such as "a(+1)" or "w*exp(z)"). The same seed gives a bit-identical panel.

panel = sol.simulate(n_agents=10_000, periods=200, seed=1)
print(panel)                        # Panel(n_agents=10000, periods=200, columns=['a', 'z', 'c'])
gini_t = panel.gini("a", by="t")    # one cross-sectional Gini per period
print(gini_t.iloc[-1])              # about 0.62, the exact value up to sampling noise
df = panel.to_frame()               # long format: id, t, a, z, c

panel.mean, panel.quantile, panel.gini and panel.top_share pool every period, or group with by="t" (or by="age" in a life cycle). panel.cross_section(t) and panel.path(i) return one period or one agent, and panel.to_microframe() hands the panel to the survey-data estimators. n_agents * periods above 5e8 raises ValueError with the memory it would need.

In a life cycle the panel runs over the ages of the horizon. Agents start as newborns and, with declared survival, an agent alive at age j lives to j+1 with probability survival[j]. panel.alive records this. The dead keep their rows but are left out of every statistic. The exact statistics pool ages with population_shares() as weights, or take one cohort with age=j.

shares = life.population_shares()   # survival 0.99: 0.022 at age 0, 0.012 at age 59
print(life.gini("a"))               # all ages pooled, about 0.73
print(life.gini("a", age=30))       # the 30-year-old cohort, about 0.50
lp = life.simulate(n_agents=5000, seed=0)
print(lp.alive[:, -1].mean())       # about 0.55 reach age 59
print(lp.mean("a", by="age")[45])   # about 7.7; life.mean("a")[45] is 7.68

Continuous-time (HJB) and Krusell–Smith solutions are simulated with the same sol.simulate(...) call:

  • For continuous-time (method="hjb"), sol.simulate(..., dt=1.0) advances the endogenous state by \(\dot{a}\,\Delta t\) interpolated on the state grid, draws Markov jump transitions from the matrix exponential \(\exp(Q\,\Delta t)\) (process_type="poisson"), or steps continuous diffusions by Euler–Maruyama with boundary reflection (process_type="diffusion").
  • For Krusell–Smith ("vfi+ks", "egm+ks"), sol.simulate(...) evolves the aggregate state path \((Z_t, K_t)\) under the converged forecast rule (sol.forecast) and interpolates the 4D policy pol[i_Z, i_e, i_a, i_K] across agents in every period. Exact stationary-distribution methods (sol.mean, sol.gini, sol.quantile, sol.top_share, sol.to_microframe) raise ValueError on Krusell–Smith solutions because there is no single stationary distribution; compute cross-sectional moments on the simulated Panel instead.

docs.title: User-registered functions
docs.text:
m.functions(**callables) registers vectorised Python/NumPy callables so model expressions in local, subject_to, aggregate, clear, and Panel evaluation can call custom schedules (such as piecewise tax-and-transfer rules) across VFI, EGM, and HJB (reward also accepts registered functions under method="vfi"). If a callable accepts an xp keyword argument, dp passes the active array backend (numpy, jax.numpy, or cupy):

m.functions(tax=lambda y, xp=np: 0.15 * y + 0.10 * xp.maximum(y - 1.0, 0.0))
m.local("y = w * exp(z)", "c = (1 + r)*a + y - tax(y) - a(+1)")

docs.title: Sequence-space HANK bridge
docs.text: An infinite-horizon single-state dp.Model supported by EGM, without a discrete choice (or its solved DPSolution), connects directly to the Auclert, Bardóczy, Rognlie & Straub (2021) sequence-space engine via dp_sequence_jacobian(model_or_sol, inputs, outputs=None, T=300, dx=1e-4) and dp_nonlinear_transition(model_or_sol, input_paths, outputs=None) in puremacro.models.hank_sequence_space, or by passing household_model=m to HANKModel, load_hank_mod, and solve_hank_bridge in puremacro.dsge.hank. See Non-Linear HANK Transitions & Effective Lower Bound for details.

docs.title: Two-asset households (5.4)
docs.text:
Two-state method="egm" supports a stationary CRRA household with liquid bonds b, illiquid assets a, and convex portfolio adjustment costs. The compiler checks the declared budget, utility and feasible set against this specialized problem; it rejects unsupported equations instead of substituting a different household problem. For example:

import numpy as np
from puremacro import dp

m = dp.Model("two_asset")
m.state("a", 40 * np.linspace(0, 1, 20)**2)
m.state("b", 10 * np.linspace(0, 1, 20)**1.5)
m.exogenous("z", dp.Markov(np.array([0.5, 1.5]),
                           np.array([[0.95, 0.05], [0.10, 0.90]])))
m.parameters(beta=0.98, gamma=1.0, r_b=0.005, r_a=0.0125,
             w=1.0, chi_0=1.0, chi_1=1.0, a_bar=0.25)
m.local("d = a(+1) - (1+r_a)*a")
m.local("chi = chi_0/(1+chi_1)*abs(d)*(abs(d)/(a+a_bar))^chi_1")
m.local("c = (1+r_b)*b + (1+r_a)*a + w*z - a(+1) - b(+1) - chi")
m.reward("crra(c, gamma)")
m.subject_to("c > 0")
m.aggregate(C="c", A="a", B="b", COST="chi")
sol = m.solve(method="egm", tol=1e-8)

The supported contract has an infinite horizon, no discrete choice or endogenous equilibrium price, at most one Markov productivity shock, at least two nodes per asset, nonnegative illiquid holdings, 0 < beta < 1, positive gamma, w, chi_0, a_bar, chi_1 >= 1, and positive gross returns. Consumption must be a local named c, cons, or consumption; utility is crra(consumption, gamma) (including a named curvature parameter or constant) or log(consumption). Log utility always has curvature one, irrespective of an unrelated parameter named gamma. The budget is recognized structurally after inlining locals; reordered sums/products, expanded products, renamed assets and the equivalent cost forms chi_0*abs(d)^(1+chi_1)/((1+chi_1)*(a+a_bar)^chi_1) and chi_0/(1+chi_1)*(abs(d)/(a+a_bar))^(1+chi_1)*(a+a_bar) are supported. Asset roles follow the recognized cost, including reversed declarations.

Price bindings accept r_b/rb/r/r_b_ss/r_ss/r_liquid, r_a/ra/r_a_ss/r_k/r_illiquid, and w/w_ss/z/y (one used parameter per role); a_bar also accepts b_bar. These same bindings apply to stationary solutions, price paths and Jacobians. Discounting may use discount("patience"). Cost parameters remain explicitly named chi_0, chi_1, and a_bar/b_bar. Arbitrary registered functions in the budget, unsupported denominators or real powers, extra budget terms, constraints, life cycles and discrete choices are rejected before solving. Numerical probes are a second check, not the proof of the budget identity. Registered functions in aggregates remain supported.

Arrays use (illiquid asset, liquid asset, productivity) order. policy("a") returns current assets; policy("a(+1)") returns the saving policy. Inspect sol.raw.converged and sol.raw.sup_norm: exhaustion of the iteration budget warns, and an infeasible consumption floor raises an error. Refine and enlarge asset grids to check numerical accuracy and top-grid mass. converged also requires the distribution's stationarity residual to be below 1e-10; finite, normalized mass alone is insufficient.

audit_result(sol) exposes budget and Euler/KKT maps, locations, stationary-weighted percentiles, separate mass/stationarity checks and upper-bound mass. Grid or horizon refinement requires explicit callbacks. The first-order bridge permits price changes to the recognized liquid return, illiquid return and income parameters; it does not authorize arbitrary cost or preference shocks.

dp_sequence_jacobian(sol, inputs=["r_b", "r_a", "w"], outputs=["C", "COST"], T=24) and dp_nonlinear_transition evaluate declared aggregates, including registered functions and their direct price dependence. Declared aggregate expressions preserve their timing: A="a" is current wealth, while A="a(+1)" is saving. Undeclared uppercase aliases A and B denote end-of-period holdings. Migration from 5.3: the one-asset bridge previously interpreted a declared A="a" as saving. Use A="a(+1)" explicitly to retain that timing; current wealth has zero impact response under a fixed initial distribution. HANKModel(..., household_model=m) supports linear general-equilibrium dynamics. Two-asset panel simulation and nonlinear general-equilibrium simulation of a declarative household are not implemented and raise NotImplementedError.

docs.title: Checking a specification
docs.text: m.check() compiles the model without solving it and raises ModelSpecError with the reason, for instance an unknown identifier or a name declared twice. solve("egm") and solve("hjb") add their own checks and raise the same error for a budget that is not of the form c + a(+1) = R*a + y(z) or a drift that is not linear in the control.

docs.title: What dp does not do yet
docs.text:
• EGM with multiple assets outside the specialized two-asset contract above (use method="vfi", which takes several states);
  • more than one price in continuous time;
  • Krusell-Smith forecast rules with more than one moment.

docs.title: Porting from vfi.Model
docs.text:
vfi.Model is deprecated and will be removed in 6.0. A vfi.Model took Python functions for the utility and the budget; dp takes expressions. Each lambda becomes its expression string, the budget becomes a local for c, and c > 0 replaces the -1e10 penalty. This is the precautionary-savings model of notebook 21, first as it was written for vfi.Model:

m = vfi.Model("Precautionary Savings Model")
m.set_param("beta", 0.96).set_param("gamma", 2.0).set_param("alpha", 0.36).set_param("delta", 0.10)
m.add_state("a", 0.1, 15.0, 60).add_shock("z", 0.90, 0.15, 5)
m.set_utility(lambda c, p: c**(1 - p["gamma"]) / (1 - p["gamma"]))
m.set_budget(lambda a, ap, z, p: np.exp(z) * a**p["alpha"] + (1 - p["delta"]) * a - ap)
res = m.solve(howard_steps=15, tol=1e-6)

and as a dp model:

pm = dp.Model("Precautionary Savings Model")
pm.parameters(beta=0.96, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.36, delta=0.10)
pm.exogenous("z", dp.AR1(rho=0.90, sigma=0.15, n=5))   # Tauchen, as add_shock
pm.state("a", np.linspace(0.1, 15.0, 60))
pm.local("c = exp(z)*a^alpha + (1 - delta)*a - a(+1)")
pm.reward("c^(1 - gamma)/(1 - gamma)")
pm.subject_to("c > 0")

ps = pm.solve(method="vfi", tol=1e-6)
print(ps.mean("a"), ps.gini("a"))   # 6.5733 and 0.3494

The budget is not of the form R*a + y(z), so this model uses method="vfi". The dp solution chooses the same next-period grid node as vfi.Model in every state, and the value functions agree to 7e-7. res["V"], res["policy_a"] and res["a_grid"] become ps.V, ps.policy("a(+1)") and ps.grids["a"]. res["mean_assets"] and res["gini"] (6.6767 and 0.3924) came from a 2000-household, 100-period simulation, and that Gini subtracted the minimum asset holding first. ps.mean("a") and ps.gini("a") are the exact values of the stationary distribution, and ps.simulate(...) gives the panel.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: The Aiyagari, Huggett, life-cycle and two-asset models written as dp models reproduce vfi.examples exactly (same prices, policies and value functions). Independent checks do not go through the compiler: two-period log-utility models match their closed form to 1e-12, the logit last period matches its closed form to 1e-12, a two-period discrete-choice model matches a 200,001-point brute-force maximisation, and the continuous-time Aiyagari equilibrium matches vfi.solve_aiyagari_continuous_hjb (r* to 1e-9). The tests are in tests/test_dp/.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text: python -m puremacro.examples.scf_aiyagari calibrates the discount factor of a dp Aiyagari model (EGM) to a wealth-to-income ratio in the Survey of Consumer Finances and compares untargeted moments with the data, with standard errors. See Survey microdata.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  • Achdou, Y., Han, J., Lasry, J.-M., Lions, P.-L. and Moll, B. (2022). Income and wealth distribution in macroeconomics: a continuous-time approach. Review of Economic Studies, 89(1), 45–86.

docs.title: Dynamic programming in .mod files
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Dynamic programs in a .mod file
docs.text:
Write the household or firm's objective and constraints as equations, save a text file, and solve it with puremacro.dp.solve_mod. The reader compiles the declarations to the existing dp.Model, so file and Python models use the same VFI, EGM and HJB solvers and return the same DPSolution objects.

This is Puremacro's DP language with Dynare-style syntax. These files are not DSGE equilibrium systems and are not executable by Dynare itself. Use puremacro.dsge.load_mod for ordinary Dynare DSGE files.

docs.title: A complete VFI model
docs.text:
Save this as growth.mod:

parameters beta alpha;
beta = 0.95;
alpha = 0.36;
state k = geomspace(0.01, 2.0, 300);

model(name='Growth by value function iteration');
  c = k^alpha - k(+1);
  reward = log(c);
end;
constraints;
  c > 0;
end;
solve(method=vfi, tol=1e-9, distribution=false);

from puremacro import dp

sol = dp.solve_mod("growth.mod")
print(sol.summary())
consumption = sol.policy("c")
next_capital = sol.policy("k(+1)")

Here k is current capital and k(+1) is next period's capital, chosen on the declared grid by VFI. The compiler supplies the Bellman problem; there is no need to write an Euler equation or a Python return-function closure. In this log-utility/full-depreciation model, the continuous exact policy is k_next = alpha*beta*k**alpha, which provides an independent accuracy check. The finite grid introduces approximation error.

The equivalent command-line calls are:

puremacro-dp growth.mod --check
puremacro-dp growth.mod
python -m puremacro.dp growth.mod --param beta=0.97

--check validates and compiles declarations but performs no numerical solve. It does not certify convergence, grid accuracy or economic assumptions.

docs.title: Income risk and saving
docs.text:
parameters beta gamma r w;
beta = 0.96; gamma = 2; r = 0.02; w = 1;
state a = 40*linspace(0, 1, 120)^2;
exogenous z = rouwenhorst(rho=0.9, sigma=0.15, n=5);

model;
  c = (1+r)*a + w*exp(z) - a(+1);
  reward = crra(c, gamma);
end;
constraints; c > 0; end;
aggregates; A = a; C = c; end;
solve(method=egm, tol=1e-9);

EGM uses continuous saving policies between grid nodes. Its supported budget and preference restrictions are unchanged; choosing another method does not change the declared economic problem. Use method=vfi for the discrete grid-search solution. Multiple state declarations and one discrete choice are supported by the underlying VFI compiler.

For one-asset EGM, the solver verifies the affine budget from the equations, including local aliases, and checks the next-asset coefficient separately from income scale. Nonlinear terms or extra constraints cannot be accepted just because they vanish at grid nodes. Custom functions of exogenous income remain supported; use VFI for general asset-dependent schedules or constraints. See the one-asset EGM restrictions.

model = dp.load_mod("household.mod")  # validates, never solves
egm = dp.solve_mod("household.mod")   # honors the file's solve options
vfi = dp.solve_mod("household.mod", method="vfi", tol=1e-10)
alternative = dp.solve_mod("household.mod", params={"r": 0.01})

Python solve options override file options. Calibration overrides apply before dependent calibrations and grids are evaluated. Names must be declared in the file. model.solve(...) uses the ordinary Python API defaults, not the optional file command; solve_mod applies that command explicitly.

docs.title: Declaration reference
docs.text:
Declaration Meaning parameters beta gamma; beta=.96; gamma=2; Declare and calibrate once, in dependency order. Arrays are allowed for age-varying parameters. state a = linspace(0, 40, 120); Endogenous state and increasing finite grid. Its next-period value is a choice. exogenous z = ar1(rho=.9, sigma=.2, n=5); Gaussian AR(1), Tauchen by default; method=rouwenhorst selects that discretization. exogenous z = markov([.5, 1.5], [.9,.1; .2,.8]); Explicit row-stochastic Markov chain. Nested lists also work. discrete h = [0, 1]; One contemporaneous discrete choice; include its reward/cost in the model. taste_shocks = sigma_h; EV1 taste shocks for the existing discrete-choice EGM solver. model; c = ...; reward = ...; end; Named local expressions and exactly one objective. # c = ... is also accepted. constraints; c > 0; end; Feasibility conditions, using the DP expression language. aggregates; A = a; C = c; end; Integrals under the solved distribution; timing follows the declared expression. price r = [-.01, .04]; clear = A - K_demand; One endogenous price bracket and scalar stationary market-clearing residual. Define demand as an expression using declared parameters/locals. discount patience; Use a calibrated parameter named patience instead of beta. horizon = 30; survival = full(30,.99); Finite horizon and optional survival vector. age starts at zero. terminal = ...; newborns = ...; Optional arrays with the shapes required by Model.horizon. control c; drift a = r*a + z - c; discount_rate rho; Continuous-time model, solved by HJB. Use jump(values, rates) for its shocks. solve(method=egm, tol=1e-9); Optional final command. Only solve_mod executes it.

Calibration expressions allow arithmetic, ^, arrays, previously calibrated parameters, linspace, geomspace, logspace, full, exp, log, sqrt, abs, and binary min/max. Matrix columns require commas; semicolons separate rows. Grids and calibration arrays are limited to one million elements by this reader, and AR(1) transition matrices are bounded by the same limit. The Python API remains available for larger inputs. Multiple independent shock chains are combined by the existing compiler; their product can still be large.

The final solve accepts method, backend, tol, howard, max_iter, distribution, xtol, and max_evals, subject to the selected engine. Explicit options that the engine would ignore are rejected: backend and howard for EGM/HJB; tol, max_iter and howard for finite horizons; and xtol/max_evals without equilibrium prices. Finite-horizon and equilibrium solves require a distribution, so distribution=false is rejected there. Python overrides are checked after merging with file options; omitted options retain the ordinary solver defaults. See DP solvers. Aggregate-risk/Krusell–Smith declarations remain available through the Python API and are not part of this file grammar.

Comments use //, %, or /* ... */. Declarations end in semicolons. The reader reports file names and statement line numbers and rejects unknown commands, duplicate declarations, incomplete blocks and unsupported options. It does not execute Python/MATLAB scripts, macros or includes. Custom economic functions can be registered explicitly with dp.load_mod(source, functions={"tax": my_tax}), under the existing Model.functions contract; a file cannot define or import such functions.

docs.title: Examples and evidence
docs.text:
Three examples ship in the installed package:

from importlib.resources import files
from puremacro import dp

source = files("puremacro.dp").joinpath("_examples/household.mod").read_text()
sol = dp.solve_mod(source)

The other names are growth.mod and lifecycle.mod. Tests compare file and Python declarations under VFI, EGM and HJB, independently enumerate a two-state Bellman maximum, check a final-age choice analytically, and compare growth policies to the closed form. These are numerical/compiler checks; they do not establish empirical validity. Use result audits and explicit grid refinement for the supported solved-result types.

docs.title: DSGE Sketchpad & Dynare
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: DSGE sketchpad: models from equations, not matrices
docs.text:
For the 5.7 nonlinear interface and a choice among local, deterministic and global solution methods, start with DSGE workflows. This page also documents the earlier sketchpad and local-solution APIs.

puremacro.dsge.klein_solve has always solved linear rational-expectations models with no Dynare and no compiler — but it takes A, B, C, and getting those means differentiating the equilibrium conditions by hand. That derivation is the step people get wrong, and it is exactly the step a tablet is worst at: no algebra system, no MATLAB, no patience.

dsge.build removes it. Write the conditions as they appear in the paper.

import numpy as np
from puremacro import dsge

def eqs(xp, x, e, p):
    # xp = t+1, x = t, e = shocks, p = params
    return [
        1 / x.c - p.beta * (p.alpha * xp.z * xp.k ** (p.alpha - 1)) / xp.c,
        x.c + xp.k - x.z * x.k ** p.alpha,
        xp.z - x.z ** p.rho * np.exp(e.eps),
    ]

m = dsge.build(
    eqs,
    variables=["c", "k", "z"],
    states=["k", "z"],
    shocks=["eps"],
    params=dict(alpha=0.33, beta=0.98, rho=0.9),
    guess=dict(c=0.5, k=0.1, z=1.0),
)
print(m.summary())
m.irf("eps", horizon=20)     # DataFrame: horizons × variables

xp, x, e and p each support attribute access (x.k), string indexing (x["k"]), positional indexing and tuple-unpacking, so a model reads the way it is written. A misspelled name raises an error listing what was declared.

docs.title: What you get back
docs.text:
LinearModel is a frozen dataclass carrying the steady state, the units, the Klein-form matrices and the underlying KleinSolution:

member meaning .steady_state pandas.Series, verified rather than trusted .units per-variable "log" or "level" .irf(shock, horizon, size) impulse responses, horizons × variables .simulate(periods, sigma, seed) stochastic simulation .policy() decision rules as a labelled table .decision_rules() / .dynare_dr DynareDR object matching Dynare's oo_.dr (ghx, ghu, ys) .theoretical_moments() analytical moments, correlations, autocorrelations & FEVD (Dynare stoch_simul) .fevd(horizons) analytical forecast error variance decomposition across finite & asymptotic horizons .solution the KleinSolution — G, F, N, L .A, .B, .C the matrices the Jacobians produced

Steady states are solved from guess=, or supplied via steady_state= and then checked against the equations (max|f(ss, ss, 0)| <= tol) rather than taken at face value. Log-linearisation is per variable, falling back to level deviations where a steady state is not strictly positive; .units records which is which.

docs.title: Complex-step differentiation, and its one restriction
docs.text:
Jacobians come from Im f(x + ih) / h with h = 1e-20 — machine-precision derivatives from one evaluation per argument, with no step-size trade-off and no cancellation error.

The catch is that this is exact only if the residual function is analytic, and it fails silently when it is not: Im through an abs() is identically zero, so the derivative comes back as zero with nothing raised anywhere. Four things break it — abs, min/max, a comparison that branches on a perturbed value, and any float() / np.real() cast that discards the imaginary part.

build therefore cross-checks every complex-step Jacobian against a finite difference in a random direction and raises ModelError naming the offending block if they disagree. Models with occasionally-binding constraints violate analyticity by construction: pass method="central" and accept ~1e-8 accuracy instead of ~1e-15. verify_derivatives=False opts out of the check.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
Equations are E_t f(z_{t+1}, z_t, u_t) = 0, matching klein_solve. An exogenous process written the usual way, z' = rho*z + eps, moves the state into the next period, so every state is zero in the h=0 row of an IRF and jumps at h=1.

Forward-looking controls are a different matter, and this trips people up: they generally do move at h=0, because the innovation is in the agents' information set and they depend on expectations of t+1. In the three-equation New Keynesian model a demand shock leaves the natural rate at zero on impact while the output gap and inflation jump immediately — agents reacting to the higher natural rate they already know is coming. That jump is Klein's L loading. Whether a control moves at h=0 is a property of the model, not of the convention; only the states are guaranteed to be zero there.

docs.title: Blanchard-Kahn as an outcome
docs.text:
Determinacy is not an assumption you assert but a property of the solve. In the worked New Keynesian example, violating the Taylor principle is a raised exception rather than a footnote:

solve(phi_pi=0.9)
# BlanchardKahnError: Blanchard-Kahn indeterminacy: 2 unstable generalised
# eigenvalues vs 3 forward-looking variables

Pass strict=False to get the Sims/gensys-style soft failure (zero matrices with eu flagged) instead.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The neoclassical growth model with full depreciation and log utility is the one textbook case with a closed form — k' = αβzk^α, c = (1−αβ)zk^α, so G = [[α, 1], [0, ρ]] and F = [α, 1] exactly. build reproduces every entry of G, F, N and L to 1e-9, and the steady state to 1e-12.

For a model with genuinely forward-looking controls, the New Keynesian block is checked the strongest way available: the whole IRF path is substituted back into the structural equations — expectations included, since the economy is deterministic after impact — and every equation holds to 1e-10.

Both live in tests/test_dsge/test_build.py; the worked example is python -m puremacro.examples.dsge_nk_sketchpad.

A note on klein_solve at 1.2.0

Building models from natural-order equations surfaced a long-standing bug in klein_solve's policy function. F used a formula inconsistent with the G returned beside it, the guard meant to catch that partitioned A and B by row when the split is over variables, and L was zero whenever a shock entered a control equation contemporaneously. All four are fixed and pinned against closed-form solutions in tests/test_dsge/test_klein_analytic.py. Measured impact on existing models: SW07 moves by 1.2e-12, and the course notebooks that call klein_solve reproduce byte-identical output — the old residual guard did fire on those, and its fallback recovered a correct F.

docs.title: Dynare Compatibility: Decision Rules & Theoretical Moments
docs.text: To match the output of Dynare's stoch_simul(order=1), LinearModel provides:

docs.title: 1. Decision Rules (m.decision_rules() / m.dynare_dr)
docs.text:
Maps Klein's state transition and policy functions into Dynare's standard representation: $\(y_t = y^* + g_{x} (x_{t-1} - x^*) + g_{u} u_t\)$

dr = m.decision_rules()
print(dr.summary())
Outputs the exact Dynare POLICY AND TRANSITION FUNCTIONS table with Constant, lagged states (k(-1), z(-1)), and structural shocks.

docs.title: 2. Theoretical Moments (m.theoretical_moments())
docs.text:
Solves the discrete Lyapunov equation \(\Sigma_x = G \Sigma_x G' + N \Sigma_u N'\) for analytical unconditional moments without relying on stochastic simulation:

mom = m.theoretical_moments(lags=5)
print(mom.summary())
Renders the 4 standard Dynare output blocks: - THEORETICAL MOMENTS: Mean, Standard Deviation, and Variance for each variable. - MATRIX OF CORRELATIONS: Full cross-correlation matrix. - COEFFICIENTS OF AUTOCORRELATION: Exact theoretical autocorrelations for lags 1 through 5. - VARIANCE DECOMPOSITION: Forecast error variance decomposition shares (in percent) across finite horizons (1, 4, 8, 16, 32) and asymptotic infinity.

docs.title: 3. Canonical Lead-Lag Interface (dsge.build_dynare)
docs.text:
Write models directly in Dynare's canonical dynamic representation: $\(E_t [ f(y_{t+1}, y_t, y_{t-1}, u_t; \theta) ] = 0\)$

Unlike dsge.build, build_dynare: - Uses the standard five-argument signature eqs(lead, curr, lag, shocks, params). - Automatically detects predetermined states: variables appearing with non-zero Jacobian in lag are classified as predetermined states, completely eliminating the manual states=[...] requirement.

from puremacro import dsge

def rbc(lead, curr, lag, shocks, p):
    return [
        curr.c**(-p.gamma) - p.beta * lead.c**(-p.gamma) * (p.alpha * np.exp(lead.a) * curr.k**(p.alpha - 1) + 1 - p.delta),
        curr.k - (np.exp(curr.a) * lag.k**p.alpha - curr.c + (1 - p.delta) * lag.k),
        curr.a - (p.rho * lag.a + shocks.eps),
    ]

m = dsge.build_dynare(
    rbc,
    variables=["k", "a", "c"],
    shocks=["eps"],
    params=dict(alpha=0.3, beta=0.99, delta=0.025, gamma=1.0, rho=0.8),
    guess=dict(k=38.0, a=0.0, c=2.0),
)
# States ('k', 'a') and control ('c',) are automatically classified!

docs.title: 4. Pure-Python Dynare .mod File Parser (dsge.load_mod)
docs.text:
Run standard Dynare .mod files directly in pure Python with zero MATLAB or Octave dependencies:

from puremacro import dsge

mod_text = """
var c k a;
varexo eps;
parameters alpha beta delta gamma rho;

alpha = 0.30;
beta  = 0.99;
delta = 0.025;
gamma = 1.0;
rho   = 0.80;

model;
  c^(-gamma) = beta * c(+1)^(-gamma) * (alpha * exp(a(+1)) * k^(alpha - 1.0) + 1.0 - delta);
  k = exp(a) * k(-1)^alpha - c + (1.0 - delta) * k(-1);
  a = rho * a(-1) + eps;
end;

initval;
  k = 38.0;
  a = 0.0;
  c = 2.0;
end;
"""

# Load from string or file path
m = dsge.load_mod(mod_text)
print(m.decision_rules().summary())
print(m.theoretical_moments().summary())

docs.title: 4b. Tier 0: The Front End — Macro Preprocessor, AST Parser & Symbolic Differentiation (v2.7.0)
docs.text: Starting with puremacro 2.7.0, the DSGE engine includes a front end for a documented subset of Dynare model files, using the core scientific-Python dependencies:

docs.title: Dynare Macro Directives
docs.text:
puremacro.dsge natively preprocesses Dynare macro directives before tokenization: - @#define VAR = EXPR: define integer, float, boolean, string, or array constants. - @#for VAR in EXPR ... @#endfor: iterate over integer ranges (1:N) or array literals (["c", "k"]). - @#if EXPR ... @#elif EXPR ... @#else ... @#endif: conditional compilation based on parameter regimes or flags. - @#include "path/to/file.mod": recursive file inclusion with relative path resolution. - @{EXPR}: string and value interpolation into equations and parameter assignments.

mod_macro = """
@#define CALIBRATION = "baseline"
@#define SECTORS = ["agr", "mfg", "srv"]

var
@#for s in SECTORS
  y_@{s} c_@{s}
@#endfor
;
...
"""
m = dsge.load_mod(mod_macro)

docs.title: Expression AST & Recursive-Descent Parser
docs.text:
• Immutable Expression DAG: Equations are converted into an immutable Directed Acyclic Graph (Const, Var, Param, UnaryOp, BinOp, Call), eliminating string manipulation and substring collision bugs.
  • Model-Local # Variables: Supports declarations like #MU = c^(-gamma); and #cbetabar = cbeta*cgamma^(-csigma);. As in Dynare (Reference Manual, §4.5), a local is a symbolic shorthand: its expression is substituted wherever it is used, shifted in time when it appears as MU(+1) or MU(-1), and it is never evaluated to a number at load time. A local built from parameters therefore follows them whenever the model is re-solved — load_mod(..., params={...}), osr, the widgets, analytic gradients, SMC and model.estimate() all see the new value (SW07's constebeta enters the model only through locals). dag.evaluate_locals(params) returns their numerical values. Up to and including 4.3.0, a local that depended only on parameters was frozen at the file's calibration, so every re-solve kept its load-time value.
  • Dated Exogenous Shocks (e(-k) and e(+k)): Lagged exogenous shocks e(-k) (\(k \ge 1\)) and anticipated news shocks e(+k) (\(k \ge 1\)) are supported in both # model-local variables and dynamic equations via automatic expansion into auxiliary state and lead variables (AUX_EXO_LAG_*, AUX_EXO_LEAD_*).
  • Parameter-dependent blocks & analytical steady_state_model evaluation: load_mod(..., params={...}) re-evaluates steady_state_model and initval at the merged parameters (Dynare re-runs steady_state_model at every parameter vector). steady_state_model; ... end; blocks are compiled into an \(O(1)\) analytical evaluator (supporting sequential local helper assignments even when a helper shares a name with a # model-local expression); compute_steady_state() checks the analytical candidate against the dynamic residuals (||f(y_ss)||_inf < tol) and automatically falls back to nonlinear root-finding or homotopy continuation (solve_algo, homotopy) if residuals exceed tol. Top-level assignments such as beta = 1/(1+r); are evaluated once when the file is read, as in Dynare, and do not follow an override of r.

  • Native .mod Command Execution (execute_mod_commands): m.execute_mod_commands(data=...) executes policy, smoothing, decomposition, and deterministic simulation commands declared in the .mod file—planner_objective; + ramsey_policy; (via solve_ramsey_lq), optim_weights; + osr_params; + osr_params_bounds; + osr; (via solve_osr), histval; + endval; (via solve_perfect_foresight), calib_smoother; (via kalman_smoother), and shock_decomposition; (via historical_decomposition)—returning a DynareCommandResults object (.ramsey, .osr, .smoother, .decomposition, .perfect_foresight, .commands_executed).

    The default legacy runner dispatches commands by category. Repeated stoch_simul declarations merge into a single invocation, and unrecognized outer statements can be skipped. Use inspect_mod for a read-only compatibility report. The opt-in load_mod(..., command_mode="ordered") and m.execute_mod_commands(ordered=True, data=...) preserve each supported fixed-calibration simulation/smoother/decomposition invocation. read_mod(...).execute_mod_commands() adds the ordered deterministic workflow without an implicit solve at load time. Unsupported state changes are rejected before solving; calibration changes and other command programs require explicit Python workflows. A successful legacy load_mod call does not validate compatibility with the entire file.

  • Any Dynare name: a parameter or variable named like a Python keyword (lambda, yield) parses and solves.

  • Special Operators: Supports STEADY_STATE(x) and diff(x). STEADY_STATE uses a fixed reference during trajectory and derivative evaluation; its expression cannot contain exogenous variables. Perfect-foresight terminal assignments follow the distinction between literal endval and endval followed by steady or endval_steady, both in direct solves and legacy execute_mod_commands() (including simul). Explicit Python endval or y_end overrides retain their documented precedence. The 5.7.0 extension supports the deterministic subset in the nonlinear model guide, with separate setup and solver snapshots. See the correctness advisory. EXPECTATION(k)(x) is parsed, but its compiled residual raises NameError, so a model that uses it cannot be solved yet.
  • Transcendental Functions: Full parsing and analytical differentiation for exp, log, sin, cos, tan, normcdf, normpdf, erf, abs, and sign.

docs.title: Symbolic Differentiation & Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE)
docs.text:
• Exact analytical first-order Jacobians (\(A_+, A_0, A_-, B_u\)) and dynamic second-order Hessians (\(H_f\)) with zero numerical difference errors.
  • Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE) prunes redundant algebraic operations by 30–70%, compiling dynamic derivatives into high-speed bytecode evaluators.

docs.title: Fast Generalized Schur Sylvester Solver
docs.text:
• Both the second-order (solve_generalized_sylvester_schur) and third-order (solve_order3_sylvester_schur) state curvature Sylvester equations \((I_{n_x^k} \otimes \hat{A}) X + (h_x^\top)^{\otimes k} \otimes (A_+ F_{x+}) X = -R\) are solved in pure real arithmetic via the recursive Real Schur (Bartels–Stewart) decomposition \(h_x = U_h T_h U_h^\top\) with \(1 \times 1\) and \(2 \times 2\) quasi-upper-triangular blocks and bounded LU caching.
  • Solves large models like Smets-Wouters (2007) in 0.028 seconds (down from 4.6s), avoiding massive dense Kronecker allocations (under 2 MB RAM vs 648 MB).

docs.title: Model Introspection & LaTeX Export
docs.text:
• Schema Diagnostics: m.model_info() or dsge.model_info(dag) provides detailed inspection of dynamic lead/lag structures, variable classifications, and Jacobian sparsity.
  • Publication-Grade LaTeX: m.write_latex_dynamic_model("model.tex") generates camera-ready LaTeX \begin{align}...\end{align} dynamic equations formatted with mathematical symbols.

docs.title: 5. Automated 2nd-Order Perturbation with Pruning (SGU 2004, Kim et al. 2008)
docs.text:
Solve second-order approximations directly from Python equations or .mod files:

# Second order: pass order=2 to load_mod / build_dynare, or re-solve an existing model
sol_2nd = m.solve(order=2)              # PrunedDSGESolution (Kim-Kim-Schaumburg-Sims pruning)
print(sol_2nd.oo_dr.summary())          # ghx, ghu, ghxx, ghxu, ghuu, ghs2 in Dynare layout

This returns a PrunedDSGESolution solving the Schmitt-Grohé & Uribe (2004) generalized Sylvester system for \((H_{xx}, G_{xx})\) and the risk correction system for \((H_{\sigma\sigma}, G_{\sigma\sigma})\).

Using the pruning algorithm of Kim, Kim, Schaumburg & Sims (2008), the state space is decomposed into first- and second-order components: $\(x_t^{(1)} = G x_{t-1}^{(1)} + N u_t\)$ $\(x_t^{(2)} = G x_{t-1}^{(2)} + \frac{1}{2} H_{xx} (x_{t-1}^{(1)} \otimes x_{t-1}^{(1)}) + \frac{1}{2} H_{\sigma\sigma} \sigma^2\)$ $\(y_t^{(1)} = F x_t^{(1)} + L u_t\)$ $\(y_t^{(2)} = F x_t^{(2)} + \frac{1}{2} G_{xx} (x_t^{(1)} \otimes x_t^{(1)}) + \frac{1}{2} G_{\sigma\sigma} \sigma^2\)$

Key capabilities: - Unconditionally Stable Simulation: sol_2nd.simulate(periods=200) avoids the explosive sample paths typical of unpruned quadratic approximations. Its sigma multiplies the shock scale already declared in shock_cov, so sigma=1 (the default) is the calibration. - Generalized Impulse Responses (GIRF): sol_2nd.girf(shock="eps", size=0.01, horizon=20) tracks state-dependent and non-linear impacts. - Ergodic mean and risky steady state: sol_2nd.ergodic_mean() (alias stochastic_steady_state()) is the unconditional mean of the pruned solution; sol_2nd.risky_steady_state() is the zero-shock fixed point, where only the risk term ½ g_σσ σ² acts; sol_2nd.risk_decomposition() splits the mean into that risk term and the curvature terms ½ g_xx vec(Ω) and ½ g_uu vec(σ²Σ_u) (see Higher-Order Perturbation, §2.4). The two can have opposite signs: in the RBC model of that section the ergodic mean of capital is above its deterministic steady state and the risky steady state is below it.

docs.title: 6. puremacro-dynare CLI Runner
docs.text:
puremacro 2.2.0 introduces the puremacro-dynare command-line executable (puremacro.dsge.cli), allowing researchers and students to parse, solve, and simulate Dynare models directly from terminal or shell scripts:

# Basic solve and display policy rules
puremacro-dynare rbc.mod

# Solve to 2nd order with pruning and generate FEVD table
puremacro-dynare rbc.mod --order 2 --fevd

# Export camera-ready tables in all formats (Markdown, LaTeX, Typst) and save IRF plots
puremacro-dynare rbc.mod --irf 20 --format all --plot

# Run historical shock decomposition from an observable dataset
puremacro-dynare rbc.mod --shock-decomp us_macro_data.csv --plot

CLI options: - --order {1,2}: Perturbation approximation order (default: 1). - --steady-only: Compute and display the steady-state vector without solving dynamics. - --irf <HORIZON>: Compute impulse response functions up to specified horizon. - --fevd: Compute analytical forecast error variance decomposition shares. - --shock-decomp <CSV>: Perform Kalman-smoothed historical shock decomposition from observable data. - --format {markdown,latex,typst,all}: Output export format for tables. - --plot: Render and display or save matplotlib impulse response plots.

docs.title: 7. OccBin: Occasionally Binding Constraints (ZLB)
docs.text:
puremacro.dsge.occbin implements the piecewise-linear solution method of Guerrieri & Iacoviello (2015) for models with occasionally binding constraints, such as the Zero Lower Bound (ZLB) on nominal interest rates or collateral borrowing constraints.

It computes the time path of regime switches between the reference (unconstrained) regime \(M_1\) and the alternative (constrained) regime \(M_2\) via backward recursion:

import numpy as np
from puremacro.dsge import build_dynare, solve_occbin, OccBinConstraint

# Three-equation New Keynesian model. The constrained regime pegs the nominal
# rate at the zero lower bound (r = -r_ss in deviations from steady state).
params = {"beta": 0.99, "sigma": 1.0, "kappa": 0.1, "phi_pi": 1.5, "phi_y": 0.125, "rho_g": 0.8, "r_ss": 0.01}
variables = ["y", "pi", "r", "g"]
shocks = ["eps_r", "eps_g"]
steady_state = {v: 0.0 for v in variables}

def nk_taylor(lead, curr, lag, shocks_v, p):
    return [
        curr.y - lead.y + (curr.r - lead.pi) / p.sigma - curr.g,          # dynamic IS
        curr.pi - p.beta * lead.pi - p.kappa * curr.y,                     # NK Phillips curve
        curr.r - p.phi_pi * curr.pi - p.phi_y * curr.y - shocks_v.eps_r,   # Taylor rule
        curr.g - p.rho_g * lag.g - shocks_v.eps_g,                         # demand shock process
    ]

def nk_zlb(lead, curr, lag, shocks_v, p):
    return [
        curr.y - lead.y + (curr.r - lead.pi) / p.sigma - curr.g,
        curr.pi - p.beta * lead.pi - p.kappa * curr.y,
        curr.r - (-p.r_ss),                                                # rate pegged at the ZLB
        curr.g - p.rho_g * lag.g - shocks_v.eps_g,
    ]

m_ref = build_dynare(nk_taylor, variables=variables, shocks=shocks, params=params, steady_state=steady_state)
# A pegged-rate regime is indeterminate on its own; OccBin only needs its Jacobians,
# so the alternative regime is built with strict=False.
m_zlb = build_dynare(nk_zlb, variables=variables, shocks=shocks, params=params,
                     steady_state=steady_state, check_steady_state=False, strict=False)

# The constraint binds when the shadow rate falls below the bound
constraint = OccBinConstraint(variable="r", threshold=-params["r_ss"], operator="<")

horizon = 30
shock_seq = np.zeros((horizon, len(shocks)))
shock_seq[0, shocks.index("eps_g")] = -0.04        # contractionary demand shock at t=0

res_occbin = solve_occbin(m_ref, m_zlb, constraint, shock_sequence=shock_seq, horizon=horizon)
print(res_occbin.summary())
print("Periods at the ZLB:", res_occbin.binding_periods)
print("Regime per period (1 = constrained):", res_occbin.regimes)
res_occbin.plot()

OccBinResult attributes: - simulation: DataFrame of time paths for all variables. - regime_history: Sequence of booleans indicating whether the constraint bound at each period \(t\). - duration: Total number of periods spent in the constrained regime. - .plot(): Time-series plot with shaded intervals for the binding regime. - .to_latex(), .to_typst(), .to_markdown(): Multi-format table exports.

docs.title: 8. Non-Linear Simulation & Perfect Foresight
docs.text:
puremacro.dsge.perfect_foresight implements the Boucekkine (1995) / Juillard (1996) stacked relaxation Newton-Raphson solver for non-linear deterministic transitions under perfect foresight.

Given a sequence of known or anticipated future shocks \(\{u_t\}_{t=1}^T\), it solves the full non-linear system \(f(y_{t+1}, y_t, y_{t-1}, u_t) = 0\) simultaneously using a block-tridiagonal sparse Jacobian solved via SuperLU:

import numpy as np
from puremacro.dsge import solve_perfect_foresight

# Deterministic Ramsey model in levels:
#   1/c_t = beta / c_{t+1} * (alpha A_t k_t^(alpha-1) + 1 - delta)
#   k_t   = A_t k_{t-1}^alpha + (1 - delta) k_{t-1} - c_t
alpha, beta, delta = 0.33, 0.96, 0.10
r_ss = 1.0 / beta - (1.0 - delta)
k_ss = (alpha / r_ss) ** (1.0 / (1.0 - alpha))
c_ss = k_ss ** alpha - delta * k_ss

def ramsey(y_plus, y_curr, y_lag, exo):
    c_p, k_p = y_plus
    c, k = y_curr
    c_m, k_m = y_lag
    A = float(np.ravel(exo)[0])
    return [
        1.0 / c - beta / c_p * (alpha * A * k ** (alpha - 1.0) + 1.0 - delta),
        k - (A * k_m ** alpha + (1.0 - delta) * k_m - c),
    ]

# A +5% TFP boost in period 5, announced at t=0: consumption jumps before the shock arrives
n_periods = 100
tfp_path = np.ones(n_periods)
tfp_path[4] = 1.05

pf_res = solve_perfect_foresight(
    ramsey,
    y_init=np.array([c_ss, k_ss]),
    y_ss=np.array([c_ss, k_ss]),
    exogenous_path=tfp_path,
    n_periods=n_periods,
    variable_names=["c", "k"],
)
print(pf_res.summary())
pf_res.plot()

docs.title: 9. Bayesian DSGE MCMC Estimation
docs.text:
puremacro.dsge.bayesian provides a complete Bayesian estimation workflow with zero external compiled dependencies:

  1. Prior Specification: Flexible prior distributions (BetaPrior, GammaPrior, InvGammaPrior, NormalPrior, UniformPrior).
  2. Mode-Finding: Numerical maximization of the log-posterior likelihood via L-BFGS-B or Nelder-Mead.
  3. Laplace Approximation: Numerical Hessian inversion at the posterior mode to construct the proposal covariance matrix \(\Sigma_{\text{prop}}\).
  4. Adaptive Random-Walk Metropolis-Hastings (RWMH): Generates posterior draws with target acceptance rate tuning (Roberts-Gelman-Gilks 1997).
  5. Convergence Diagnostics: Split-\(\hat{R}\) (Gelman-Rubin) and Geweke spectral convergence tests, with the spectral density at zero estimated from a fitted AR model, as in R's coda.
import numpy as np
from puremacro.dsge import estimate_dsge_bayesian
from puremacro.dsge.priors import BetaPrior, InvGammaPrior
from puremacro.state_space import StateSpaceModel, kalman_filter

# Observable: y_t = rho y_{t-1} + sigma eps_t, T = 300 (stand-in for your model's likelihood)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
y = np.zeros(300)
for t in range(1, 300):
    y[t] = 0.7 * y[t - 1] + 0.4 * rng.standard_normal()
y = y[:, None]

def log_likelihood(params):
    rho, sigma = (params["rho"], params["sigma"]) if isinstance(params, dict) else (params[0], params[1])
    ssm = StateSpaceModel(T=np.array([[rho]]), Z=np.array([[1.0]]), R=np.array([[1.0]]),
                          Q=np.array([[sigma ** 2]]), H=np.array([[1e-6]]))
    return kalman_filter(y, ssm)["loglik"]

priors = {
    "rho": BetaPrior(mean=0.6, std=0.15, lb=0.01, ub=0.99),
    "sigma": InvGammaPrior(mean=0.3, std=2.0, lb=0.01, ub=3.0),
}

bayes_res = estimate_dsge_bayesian(
    log_likelihood, priors,
    initial_params=np.array([0.6, 0.3]),
    n_draws=1000, n_burn=200, n_chains=2, seed=42,
)
print(bayes_res.summary())

# Prior vs posterior densities, and a camera-ready table
bayes_res.plot_priors_posteriors()
print(bayes_res.to_latex())

docs.title: 10. FEVD & Historical Shock Decomposition
docs.text:
puremacro.dsge.decomposition provides analytical Forecast Error Variance Decomposition and Kalman-smoothed Historical Shock Decomposition:

# 1. Analytical FEVD across horizons [1, 4, 8, 16, 40]
fevd_res = m.fevd_result(horizons=[1, 4, 8, 16, 40])
print(fevd_res.summary())
print(fevd_res.to_latex())

# 2. Historical shock decomposition of a sample (here simulated from the model;
#    pass your observed data with one column per variable)
data = m.simulate(periods=80, seed=1)
decomp_res = m.shock_decomposition(data)
print(decomp_res.summary())

# Stacked bar chart of the historical shock contributions
decomp_res.plot(variable="c")

docs.title: Estimating a Dynare .mod file
docs.text:
Until 2.6.0 puremacro could solve a .mod file and could not estimate one. Every piece was present — priors that read Dynare's estimated_params conventions, a Kalman filter and smoother with exact diffuse initialisation, an audited Metropolis driver — and one connector was missing: nothing turned a varobs declaration into a measurement equation. In practice that meant writing seventy lines of index arithmetic per model, which nobody does for their own model.

That connector now exists. A .mod file that declares varobs and estimated_params goes straight to a posterior.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from puremacro.dsge import load_mod

MOD = """
var y a;
varexo eps;
parameters rho;
rho = 0.7;
model;
  y = a;
  a = rho * a(-1) + eps;
end;
initval; a = 0; y = 0; end;
shocks; var eps; stderr 0.5; end;
varobs y;
estimated_params;
  rho, beta_pdf, 0.5, 0.2;
  stderr eps, inv_gamma_pdf, 0.5, 2;
end;
"""

model = load_mod(MOD)

# Data simulated at rho = 0.7, sigma = 0.5, started from the stationary
# distribution rather than from zero (a series that starts away from its own
# stationary distribution biases the estimate down, which is a property of the
# sample, not of the estimator).
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
burn, T = 200, 400
eps = rng.standard_normal(burn + T) * 0.5
a = np.zeros(burn + T)
for t in range(1, burn + T):
    a[t] = 0.7 * a[t - 1] + eps[t]
data = pd.DataFrame({"y": a[burn:]})

res = model.estimate(data, n_draws=400, n_chains=1, burn_in=500, seed=0)
print(res.summary().round(3))

priors and varobs default to the file's own blocks, so nothing is declared twice. Pass them explicitly to override.

docs.title: What the file has to declare
docs.text:
varobs names the observed series, in any order; the data frame supplies a column per name. estimated_params names what is estimated and how.

estimated_params;
  // NAME, INITVAL, LB, UB, PRIOR_SHAPE, P1, P2, P3, P4, JSCALE;
  alpha, 0.35, beta_pdf, 0.35, 0.02;
  rho, , 0, 1, beta_pdf, 0.5, 0.2;
  stderr eps_a, inv_gamma_pdf, 0.1, 2;
  corr eps_a, eps_b, normal_pdf, 0, 0.2;
end;

The grammar is positionally ambiguous — NAME, 0.35, beta_pdf, … and NAME, beta_pdf, … differ only by a leading field — and corr a, b carries a comma inside its target. Both are resolved by consuming any stderr/corr keyword first, then locating the first *_pdf field: what precedes it is read by length, what follows by position. Shape names are matched case-insensitively, because real files write INV_GAMMA_PDF while the manual writes inv_gamma_pdf.

Dynare shape puremacro notes beta_pdf BetaPrior P3/P4 give the generalised beta on [P3, P4] gamma_pdf GammaPrior P3 is the lower bound normal_pdf NormalPrior P3/P4 truncate inv_gamma_pdf, inv_gamma1_pdf InvGammaPrior a prior on a standard deviation inv_gamma2_pdf InvGammaPrior(kind="type2") a prior on a variance uniform_pdf UniformPrior (P1, P2) as mean/std, or (P3, P4) as bounds weibull_pdf WeibullPrior

In every family P1 and P2 are the mean and standard deviation of the actual variable, shift and scale included — Dynare's beta_specification / gamma_specification convention. Reversing that silently re-specifies a whole block.

Estimated objects are named the way Dynare displays them: SE_<shock>, CORR_<s1>_<s2>, ME_<obsvar>.

ep = model._estimated_params
print([s.name for s in ep.specs])
print({s.name: s.kind for s in ep.specs})

That kind is not cosmetic. Only "param" enters the model's equations, so only "param" forces a re-solve; a shock standard deviation, a shock correlation and a measurement-error standard deviation are written straight into Q and H.

docs.title: The measurement equation
docs.text:
A solved model reports v_t = ys + C x_t + D u_t, so an observable loads the contemporaneous innovation, while a standard state space assumes measurement noise independent of the state shock. There is no exact way to write D u_t as measurement noise, so the innovation is carried in the state:

\[\alpha_t = \begin{bmatrix} x_t \\ u_t \end{bmatrix},\quad T = \begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix},\quad R = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ I\end{bmatrix},\quad Z = \begin{bmatrix} C_O & D_O\end{bmatrix},\quad d = ys_O\]

Two things fall out of that choice. Growth-rate observables need no special handling — dy = y - y(-1) + ctrend is a declared variable, so it is a row of (C, D) like any other. And the smoothed structural shocks are literally the last rows of the smoothed state, so no disturbance smoother is involved.

from puremacro.dsge import make_state_space_from_varobs

ssm = make_state_space_from_varobs(model, ["y"])
print(ssm.T.shape, ssm.R.shape, ssm.Z.shape, ssm.d)

Measurement error is zero by default, as in Dynare. Pass measurement_error={"y": 0.01} for a standard deviation, or ridge= for pure conditioning. If the observables cannot be generated by the shocks the model has, that is reported as the specification error it is before any sampling starts, not as a bad starting point.

docs.title: Smoothing and forecasting at calibrated parameters
docs.text:
smoother is Dynare's calib_smoother.

sm = model.smoother(data)
print(sm.shocks.head(3).round(4))
print(f"log-likelihood {sm.loglik:.3f}")
print(sm.summary())

sm.states, sm.shocks, sm.smoothed_obs and sm.filtered_states are data frames indexed like the input. sm.shock_decomposition() gives the historical decomposition for the same model and data.

fc = model.forecast(horizon=12, data=data, ci=0.90)
print(fc.mean.head(3).round(4))

The band reflects shock uncertainty only — the parameters are held fixed at the values the model was solved with.

Carrying the innovation in the state makes the predicted covariance structurally rank-deficient (the augmented state has n_states + n_shocks dimensions driven by n_shocks innovations), so kalman_smoother uses the Durbin–Koopman backward recursion, which inverts only the innovation covariance F_t and never the predicted state covariance. Up to 4.6.0 it used the Rauch–Tung–Striebel gain built from numpy.linalg.pinv of that matrix; on a small RBC its smallest singular value sat at pinv's default cutoff, so the first smoothed period differed by up to ~3e-06 between LAPACK builds. With no measurement error the fitted observables now reproduce the data at every period, the first included.

docs.title: Checking the mode
docs.text:
estimate_dsge used to do one bounded L-BFGS-B run, and a 2.5.0 audit caught it returning the starting values while reporting convergence. mode_compute now selects among lbfgs (the default), simplex, csminwel, cmaes and none.

The cheapest way to see that a reported mode is not one is to look at it along each parameter:

from puremacro.dsge import mode_check
from puremacro.dsge.priors import log_prior

names = tuple(res.param_names)
priors = model._estimated_params.priors()

def neg_log_post(v):
    """The posterior, built from public pieces: re-solve, filter, add the prior."""
    theta = dict(zip(names, map(float, v)))
    m = load_mod(MOD, params={"rho": theta["rho"]})
    ll = m.smoother(data, shock_cov=np.array([[theta["SE_eps"] ** 2]])).loglik
    return -(ll + log_prior(theta, priors))

mc = mode_check(
    neg_log_post,
    np.array([res.mode[n] for n in names]), names,
    n_points=11, cov=res.mode_hessian_inv,
)
print(mc.summary())

A slice that improves away from the reported mode means the point is not a mode in that direction. mc.summary() names the offenders; passing is necessary, not sufficient, since these are one-parameter slices and say nothing about directions in between.

docs.title: Marginal likelihood and model comparison
docs.text:
print(f"Laplace  log p(y) = {res.log_mdd('laplace'):.3f}")

Two estimators, and they are not equivalent. Laplace is exact when the posterior is Gaussian and only as good as the mode otherwise — check the mode first. Geweke's modified harmonic mean reweights the draws by a truncated normal and is evaluated at every truncation level, with the spread across levels returned rather than hidden: the estimator is supposed to be invariant to the truncation, so a swing past one log point means it has not converged, and it says so.

model_comparison scores every model by the same estimator and refuses when one cannot supply it. A Laplace value and a harmonic-mean value are not on the same footing, and mixing them silently is how a Bayes factor becomes fiction.

docs.title: Model Diagnostics & Residual Analysis
docs.text: Before estimating a model or trusting policy simulations, puremacro provides three diagnostic entry points matching and extending Dynare's diagnostic toolkit: check(), resid(), and model_diagnostics().

docs.title: Blanchard-Kahn Determinacy & Eigenvalues (check())
docs.text:
model.check() evaluates the generalized eigenvalue spectrum of the companion pencil, classifies roots into stable, unit-root, and explosive categories, and verifies the Blanchard-Kahn order and rank conditions:

table = model.check()
print(table.summary())

When determinacy fails (indeterminacy or explosiveness), check() goes beyond a scalar count: it computes the generalized eigenvectors associated with the offending roots and isolates the top variable loadings, naming which economic variables drive the failure:

EIGENVALUES & BLANCHARD-KAHN DIAGNOSTICS (qz_criterium=1.000001)
========================================================================
Status       : 1 explosive roots for 2 forward-looking variables; missing root at |lambda| = 0.9421 loads chiefly on pi, y (indeterminacy).
Determinacy  : DETERMINACY FAILED
Forward vars : 2
Explosive    : 1
Stable       : 3
Unit roots   : 0

Visualizing the spectrum against the complex unit circle:

fig = table.plot()  # plots stable, unit, and explosive roots with unit circle

docs.title: Steady-State Residuals (resid())
docs.text:
model.resid() evaluates the dynamic equilibrium equations at steady state, \(f(ss, ss, ss, 0)\), and returns a pd.Series of residuals sorted descending by absolute magnitude:

resids = model.resid()
print(resids.head(5).round(6))

Equation labels and tags from the .mod file are preserved, allowing immediate isolation of equations with non-zero steady-state residuals (e.g. diagnosing calibration discrepancies).

docs.title: Structural Model Diagnostics (model_diagnostics())
docs.text:
model.model_diagnostics() performs comprehensive static and dynamic structural checks: - Static Jacobian rank analysis: evaluates \(\text{rank}(J_{\text{static}})\) against the number of variables. - Collinear equations & variables: uses Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to pinpoint exact collinear equation subsets and unconstrained variables. - Numeric incidence matrix: computes the union incidence across neighbourhood perturbations to detect unused variables and redundant equations. - Dynamic matrix pencil regularity: verifies that \(\det(B - \lambda A) \not\equiv 0\). - Stochastic singularity: flags if the number of declared varobs exceeds the number of shocks plus measurement errors.

diag = model.model_diagnostics()
print(diag.summary())

# Plot the boolean incidence matrix
fig = diag.plot()

docs.title: Robust Block-Triangular Steady-State Solving
docs.text:
Computing deterministic steady states in medium- and large-scale DSGE models frequently fails under naive multidimensional Newton solvers. Puremacro implements a block-triangular decomposition engine (puremacro.dsge.steady):

  1. Hopcroft-Karp Bipartite Matching: finds a maximum cardinality matching between equations and variables in \(O(|E|\sqrt{|V|})\) time.

  2. Dulmage-Mendelsohn Singularity Decomposition: decomposes the incidence bipartite graph into over-determined, under-determined and well-determined subsets. When a complete matching does not exist at the guess, steady() runs one full-system hybr solve and checks the matching again at the point it reaches. If the matching is complete there, the gap was local to the guess and the root is returned (info["fallback_reason"] == "incomplete_matching_at_guess"). Otherwise the model is structurally singular and its steady state is not locally unique:

  3. If every over-determined equation reads 0 = 0 (the static form of a unit-root law of motion such as z = z(-1) + e), the point is returned with a StructuralSingularityWarning naming the free variables and info["structurally_singular"] = True, as Dynare does for unit-root models.

  4. Any other structure (structurally duplicated equations, i.e. a subset of equations involving fewer variables than equations, or a variable that enters no equation) raises StructuralSingularityError. The error names the over- and under-determined subsets and carries the checked root as hybr_point. To accept the point instead, pass allow_singular=True to steady(), build(), build_dynare() or load_mod(), or wrap the call in with allow_structural_singularity(): after from puremacro.dsge.steady import allow_structural_singularity. The context manager's setting applies to the current thread (or asyncio task) only.
  5. allow_singular=False makes unit roots raise too.
  6. An inconsistent system raises in every mode.

The check is structural, like Dynare's dmperm: numerically collinear equations with a complete incidence (e.g. x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 4) are not detected. When the block pass leaves a residual above tol, a full-system hybr polish runs and is recorded in info["full_system_polish"], as well as in an INFO log record. A model built by build(), build_dynare() or load_mod() keeps that info dict as model.steady_state_info (None when the steady state was supplied rather than solved for).

# requires: standalone snippet
from puremacro.dsge.steady import StructuralSingularityError, steady

try:
    ss, info = steady(equations, variables, guess, params)
except StructuralSingularityError as err:
    print("Overdetermined equations :", err.overdetermined_equations)
    print("Underdetermined variables:", err.underdetermined_variables)
    print("Checked root             :", err.hybr_point)
3. Tarjan Strongly Connected Components (SCC): decomposes the matching-directed dependency graph into topological sub-blocks solved in sequence. Singletons are solved with 1D scalar root finders (Brent / secant), while coupled sub-blocks use multidimensional solvers.

docs.title: Solver Menu & Homotopy Continuation
docs.text:
The solve_algo parameter selects among numerical algorithms: - "block" (default): block-triangular recursive solver. - "hybr": MINPACK Powell hybrid method. - "lm": Levenberg-Marquardt least-squares solver. - "df-sane": derivative-free spectral method for large-scale systems.

When non-linear solvers fail from a distant initial guess, adaptive homotopy continuation traces a parameter path with automatic step bisection:

# requires: standalone snippet
from puremacro.dsge.steady import steady

# Continuation from alpha=0.20 to alpha=0.36
ss, info = steady(
    equations,
    variables,
    guess,
    params={"alpha": 0.36, "beta": 0.99},
    solve_algo="block",
    homotopy={"alpha": (0.20, 0.36)},
    homotopy_steps=10,
)

docs.title: Parameter Identification Analysis
docs.text:
Following Iskrev (2010) and Ratto (2011), model.identification() assesses whether structural parameters can be uniquely recovered from the declared observables varobs:

# requires: standalone snippet
ident = model.identification(varobs=["y", "pi", "i"], lags=2)
print(ident.summary())

The analysis evaluates two fundamental Jacobians: 1. \(J_1\) (State-space solution Jacobian): \(\frac{\partial \text{vec}(T, R, Q, Z, H)}{\partial \theta}\). 2. \(J_2\) (Theoretical moment Jacobian): \(\frac{\partial m(\theta)}{\partial \theta}\), where \(m(\theta)\) stacks model autocovariances up to lags.

The returned IdentificationResult reports: - Rank deficiency: whether \(J_1\) and \(J_2\) are full rank, and the dimension of their null spaces. - Null-space parameter combinations: exact linear combinations spanning the null space (e.g. 0.7071 * theta1 - 0.7071 * theta2 = 0), revealing redundant or proportional parameters. - Multi-way collinearity (\(R^2\)): \(R^2\) from regressing each Jacobian column on all others; values near \(1.0\) flag collinear parameters. - Identification strength: Ratto's sensitivity and normalized strength measures.

# requires: standalone snippet
# Visualize collinearity R^2 vs identification strength
fig = ident.plot()

docs.title: Where the Jacobians are evaluated
docs.text:
Local identification is a property of the Jacobian at one parameter vector \(\theta_0\): the rank condition is \(\operatorname{rank} J(\theta_0) = n_\theta\). Every column of \(J_1\), \(J_2\), \(J_H\) and \(J_S\) is taken at the same \(\theta_0\). The model is re-solved once at \(\theta_0\), and column \(j\) perturbs \(\theta_j\) alone, with every other parameter held at its \(\theta_0\) value. \(\theta_0\) is the model's calibration and declared shock covariance, overridden by fixed_params, and then by the value of each analysed parameter:

params Value of each analysed parameter a mapping {name: value} (or p_dict=) the value given a list of names its current value: the calibration for a structural parameter, \(\sqrt{\Sigma_{u,ii}}\) for SE_<shock> (1.0 when no covariance is declared), the declared correlation for CORR_<s1>_<s2> (0.0 when none), the measurement_error entry for ME_<obs> (0.0 when none) EstimatedParams / EstimatedParamSpecs the spec's start: its INITVAL when declared, else its prior mean omitted, on a .mod model with estimated_params each declared parameter at its start, as in the row above omitted, on any other model every calibrated parameter at its calibration

A list of names that the estimated_params block declares also takes each spec's start.

fixed_params (structural values held at \(\theta_0\) but not analysed) and measurement_error (fixed measurement-error standard deviations by observable) are keywords of both the method model.identification() and the function puremacro.dsge.identification(model, ...).

How this differs from Dynare. Dynare's identification command defaults to parameter_set = prior_mean. puremacro's default matches that only when the block declares no INITVAL. To pick the point explicitly, pass it:

# requires: standalone snippet
ep = model._estimated_params
at_prior_mean = model.identification(params={s.name: s.prior.mean for s in ep.specs})
at_calibration = model.identification(params={n: model._params[n] for n in ["kappa", "rho_u"]})

SE_ values are innovation standard deviations (\(Q_{ii} = \sigma_i^2\)). CORR_ values are correlations (\(Q_{ij} = \rho_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j\), using the standard deviations at \(\theta_0\)). ME_ values are measurement-error standard deviations (\(H_{ii} = \sigma^2\)). This is the same mapping estimate() applies to a draw. A declared off-diagonal covariance that no CORR_ parameter names stays fixed as a covariance when an SE_ moves. Dynare instead keeps a declared correlation fixed as a correlation.

Structural columns are central differences with step \(h = \max(10^{-5}, 10^{-4}|\theta_j|)\). The exception is when \(\theta_j \pm h\) crosses a declared bound or a solve fails. The column is then a second-order one-sided difference taken on a side whose points stay inside the bounds, away from the active bound. A step never crosses a declared bound. Shock and measurement-error columns are analytic.

State set of a .mod / build_dynare model. build_dynare finds the predetermined variables numerically: a variable is a state when its lag has a non-zero coefficient at the calibration. A lag whose coefficient is calibrated to 0, such as SW07's crhoms, crhopinf, crhow, cmap and cmaw, is therefore not a state of the calibrated model. Every solve in one identification analysis uses the same state set: the model's states, plus the lags that are active at \(\theta_0\), plus the lags that any analysed structural parameter switches on when it moves. When that set differs from the model's own, the model is re-solved with it, even at the calibration. The observables' moments and spectra are unchanged by the extra states; their derivatives are not. Models from build() keep the states you declared.

prior_mc=N repeats the rank analysis at N draws of \(\theta_0\) from the priors, truncated to the declared bounds. Each draw is analysed at its own full point. Draws the model cannot be solved at are skipped and counted in prior_mc_results["n_failed"]; n_draws counts the draws that were analysed. If no draw can be solved, the rates are NaN and a RuntimeWarning is raised.

docs.title: Pre-Flight Identification Check in Estimation
