    method="piecewise_kalman",
    occbin_regimes=[constraint],
    n_draws=2000,
    burn_in=500,
)

print(res_est.summary())

docs.title: 5.1 The Herbst & Schorfheide (2014, 2015) SMC Algorithm
docs.text:
Standard Random Walk Metropolis-Hastings (RWMH) algorithms struggle on complex macroeconomic likelihood surfaces characterized by multiple local modes, ridge collinearities, and flat parameter directions.

Puremacro implements the Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm of Herbst & Schorfheide (2014, Journal of Applied Econometrics; 2015, Princeton University Press). SMC bridges the prior \(\pi(\theta)\) to the posterior \(p(\theta|Y)\) through a sequence of \(N\) intermediate tempered distributions:

\[\pi_n(\theta) \propto \pi(\theta) \left[ p(Y \mid \theta) \right]^{\phi_n}, \quad 0 = \phi_0 < \phi_1 < \dots < \phi_N = 1\]

Key features: 1. Adaptive Tempering: Instead of a fixed grid, puremacro dynamically chooses \(\phi_{n+1}\) by solving:

\[\text{ESS}(\phi_{n+1}) = \alpha^* \cdot N_{\text{particles}}\]

using a 1D bisection solver, ensuring optimal particle diversity across stages. 2. Systematic Resampling: Particles with low weights are resampled when effective sample size falls below the threshold \(ESS < 0.5 N_{part}\). 3. Particle Mutation: Resampled particles mutate through multiple steps of Metropolis-Hastings with empirical covariance matrix \(\Sigma_n = \text{Cov}_\pi(\theta)\) and adaptive scaling factor \(c_n\).

docs.title: 5.2 Exact Marginal Data Density (MDD)
docs.text:
A decisive advantage of SMC over MCMC is the exact computation of the Marginal Data Density (MDD) \(\ln p(Y)\) as a cumulative product of stage normalizing constants:

\[\ln \hat{p}(Y) = \sum_{n=1}^N \ln \left( \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M w_n^{(m)} \right)\]

where \(w_n^{(m)} = [p(Y \mid \theta_{n-1}^{(m)})]^{\phi_n - \phi_{n-1}}\) are the incremental importance weights. Puremacro also reports the asymptotic numerical standard error \(\text{SE}(\ln \hat{p}(Y))\).

docs.title: 5.3 Nonlinear Bootstrap Particle Filter
docs.text:
For nonlinear DSGE models (orders 2 and 3) or non-Gaussian measurement densities, puremacro provides a native pure-NumPy Bootstrap Particle Filter: - Propagates particles through the pruned nonlinear state equations. - Reweights particles against empirical observation densities. - Evaluates the exact nonlinear log-likelihood with systematic resampling.

from puremacro.dsge import load_mod
from puremacro.dsge.smc import SMCSampler

model = load_mod("smets_wouters_07.mod")

# Configure SMC Sampler
smc = SMCSampler(
    model,
    data=macro_data,
    varobs=["dy", "dc", "dinve", "dw", "pinf", "robs", "labobs"],
    n_particles=2000,
    n_stages=50,
    adaptive_tempering=True,
    target_ess=0.5,
    seed=123,
)

# Sample posterior
res_smc = smc.sample()

print(f"Log Marginal Data Density (MDD): {res_smc.mdd:.3f} +/- {res_smc.mdd_se:.3f}")
print(res_smc.posterior_summary)

# Visual stage diagnostics
res_smc.plot_stages()
res_smc.plot_posterior()

docs.title: 6. Nonlinear Ramsey Optimal Policy & BGP Detrending
6.1 Automated Ramsey Optimal Policy
docs.text:
Under commitment, a benevolent policymaker maximizes intertemporal household welfare subject to the decentralized structural equilibrium conditions of the economy:

\[\max_{\{y_t\}_{t=0}^\infty} \mathbb{E}_0 \sum_{t=0}^\infty \beta^t U(y_t) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbb{E}_t f(y_{t+1}, y_t, y_{t-1}, u_t) = 0\]

Puremacro's ramsey_model (puremacro.dsge.ramsey) sets this problem up from an objective string and solves its linear-quadratic approximation: 1. Forms the planner's Lagrangian:

\[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_0 \sum_{t=0}^\infty \beta^t \left[ U(y_t) + \lambda_t^\top f(y_{t+1}, y_t, y_{t-1}, u_t) \right]\]
  1. Derives the First-Order Conditions (FOCs) symbolically over the expression DAG, with respect to every endogenous variable \(y_{i,t}\) and Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda_{j,t}\). They are for display only: focs holds them as readable equations in Dynare syntax and foc_nodes as expression trees.
\[\frac{\partial U(y_t)}{\partial y_{i,t}} + \left[ \frac{\partial f(y_{t+1}, y_t, y_{t-1}, u_t)}{\partial y_{i,t}} \right]^\top \lambda_t + \beta^{-1} \left[ \frac{\partial f(y_t, y_{t-1}, y_{t-2}, u_{t-1})}{\partial y_{i,t}} \right]^\top \lambda_{t-1} + \beta \mathbb{E}_t \left[ \frac{\partial f(y_{t+2}, y_{t+1}, y_t, u_{t+1})}{\partial y_{i,t}} \right]^\top \lambda_{t+1} = 0\]
  1. Assembles the system it actually solves numerically, a linear-quadratic one: the constraints linearized at the steady state (the model's linear matrices, or the .mod equations differentiated at the steady state) and the Hessian of the objective at the steady state, with the steady-state multipliers set to zero. The state vector is augmented with the multipliers \(\lambda_t\).
  2. Solves the saddle-path equilibrium with Klein QZ. The law of motion is the same for the Ramsey plan chosen at \(t_0\) and for the timeless-perspective rule (Woodford 2003); impulse responses start from the steady state with \(\lambda_{-1} = 0\), where the two coincide (see DSGE Frontier, §1.3).

The solution is exact when the objective is a quadratic loss centred on the steady state, as in the example below. For a nonlinear welfare objective whose steady-state multipliers are not zero, it is only a linear-quadratic approximation, without the second-order terms of a full Ramsey linearization. On a linear model, ramsey_model shares the matrices and the QZ solver with lq_commitment.

The model below has two equations for three variables: the interest rate i is the instrument and has no rule. load_mod needs as many equations as variables, so the .mod text goes to ramsey_model directly, with the instrument named.

from puremacro.dsge import ramsey_model

# Canonical 3-equation New Keynesian model without a policy rule: the planner's
# constraints are the IS curve and the Phillips curve, and i is the instrument.
NK_MOD = """
var x pi i;
varexo eps_u;
parameters beta sigma kappa;
beta = 0.99; sigma = 1.0; kappa = 0.15;

model;
  x = x(+1) - (1/sigma) * (i - pi(+1));
  pi = beta * pi(+1) + kappa * x + eps_u;
end;
"""

# Optimal commitment policy minimizing the quadratic loss L = pi^2 + 0.1 * x^2
ramsey_res = ramsey_model(
    NK_MOD,
    objective="pi^2 + 0.1 * x^2",
    planner_discount=0.99,
    instruments=["i"],
)

print("Ramsey FOCs (for display):")
for eq in ramsey_res.focs:
    print(" ", eq)

# Responses to a cost-push shock satisfy the commitment target criterion
# pi_t = -(0.1 / kappa) * (x_t - x_{t-1}): pi_0 = 0.6274, x_0 = -0.9411
print(ramsey_res.irf("eps_u", horizon=4).round(4))

# Impulse responses of the endogenous variables and the multipliers
fig = ramsey_res.plot(shock="eps_u", horizon=20)

docs.title: 6.2 Balanced Growth Path (BGP) Detrending
docs.text:
Empirical macro models often feature non-stationary deterministic trends (e.g. labor-augmenting technological growth \(A_t = \gamma^t A_0\) or investment-specific technical progress).

Puremacro provides automated Balanced Growth Path (BGP) stationarization: - Declare trend variables: trend_var A; or log_trend_var a; - Assign deflators to trending variables: var(deflator=A) Y C I; - Puremacro automatically generates the stationary transformed system \(y_t^* = Y_t / A_t\) and derives the steady state along the balanced growth path.

docs.title: Inspecting and executing .mod command programs
docs.text:
inspect_mod inventories the syntax and execution support of a Dynare-style file without evaluating calibration or steady-state expressions, compiling residuals/derivatives, solving, estimating, simulating, importing plotting tools, or changing the RNG. It reads the source and its explicitly requested local macro includes. This is a compatibility report, not a determinacy, numerical accuracy or economic-validity check.

from puremacro.dsge import inspect_mod

report = inspect_mod("study.mod", ordered=True)
print(report.summary())
print(report.to_json())

puremacro-dynare inspect study.mod --ordered
puremacro-dynare inspect study.mod --ordered --format json
puremacro-dynare inspect study.mod --entry-point load_mod --output report.txt

The CLI writes only to stdout unless --output is supplied. Exit codes are 0 for a complete report without findings, 1 for compatibility findings or required caller input, and 2 for incomplete inspection or unreadable input. JSON and text expose the same statements and findings; JSON also provides the complete source hashes, option statuses and provenance records.

The default entry point is execute_mod_commands; load_mod and load_hank_mod can be selected explicitly. Loading a model does not itself run its stoch_simul, smoothing or decomposition commands. An option accepted by the parser is reported as supported only if the selected runner consumes it. Unknown scripts, MATLAB control flow, unsupported options, EXPECTATION, and STEADY_STATE applied to an exogenous variable receive named findings. hetagent_block is identified as a puremacro extension requiring the HANK entry point, not as native Dynare syntax. That loader uses its configured built-in household unless household_model is supplied. Fields retained but not consumed by HANKModel receive separate findings.

Each statement includes its original source location, expanded location, excerpt, status, explicit options and requested variables. Equation and model-local entries are children of the enclosing model block. Comments are inventoried too. Macro directives, including inactive branches, follow the expanded statement inventory and carry original positions rather than an invented expanded position. Included lines retain their include chain. Loop expansions have distinct instance identifiers even when they originate from the same source line. Columns are null when interpolation prevents an exact mapping; a statement spanning multiple origins also carries the individual origin spans. Input hashes use SHA-256 of the original UTF-8 bytes, including line endings; parsing normalizes LF, CRLF and CR separately. Reports contain no timestamps.

Macro preprocessing is the only expression-evaluation step in inspection; it uses the existing macro engine with a work budget (macro_limit=100_000) and 2 MB source/expansion limits. Oversized expansions, failed includes, malformed syntax, and incomplete blocks produce incomplete coverage. Reports never substitute a successful compatibility verdict for those failures. Parameter expressions remain unevaluated, including invalid numerical expressions such as log(-1); a clear report therefore does not establish that calibration or a solve will succeed.

For smoothing and decomposition, data= optionally checks the DataFrame's columns, numeric conversion, duplicates and infinities. NaNs are allowed. The likelihood and identification are not evaluated. Without data, the report names the missing input. A datafile option does not implicitly read a file.

docs.title: Opt-in ordered execution
docs.text:
Use ordered loading to reject unsupported programs before any solve:

from puremacro.dsge import load_mod

model = load_mod("study.mod", command_mode="ordered")
results = model.execute_mod_commands(ordered=True, data=data)
for invocation in results.invocations:
    print(invocation.command, invocation.explicit_options,
          invocation.effective_options, invocation.requested_variables)
    # Full numerical result and selected presentation are kept separately.
    full = invocation.result
    selected = invocation.selected_result

For a simulation-only program, omit data. Ordered loading returns a first-order LinearModel; each stoch_simul invocation requests its own order through the existing solver. Do not pass order=2 or order=3 to ordered loading itself. The loader consumes the expanded source snapshot that was inspected, and later execution uses that report even if an included file changes. Macro programs must be loaded with command_mode="ordered" to retain this provenance. For plain text, execute_mod_commands(ordered=True) can also check an already loaded model, but loading has already performed its solve.

The stochastic subset supports repeated stoch_simul, calib_smoother and shock_decomposition at a fixed calibration. The extension introduced in 5.7.0 also replays deterministic boundary blocks, shock declarations and repeated perfect-foresight setup/solver commands, including mixed deterministic and stochastic programs. Use read_mod(source).execute_mod_commands() to start without an implicit steady-state or perturbation solve; see the nonlinear model guide for the supported options and snapshots. Interleaved parameter assignments, policy commands and HANK commands remain unsupported in ordered execution. Known incompatibilities, supplied data schema and requested samples are checked before the first numerical command.

Command Supported explicit options Effective behavior stoch_simul order, irf, periods, ar, drop, hp_filter, pruning, nograph Initial defaults: order 2, irf 40, periods 0, ar 5, drop 100, no filter; nograph must be enabled. calib_smoother prefilter, first_obs, nobs Default prefilter off, first observation 1, all remaining observations. shock_decomposition first_obs, nobs Uses the supplied sample and full underlying state system.

Options use literal values in this subset. A symbolic value is unresolved in inspection, rather than silently evaluated or substituted. first_obs is one-based and nobs is a count. Shock standard deviations can be overridden with execute_mod_commands(sigma=...); the override reaches all three handlers.

Supported settings persist within one program, with two explicit exceptions: omitting order on each stoch_simul resets it to 2, and omitting an output-variable list selects all available outputs for that invocation. ar, irf, filtering and simulation settings otherwise persist; sample settings first_obs/nobs are shared by smoothing and decomposition. prefilter persists too. Because the native decomposition method does not implement prefiltering, a decomposition following calib_smoother(prefilter=1) is rejected unless a preceding smoother explicitly resets prefilter=0. Independent executions start from fresh option defaults.

For example:

stoch_simul(order=1, irf=3, ar=1) y;
stoch_simul(order=1, irf=7) x;
stoch_simul(irf=9);

This produces three entries, with (order, irf, ar) equal to (1,3,1), (1,7,1), and (2,9,1). Their selected outputs are y, x, and all variables. A stoch_simul selected result narrows displayed moments/IRFs but retains the complete decision rules. Smoother selections narrow available state/observable presentation frames; a requested variable absent from both is rejected before execution. Decomposition selections narrow component tables.

Each DynareCommandInvocation retains source location, explicit/effective options, requested selection, input/calibration fingerprint, status, and result snapshots. results.stoch_simul, .smoother, and .shock_decomposition remain conveniences for the last successful full result of that kind. Results from earlier calls are not overwritten. ModExecutionError.results retains all completed entries and the failed invocation if a numerical method fails; ModCompatibilityError.report contains the preflight findings.

The legacy defaults remain available: load_mod(...) and execute_mod_commands() still aggregate by command category. Inspection names that mode's repeated-command collapse and ignored output-variable selections.

docs.title: External evidence and limits
docs.text:
The small offline corpus in tests/fixtures/dynare_commands/ stores a Dynare 7.0 generated MATLAB driver excerpt and its source hash. It verifies per-command order reset, persistent ar/irf, fresh output selections, and shared sample settings. It is preprocessor evidence, not a numerical Dynare comparison. Tests additionally compare each supported puremacro invocation with its direct Python numerical method and exercise partial failures and unsupported sequences.

The Dynare manual describes output selections and defaults. The fixed Dynare 7.2 statement writer and runtime also establish why defaults must not be interpreted as resetting every option. This subset does not claim general Dynare command-program parity, global MATLAB options_ compatibility, or support for scripts and mutable model programs. Use check, resid, and model_diagnostics after solving for numerical/model diagnostics.

docs.title: One nonlinear specification, explicit solution methods
docs.text:
read_mod compiles a .mod file into a NonlinearModel without computing a steady state or solving a local rational-expectations approximation. You choose the numerical problem afterward. The same specification can supply nonlinear residuals to perfect foresight, perturbation and an explicitly constructed global equilibrium problem.

For method selection and the course sequence, start with the DSGE workflow guide.

Task Entry point What is computed Inspect syntax and command compatibility inspect_mod(source, ordered=True) A report; no numerical solution Retain equations and calibration read_mod(source, params=...) A compiled NonlinearModel; declarations may be evaluated Find a static equilibrium model.steady(...) A checked dictionary of endogenous levels Obtain a local policy rule model.solve(order=1), 2 or 3 The existing perturbation solution Solve a specified deterministic path model.solve_perfect_foresight(...) Endogenous values at dates 1 through T Run supported commands in file order model.execute_mod_commands() A command history and retained result snapshots Keep the established load-and-solve workflow load_mod(source, order=...) A local solution immediately

A finite boundary problem can be solvable even when the local policy-rule solver rejects the model. Conversely, successful compilation does not establish existence, uniqueness, determinacy or convergence. Perfect foresight still requires a well-posed system, appropriate boundaries and a feasible numerical path.

docs.title: Start with an exact deterministic path
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from puremacro.dsge import read_mod, NonlinearModel

model = read_mod("""
var x;
model; [name='accumulation'] x=0.5*x(-1); end;
initval; x=1; end;
""")
assert model.shocks == ()
assert model.equation_names == ("accumulation",)
steady = model.steady()
path = model.solve_perfect_foresight(y_init=[1], y_end=[0], periods=8)
assert path.converged
np.testing.assert_allclose(path.path.x, 0.5 ** np.arange(1, 9), atol=1e-10)

This is depreciation without investment: the date-zero stock is 1 and each period retains half of the previous stock. No varexo declaration is needed. path.path contains eight rows, excluding the supplied date-zero and date-nine boundaries. In this backward-looking example the terminal value does not enter any equation; a forward-looking equation would use it.

steady() returns the verified static equilibrium, here {"x": 0.0}. It does not change model.guess or model.steady_state. The latter, when present, is a supplied analytical declaration, not a numerical convergence certificate. Pass the returned values explicitly when they are needed as boundaries or as the reference for a subsequent calculation.

A purely forward-looking finite boundary problem also needs no prior local policy rule. Here the specified terminal price is 1 at date 5, and backward substitution determines the four reported prices. The initial value does not enter this equation:

forward_only = read_mod("var p; model; p=2*p(+1); end;")
finite_path = forward_only.solve_perfect_foresight(
    y_init=[0], y_end=[1], periods=4,
)
assert finite_path.converged
np.testing.assert_allclose(finite_path.path.p, [16, 8, 4, 2], atol=1e-10)

This example establishes a finite path under the supplied terminal value; it does not select an infinite-horizon economic solution.

docs.title: Migrate from load_mod deliberately
docs.text:
Existing load_mod calls keep their behavior. Use read_mod when the next task needs the original equations without requiring a local solution first. Obtain a local solution explicitly when you need decision rules, IRFs or moments:

from puremacro.dsge import load_mod

local_source = """
var x; varexo e; parameters rho; rho=0.7;
model; x=rho*x(-1)+e; end;
initval; x=0; end;
shocks; var e; stderr 0.1; end;
"""
legacy = load_mod(local_source, order=1)
specification = read_mod(local_source)
local = specification.solve(order=1)
np.testing.assert_allclose(local.decision_rules().ghx,
                           legacy.decision_rules().ghx, atol=1e-12)
assert specification.steady_state is None

There are three migration details to preserve:

  • read_mod(...).solve() defaults to order 1. It does not select its order from a stoch_simul command. Set order=2 or 3 explicitly when that is the intended approximation. load_mod(order=None) retains its existing command-derived order behavior.
  • Ordered execution is the default on NonlinearModel. On a model returned by load_mod, use execute_mod_commands(ordered=True) explicitly; loading with command_mode="ordered" performs compatibility preflight before its local solve. For a deterministic-only task, read_mod avoids that extra solve.
  • read_mod(params=...) re-evaluates analytical steady-state, initial-value and shock-covariance expressions at the merged calibration. Ordered dated-shock expressions are also evaluated at that calibration. Legacy load_mod keeps its existing shock-covariance behavior; use its shock_cov= argument when changing that covariance explicitly.

Calibrate every parameter and override only declared names. An override does not re-run dependent top-level assignments: if the source contains r=0.04; beta=1/(1+r);, overriding r alone leaves the calibrated beta unchanged. Override both, or use a parameter-dependent # model-local expression where an identity should remain symbolic. For another calibration, create another specification with read_mod(source, params=...); this also keeps the experiment's provenance clear.

A Path or a string without semicolons/newlines denotes a file. Raw source containing relative macro includes can use base_dir=. Reading retains the expanded source snapshot: changing an included file afterward does not change an already read command program. Read it again to use the new contents.

docs.title: Array timing and the callback contract
docs.text:
For n compiled endogenous variables and m shocks, the residual interface is

\[F(y_{t+1},y_t,y_{t-1},e_t;\theta,\bar y)=0.\] Argument or result Shape Meaning lead (n,) All endogenous values at t+1 current (n,) All endogenous values at t lag (n,) All endogenous values at t−1 shocks (m,) Current exogenous values/innovations, in declared order steady_state (n,) when supplied A fixed endogenous reference for STEADY_STATE() Returned residual (n,) One residual per compiled equation, in equation order PF shocks path (T, m) Exogenous values at dates 1 through T PF initial_path (T, n) Newton's starting guess, separate from the boundaries

model.residuals(...) accepts these one-dimensional arrays or mappings with all required names. It is a single-date evaluator, not a batch evaluator. When there are no shocks, pass [] or an array of shape (0,). Residual arrays preserve complex inputs, which allows suitable smooth callbacks to participate in complex-step differentiation. Avoid casting callback inputs to float or using absolute-value/branching operations when requesting that derivative method.

The model uses the timing written in the equations. For example, y=exp(a)*k(-1)^alpha; k=(1-delta)*k(-1)+i; makes k the end-of-period stock; production at t uses the inherited stock. Pass the complete endogenous vector at each date, not just the state variables selected by a perturbation solver.

from_equations wraps the same interface. Its callback receives four positional arrays and may explicitly declare params and/or steady_state; those optional arguments are passed only when named in the callback signature. params is a mapping. steady_state is an array or None. The callback supplies equations already arranged as residuals equal to zero:

def accumulation(lead, current, lag, shocks, *, params):
    return current - params["rho"] * lag

callback = NonlinearModel.from_equations(
    accumulation, variables=["x"], params={"rho": 0.5},
    equation_names=["accumulation"], guess=[0],
)
other_path = callback.solve_perfect_foresight(
    y_init=[1], y_end=[0], periods=8, linear_solver="krylov",
)
np.testing.assert_allclose(other_path.path, path.path, atol=1e-10)

variables must be nonempty, and endogenous and shock names must be distinct. Optional equation_names has one distinct name per variable. Optional timing records your declared timing; it does not shift or rewrite a Python callback. guess, steady_state and shock_cov provide explicit initial-value, reference and covariance metadata. A callback model has no .mod source to execute; use its numerical methods directly.

A mixed backward/forward system shows why all three endogenous vectors matter. Let z follow an AR(1) and let q be a deterministic discounted value of z, with a zero terminal value. The following callback and .mod specification produce the same finite-horizon path:

def valuation_equations(lead, current, lag, shocks, *, params):
    z, q = current
    return np.array([
        z - params["rho"] * lag[0] - shocks[0],
        q - z - params["beta"] * lead[1],
    ])

valuation = NonlinearModel.from_equations(
    valuation_equations, variables=["z", "q"], shocks=["e"],
    params={"rho": 0.5, "beta": 0.8},
    equation_names=["state", "valuation"],
    timing={"z": [-1, 0], "q": [0, 1]}, guess=[0, 0],
)
valuation_mod = read_mod("""
var z q; varexo e; parameters rho beta; rho=0.5; beta=0.8;
model;
[name='state'] z=rho*z(-1)+e;
[name='valuation'] q=z+beta*q(+1);
end;
""")
innovations = np.zeros((8, 1))
innovations[0, 0] = 1
arguments = dict(y_init=[0, 0], y_end=[0, 0], periods=8, shocks=innovations)
callback_path = valuation.solve_perfect_foresight(**arguments)
compiled_path = valuation_mod.solve_perfect_foresight(**arguments)
assert callback_path.converged and compiled_path.converged
np.testing.assert_allclose(callback_path.path, compiled_path.path, atol=1e-10)
expected_z = 0.5 ** np.arange(8)
expected_q = np.zeros(9)
for t in range(7, -1, -1):
    expected_q[t] = expected_z[t] + 0.8 * expected_q[t + 1]
np.testing.assert_allclose(compiled_path.path.z, expected_z, atol=1e-10)
np.testing.assert_allclose(compiled_path.path.q, expected_q[:-1], atol=1e-10)

docs.title: Names, references and augmented equations
docs.text:
Attribute Interpretation variables, shocks The authoritative array order used by the compiled specification parameter_values The current fixed calibration equation_names Equation tags such as [name='Euler'], or generated names timing Endogenous dates appearing in the compiled equations equation_sources Locations of original source equations source_hashes Hashes identifying the source snapshot and included files

The parser can augment higher leads/lags and dated exogenous variables with auxiliary equations. Consequently, model.variables can be longer than the source var list. Inspect it before constructing arrays; auxiliary rows may not have their own original source-equation span. For nonconstant historical paths, provide a consistently augmented state through Python. The ordered boundary subset accepts only unindexed values or date zero, not a complete multi-date histval calendar.

For a dynamic residual audit, supply the fixed steady_state reference explicitly when the equations contain STEADY_STATE(). Calling residuals without it uses the current vector for that operator, which is appropriate for a static residual calculation. The attribute model.steady_state is not implicitly substituted by residuals. In a perfect-foresight solve, y_end provides both the terminal boundary and the fixed reference:

reference_model = read_mod("""
var p;
model; p=0.5*p(+1)+0.5*STEADY_STATE(p); end;
""")
fixed = reference_model.residuals([3], [2], [0], [], steady_state=[1])
static_reference = reference_model.residuals([3], [2], [0], [])
np.testing.assert_allclose(fixed, [0])
np.testing.assert_allclose(static_reference, [-0.5])

docs.title: Steady states and positive domains
docs.text:
model.steady(exo_values=..., guess=..., tol=...) solves the static original equations and checks the resulting residual against tol. exo_values is a mapping by shock name or a shock-order vector; it specifies the constant exogenous levels at this equilibrium. A guess is a starting point, not a restriction on the solution. Without an explicit guess the method uses an analytical declaration, then initval, when available.

For log, reciprocal or fractional-power equations, provide a feasible guess. In an ordered program a steady_state_model declaration supplies the analytical seed even when initval is absent. The equations are still solved and verified at the active exogenous values. A changed terminal exogenous level therefore cannot be replaced silently by the initial equilibrium.

This positive level model has the exact static relation x=center*exp(e/0.8). The overridden center is 3, and the permanent terminal shock raises the steady state to 12:

positive_program = read_mod("""
var x; varexo e; parameters center; center=2;
model; log(x)=0.2*log(x(-1))+0.8*log(center)+e; end;
steady_state_model; x=center; end;
steady;
endval; e=0.8*log(4); end;
steady;
perfect_foresight_setup(periods=3);
perfect_foresight_solver(tolf=1e-10);
""", params={"center": 3})
positive_results = positive_program.execute_mod_commands()
static_results = [entry.result for entry in positive_results.invocations
                  if entry.command == "steady"]
np.testing.assert_allclose([value.x for value in static_results], [3, 12])
expected = 3 * 4 ** (1 - 0.2 ** np.arange(1, 4))
np.testing.assert_allclose(positive_results.perfect_foresight.path.x,
                           expected, atol=1e-8)

perfect_foresight_setup(endval_steady, periods=...) can request the terminal static solve as part of setup. This native option prepares a checked endpoint; it does not promise Dynare's full homotopy or terminal-steady-state algorithm. For nonlinear continuation and independent horizon checks, use the transition workflow.

docs.title: Execute deterministic commands in source order
docs.text:
The commands use concepts described in the Dynare manual's initial and terminal conditions and deterministic simulation sections. The tables below define the native puremacro subset. Dynare provides additional command forms and algorithms beyond this subset.

The first experiment below is transitory. The second changes the constant exogenous level and computes the associated terminal steady state. A shock redeclared after the first setup deliberately demonstrates its snapshot semantics:

program = read_mod("""
var x; varexo e; parameters rho; rho=0.5;
model; x=rho*x(-1)+e; end;
initval; x=0; e=0; end;
steady;
shocks; var e; periods 1; values 1; end;
perfect_foresight_setup(periods=4);
shocks; var e; periods 1; values 9; end;
perfect_foresight_solver(tolf=1e-10);
endval; x=8; e=1; end;
steady;
shocks(overwrite); end;
perfect_foresight_setup(periods=8);
perfect_foresight_solver;
""")
results = program.execute_mod_commands()
solves = [entry for entry in results.invocations
          if entry.command == "perfect_foresight_solver"]
np.testing.assert_allclose(solves[0].result.path.x, [1, .5, .25, .125], atol=1e-10)
np.testing.assert_allclose(solves[1].result.path.x,
                           2 * (1 - .5 ** np.arange(1, 9)), atol=1e-10)
print(results.to_frame())

The first solved path still begins at 1: its setup was prepared before the value 9 was declared. The second setup uses the updated terminal equilibrium and the cleared dated-shock declarations. endval; x=8; e=1; end; steady; produces terminal x=2, because steady solves x=0.5*x+1. Omitting that steady would retain the literal terminal value 8.

docs.title: Boundary and shock state
docs.text:
Statement Effect when reached initval Starts a new initial/terminal experiment; omitted endogenous and exogenous values become zero; clears historical and terminal assignments steady before endval Replaces initial endogenous values with their static equilibrium at the current initial exogenous levels histval Supplies the historical endogenous boundary, overriding initial values there; supported dates are unindexed or zero endval Updates the terminal values; omissions inherit the existing terminal context or initial values steady after endval Replaces terminal endogenous values with the equilibrium at terminal exogenous levels shocks Accumulates dated assignments and covariance declarations; a redeclared date replaces only that date shocks(overwrite) Clears previous dated shocks and covariance declarations before reading the new block perfect_foresight_setup Copies boundaries, exogenous path and initial iterate for the selected horizon perfect_foresight_solver Solves that prepared experiment; a repeated successful solve starts from its previous path simul Prepares and solves the current experiment in one command

The runner begins with zero initial values. An endval by itself does not set the historical boundary in this subset: use an explicit initval or initial steady. initval does not clear shock declarations; use shocks(overwrite) when starting an experiment that should discard them. The subset rejects histval and endval together within one initial-value experiment.

A setup contains y_init at date 0 and y_end at T+1. Its initial Newton path repeats the terminal endogenous vector at dates 1 through T. Its exogenous path uses the terminal exogenous levels, or initial levels when there is no endval, with dated assignments replacing those levels at the specified dates. These are exogenous levels/innovations as written in the equations; there is no automatic conversion to percentage changes.

Dated values can use finite expressions of the preceding calibrated parameters. Dates are positive integers within the setup horizon. A single value may fill all dates in a declared range; otherwise supply one value for every expanded date. For portability, avoid combining multiple ranges with range-specific values; write separate shock stanzas instead.

A stderr or covariance declaration controls stochastic variance; it does not create a deterministic realization. Conversely, a block containing only dated shocks leaves unspecified stochastic variances at zero and may produce a parser warning to that effect. Keep both kinds of declarations explicit in programs that also use stoch_simul. The mixed ordered runner requires zero exogenous reference values for stochastic commands; recenter the model before running a stochastic experiment around a nonzero exogenous baseline.

docs.title: Supported options and compatibility boundaries
docs.text:
The following defaults belong to puremacro's ordered runner. Options must be supported literals; arbitrary expressions in command options are not evaluated by compatibility inspection.

Command Accepted options Initial defaults steady in a deterministic program tol or tolf Residual tolerance 1e-10 perfect_foresight_setup periods, endval_steady 100, false perfect_foresight_solver tol or tolf; maxit or max_iter; matching periods; stack_solve_algo; linear_solver; mcp 1e-8, 50, 100, 0, 'direct', false simul Setup and solver options together Same PF defaults

PF option values persist when omitted later in the same program. A later tol= replaces an earlier tolf= value and vice versa; likewise for the iteration-limit aliases. Supplying both aliases in one command is rejected. The initial steady tolerance is separate from the PF solver tolerance. Changing a solver's periods without preparing that horizon first is rejected. A new setup replaces the previous prepared path; a repeated solver on the same setup reuses the last successful path.

Feature Native ordered support or required alternative Sparse direct stacked Newton stack_solve_algo=0 or linear_solver='direct' Newton–Krylov linear_solver='krylov'; omit explicit stack_solve_algo Complementarity tags Native mcp with direct backend; simple variable/parameter bound expressions Full Dynare algorithm IDs Values other than stack_solve_algo=0 are rejected; no numerical-equivalence claim tolx, lmmcp, solver/homotopy option families Outside the ordered subset; use supported native Python controls Parameter changes between experiments Create separate specifications with params=; repeated/top-level reassignment is rejected Historical date calendars Only unindexed/date-zero boundary assignments; provide an augmented state through Python varexo_det, trend/regime/estimation declarations May be parsed or reported, but are not executed by this ordered route Expectation-error, learned-shock and calendar commands Not implemented by this ordered route MATLAB/Octave scripts and external helper execution Not executed; move the study logic to Python Ramsey/OSR or heterogeneous-agent programs Use the corresponding explicit APIs/entry points; they are outside this ordered subset

MCP tags such as [mcp='r > floor'] keep the original LHS-minus-RHS equation orientation. At a lower bound the associated residual must have the nonnegative sign required by the complementarity condition. The tag does not infer or correct your economic inequality. Repeated bounds for one variable, dynamic-bound expressions and unsupported tag syntax are rejected. Native MCP is not a lmmcp alias, and it cannot be combined with Krylov.

The compiled specification uses the existing parser and supported bounded macro preprocessing. It is not a general MATLAB interpreter. Boundary assignment expressions must be evaluable in the available calibration/value context; expressions that depend on a previous numerical solution may fail already during reading. For such studies, solve in Python and pass the resulting arrays explicitly. Treat the compatibility report for the exact entry point as authoritative: recognition of a keyword alone does not imply its execution is supported.

docs.title: Inspect, diagnose and recover
docs.text:
Compatibility inspection is separate from solving. coverage="complete" means the syntax was collected completely; exit_code==0 means the selected execution route has no compatibility findings. Neither certifies a numerical solution. The report identifies source locations, unsupported option names and suggested remedies. read_mod can retain a specification whose commands are unsupported; execution performs the compatibility check before starting its numerical commands.

from puremacro.dsge import inspect_mod, ModCompatibilityError, ModExecutionError

unsupported_source = """
var x; model; x=0.5*x(-1); end;
initval; x=1; end;
simul(periods=4, tolx=1e-8);
"""
report = inspect_mod(unsupported_source, ordered=True)
assert report.coverage == "complete" and report.exit_code != 0
assert any(issue.code == "UNSUPPORTED_OPTION" for issue in report.issues)
try:
    read_mod(unsupported_source).execute_mod_commands()
except ModCompatibilityError as error:
    assert any(issue.code == "UNSUPPORTED_OPTION" for issue in error.report.issues)
else:
    raise AssertionError("An unsupported option must not be ignored")

Once a numerical command starts, a failure raises ModExecutionError with .report and .results. Completed entries and the failed entry remain available. A failed PF result is retained when the solver returned one; a failed static solve need not have a numerical result. This deliberately impossible real-valued static equation demonstrates the distinction:

impossible = read_mod("""
var x; model; x^2+1=0; end;
initval; x=0; end;
steady;
simul(periods=3);
""")
try:
    impossible.execute_mod_commands()
except ModExecutionError as error:
    partial = error.results
    assert partial.invocations[-1].status == "failed"
    assert partial.invocations[-1].command == "steady"
    assert "SteadyStateError" in partial.invocations[-1].error
else:
    raise AssertionError("An unverified steady state must not be accepted")
Symptom Check and recovery A local QZ/determinacy failure blocks a deterministic study Load with read_mod; independently check that the finite boundary system is well posed ModelError during reading Check declarations, parameter expressions, equation count, includes and parser coverage; unsupported source constructs cannot be fixed by increasing iterations ModCompatibilityError Read .report; replace the unsupported option/command or move that operation to its explicit Python API A log/power/division produces nonfinite residuals Check positivity and denominators in guesses, boundary values and all trial paths; use a feasible analytical seed SteadyStateError Inspect the static original equations and calibration; a supplied analytical declaration must satisfy them too PF does not converge Inspect the failed entry's result and solver_diagnostics; check timing, independent equations, boundary consistency and scaling before increasing maxit A changed shock appears to have no effect Check the setup snapshot; declarations after setup require another setup Tiny residual but a questionable transition Recompute original residuals, compare longer horizons and inspect economic feasibility; convergence alone does not verify the terminal approximation

The direct Python PF method may return converged=False; the ordered runner turns that outcome into ModExecutionError and retains the failed result. Always check convergence when calling numerical methods directly. For domain checks, continuation, terminal-policy boundaries and horizon studies, see transition controls and trajectory audits.

docs.title: Retain and export the experiment
docs.text:
DynareCommandResults.invocations contains numerical command snapshots, including steady and setup. Declaration blocks update the input state and do not each create a numerical result. Each invocation records its command, source location, explicit/effective options, input fingerprint, status, complete result, and selected_result. A variable selection narrows presentation; it does not solve a smaller equilibrium system.

effective_options["input_state"] retains calibration, initial/terminal values, historical values, dated shocks and covariance. Solver entries also retain the prepared inputs. Each PerfectForesightSetup exposes periods, variable_names, shock_names, y_init, y_end, exogenous_path, initial_path and parameters. Its arrays have the dimensions listed above.

Snapshots are copied between invocations; later source declarations and later solves do not overwrite earlier results. The convenience alias results.perfect_foresight is a separate copy of the last successful PF result. Arrays and DataFrames inside a snapshot remain ordinary mutable objects: make your own copy before editing a retained experiment.

setups = [entry.result for entry in results.invocations
          if entry.command == "perfect_foresight_setup"]
first_setup = setups[0]
np.testing.assert_allclose(first_setup.to_frame().e, [1, 0, 0, 0])
assert first_setup.to_dataframe().equals(first_setup.to_frame())
print(first_setup.summary())
print(results.to_frame())
markdown_shocks = first_setup.to_markdown()
latex_shocks = first_setup.to_latex()
typst_shocks = first_setup.to_typst()
assert "e" in markdown_shocks and "tabular" in latex_shocks and "#table" in typst_shocks
Result Tables and reports PerfectForesightSetup summary() describes dimensions; to_frame()/to_dataframe() return the dated shock path; Markdown/LaTeX/Typst exporters render that table DynareCommandResults summary() and to_frame() describe execution history; to_markdown(), to_latex(), to_typst() export it PerfectForesightResult path/to_frame() contain endogenous trajectories; summary() includes convergence evidence; table exporters and plot() support presentation MCPResult Adds binding periods and complementarity diagnostics to its path and convergence information

terminal_error measures the distance between the last simulated endogenous row and the supplied terminal vector. It is not a transversality test or an estimate of every truncation error. Compare paths at economically relevant early dates across horizons, alongside original-equation residuals.

docs.title: MAV T02_A: one specification for a permanent productivity change
docs.text:
The course file uses log productivity a_t=rho_a*a_(t-1)+e_a. Keeping productivity at 1.02 requires a first innovation log(1.02) and subsequent innovations (1-rho_a)*log(1.02). A single innovation to an AR(1) with rho_a<1 instead decays. The same source equations can be retained for local and deterministic studies.

Run the following block from the matching repository root; the course model file is a source-checkout dependency rather than an installed-package data file:

# requires: matching source checkout with curso/notebooks/
from pathlib import Path

source = Path("curso/notebooks/modelos/neoclasico_prevision_perfecta.mod").read_text()
experiment = read_mod(source + """
endval; e_a=(1-rho_a)*log(1.02); end;
steady;
shocks; var e_a; periods 1; values log(1.02); end;
perfect_foresight_setup(periods=80);
perfect_foresight_solver(tolf=1e-10);
perfect_foresight_setup(periods=160);
perfect_foresight_solver;
""")
study = experiment.execute_mod_commands()
transitions = [entry.result for entry in study.invocations
               if entry.command == "perfect_foresight_solver"]
assert all(result.converged for result in transitions)
np.testing.assert_allclose(transitions[0].path.a, np.log(1.02), atol=1e-10)
early_difference = np.max(np.abs(
    transitions[0].path.iloc[:20].to_numpy() -
    transitions[1].path.iloc[:20].to_numpy()
))
print(early_difference)

The original course file's first-order stoch_simul executes before the appended transition commands. The two setup/solver pairs retain their separate horizons and endpoints. Inspect early_difference and the residual evidence; a small stacked residual alone does not certify an infinite-horizon solution.

For a local/global comparison, build an EquilibriumProblem.from_model with explicit state, control, transition and expectation mappings; see global equilibrium methods. A .mod file does not by itself identify that recursive formulation or a planner's objective. For better finite-path initialization, continuation and terminal audits, continue with nonlinear transitions. These routes reuse the equations while making their distinct information sets and approximation assumptions explicit.

docs.title: DSGE Parity Surface, Advanced Simulation & Parity Dashboard
docs.text:
This page describes selected DSGE simulation and comparison interfaces. It does not establish the full Dynare surface or general numerical parity. See structural validation status for independently checked cases and current limitations.

This milestone delivers four core macroscopic capabilities: 1. stoch_simul Filtering & Simulation Surface: Spectral density integration via Gauss-Legendre quadrature for theoretical HP and bandpass filtering, one-sided recursive Kalman HP filter, full cross-variable autocorrelation matrices, contemporaneous correlations, and empirical simulation moments (simul_replic). 2. Extended Path Non-Linear Stochastic Simulation (Fair & Taylor 1983): Global dynamic simulation without perturbation Taylor truncations, driven by a sparse SuperLU stacked Newton boundary-value solver with exact linear model invariance. 3. Advanced Forecasting & Shock Decompositions: Waggoner & Zha (1999) conditional forecasting via structural shock inversion, .mod shock_groups; grammar blocks with exact machine-precision adding-up decompositions, Bayesian impulse response function (IRF) fan charts, prior predictive analysis, and tunable qz_criterium for unit-root and cointegrated systems. 4. Dynare Parity Dashboard: Comparison of caller-supplied oo_.dr mappings and actual supplied moments. The caller reads any MAT file. The CLI cannot consume reference results and is unavailable; use the Python API.

docs.title: 1. Overview & Architecture
docs.text:
The puremacro DSGE engine bridges exact analytical solutions, higher-order perturbation with state pruning, and non-linear sequence-space transitions. Supported syntax and numerical methods form a subset; migration requires model-specific checks.

Module Core Capability Key Method / Algorithm Benchmark Reference puremacro.dsge._moments Spectral filtering & simulation moments Gauss-Legendre quadrature & forward Kalman filter Hodrick & Prescott (1997); Stock & Watson (1999) puremacro.dsge.extended_path Extended Path non-linear simulation Stacked SuperLU Newton engine with zero future shock expectations Fair & Taylor (1983); Adjemian & Juillard (2014) puremacro.dsge.conditional Conditional forecasting Structural shock inversion (\(U = R^{-1} d\)) Waggoner & Zha (1999) puremacro.dsge.shock_groups Grouped shock decompositions Exact historical attribution with adding-up balance Dynare 4.6+ / 5.x / 6.x specification puremacro.dsge.bayesian Bayesian IRFs & Prior Predictive Posterior fan charts & prior simulation Geweke (1999); Herbst & Schorfheide (2015) puremacro.dsge.parity Parity Dashboard & Verification Automated golden comparisons & scorecard generation Pfeifer (2014); Dynare Benchmark Suite puremacro.dsge.cli Parity CLI unavailable Use the Python API with references No comparison is executed

docs.title: 2.1 Theoretical Spectral Density Filtering
docs.text:
In linear or linearized DSGE models, the state-space representation dates state deviations \(x_t\) and observed/target variables \(v_t\):

\[x_{t+1} = G x_t + N u_t, \quad v_t = M_x x_t + M_u u_t, \quad u_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma_u)\]

The continuous spectral density matrix of \(v_t\) at frequency \(\omega \in [-\pi, \pi]\) is:

\[S_v(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi} H(e^{-i\omega}) \Sigma_u H(e^{i\omega})^\top\]

where the transfer function is \(H(e^{i\omega}) = M_x (e^{i\omega} I_{n_x} - G)^{-1} N + M_u\).

When a linear filter with squared frequency-response gain \(|\Phi(\omega)|^2\) is applied, the theoretical filtered autocovariance at lag \(k\) is evaluated by integrating over frequencies:

\[\Gamma_k^{filtered} = \int_{-\pi}^\pi |\Phi(\omega)|^2 S_v(\omega) e^{i\omega k} \, d\omega = 2 \int_0^\pi |\Phi(\omega)|^2 \operatorname{Re}\left[ S_v(\omega) e^{i\omega k} \right] \, d\omega\]

Puremacro integrates this spectral density using \(n_{quad} = 256\) Gauss-Legendre quadrature nodes and weights mapped to the interval \([0, \pi]\).

docs.title: Supported Spectral Filters
docs.text:
1. Hodrick-Prescott Filter (hp_filter = lambda): $\(|\Phi_{HP}(\omega)|^2 = \left(\frac{4\lambda (1 - \cos\omega)^2}{1 + 4\lambda (1 - \cos\omega)^2}\right)^2\)$ where \(\lambda = 1600\) for quarterly data, \(\lambda = 6.25\) for annual data, and \(\lambda = 129600\) for monthly data.
  2. Frequency Bandpass Filter (bandpass_filter = [low, high]): Ideal bandpass filter retaining periodicities between periods \(p_{high} = 2\pi/\omega_{low}\) and \(p_{low} = 2\pi/\omega_{high}\) (e.g. \([6, 32]\) quarters for business cycles): $\(|\Phi_{BP}(\omega)|^2 = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \omega_{low} \le \omega \le \omega_{high} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

docs.title: 2.2 One-Sided Recursive Kalman HP Filter
docs.text:
While the standard two-sided HP filter relies on future data and cannot be applied in real-time causal contexts, the one-sided HP filter (one_sided_hp_filter) solves the recursive state-space model:

\[\Delta^2 \tau_t = \eta_t, \quad y_t = \tau_t + \varepsilon_t, \quad \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{\sigma_\eta^2} = \lambda\]

Writing in state space with state vector \(s_t = [\tau_t, \tau_{t-1}]^\top\):

\[s_t = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} s_{t-1} + \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \eta_t, \quad y_t = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} s_t + \varepsilon_t\]

Puremacro estimates the causal trend \(\tau_{t|t}\) forward using the discrete Kalman filter with backwards linear extrapolation initialization matching Dynare.

docs.title: 2.3 Cross-Variable Autocorrelations & Contemporaneous Correlations
docs.text:
Given theoretical or filtered autocovariances \(\Gamma_k\), the contemporaneous correlation matrix \(R(0)\) and cross-variable autocorrelation matrices \(R(k)\) for lags \(k = 1, \dots, n\) are defined as:

\[D = \operatorname{diag}(\Gamma_0), \quad R(0) = D^{-1/2} \Gamma_0 D^{-1/2}, \quad R(k) = D^{-1/2} \Gamma_k D^{-1/2}\]

All diagonal entries of \(R(0)\) are strictly 1.0, and values are constrained to the mathematical domain \([-1, 1]\).

docs.title: 2.4 Empirical Simulation Moments (simul_replic = M)
docs.text:
When simul_replic = M is specified in stoch_simul: 1. The engine simulates \(M\) independent Monte Carlo sample paths of length periods. 2. Any requested trajectory filter (e.g., two-sided HP or one-sided HP) is evaluated on each replication path. 3. Sample means, standard deviations, variances, and cross-variable autocorrelations are computed across paths. 4. Monte Carlo standard errors \(\sigma / \sqrt{M}\) are reported alongside point estimates.

# requires: standalone snippet
from puremacro.dsge import load_mod

# Solve model and compute theoretical HP moments with autocorrelation matrix
m = load_mod("rbc.mod")
m.solve()

# Theoretical moments filtered with HP(1600) and order 4 autocorrelations
res = m.stoch_simul(hp_filter=1600.0, ar=4, contemporaneous_correlation=True)
print(res.summary())

# Empirical Monte Carlo simulation with M=500 replications
res_mc = m.stoch_simul(periods=200, simul_replic=500, hp_filter=1600.0)
print(res_mc.simulated_moments)

docs.title: 3.1 The Fair & Taylor (1983) Algorithm
docs.text:
The Extended Path algorithm (extended_path) simulates non-linear dynamic macroeconomic models under rational expectations without Taylor series truncations or dynamic programming grid discretization.

At each simulation date \(t = 0, \dots, T-1\): 1. A structural innovation vector \(u_t\) is drawn or supplied. 2. Agents are assumed to expect all future innovations beyond period \(t\) to be zero: $\(\mathbb{E}_t[u_{t+s}] = 0 \quad \text{for } s \ge 1\)$ 3. The forward deterministic boundary problem is stacked over horizon \(T_H\): $\(f(y_{t+1|t}, y_{t|t}, y_{t-1}, u_t) = 0\)$ $\(f(y_{t+s+1|t}, y_{t+s|t}, y_{t+s-1|t}, 0) = 0 \quad \text{for } s = 1, \dots, T_H - 1\)$ with terminal condition \(y_{t+T_H|t} = y_{ss}\). 4. The system is solved simultaneously using the sparse SuperLU stacked Newton-Raphson engine from puremacro.dsge.perfect_foresight. 5. The contemporaneous realization \(y_t = y_{t|t}\) is saved, the historical state is updated (\(y_{t-1} \leftarrow y_t\)), and the solver moves to date \(t+1\) warm-starting from the previous path.

docs.title: 3.2 Linear Model Invariance
docs.text:
A fundamental correctness property of the Fair-Taylor algorithm is linear model invariance: when the model equations \(f\) are linear in \((y_{t+1}, y_t, y_{t-1}, u_t)\), the extended path trajectory is mathematically identical to the first-order linear state space simulation:

\[\| y_t^{EP} - y_t^{Linear} \|_\infty \le 10^{-10}\]

Puremacro rigorously verifies this invariance property in its continuous test suite.

# requires: standalone snippet
from puremacro.dsge.extended_path import extended_path

# Run non-linear stochastic simulation over 150 periods with horizon 80
ep_res = extended_path(
    model_or_equations=m,
    periods=150,
    horizon=80,
    seed=42,
    tol=1e-8,
)

# Access simulated paths and generate publication figures
df_sim = ep_res.to_frame()
fig = ep_res.plot(variables=["c", "k", "y", "r"])

docs.title: 4.1 Conditional Forecasting (Waggoner & Zha 1999)
docs.text:
In economic policy analysis, central banks frequently construct forecasts conditioned on hypothetical trajectories of specific target variables (e.g., conditioning on a policy interest rate path remaining fixed for 4 quarters).

Following Waggoner & Zha (1999, Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control), the conditional forecast solves for the structural innovation sequence \(U = [u_1^\top, \dots, u_H^\top]^\top\) satisfying:

\[R \, U = d\]

where \(R\) is the stacked impulse response mapping from structural shocks to target variables, and \(d\) is the gap between unconditional baseline forecasts and the specified target trajectory.

docs.title: Solution Methods:
docs.text:
• Covariance-Weighted (method="covariance_weighted"): Minimizes the Mahalanobis distance \(U^\top \Sigma_U^{-1} U\), weighting shocks by their structural probability: $\(U = \Sigma_U R^\top \left( R \Sigma_U R^\top \right)^{-1} d\)$
  • Minimum Energy (method="minimum_energy"): Minimizes the Euclidean 2-norm \(\|U\|_2\): $\(U = R^\top \left( R R^\top \right)^{-1} d\)$
# requires: standalone snippet
from puremacro.dsge.conditional import conditional_forecast

# Enforce interest rate 'r' to 0.015 for the first 4 quarters
cf_res = conditional_forecast(
    model=m,
    conditions={"r": [0.015, 0.015, 0.015, 0.015]},
    horizon=12,
    controlled_shocks=["eps_r"],
    method="covariance_weighted",
)

# Inspect implied structural shocks and fan chart
print(cf_res.shocks)
fig = cf_res.plot(variables=["y", "pi", "r"])

docs.title: 4.2 Grouped Historical Shock Decompositions (shock_groups;)
docs.text:
In .mod files, users can declare shock group categories:

shock_groups;
  'Supply' = ea, eb;
  'Demand' = eq, ec;
  'Monetary Policy' = em;
end;

puremacro.dsge.shock_groups decomposes historical observed series into these economic categories plus initial condition contributions:

\[y_t^{obs} = \sum_{g \in \text{groups}} y_t^{(g)} + y_t^{(init)}\]

This decomposition preserves exact adding-up balance to machine precision (\(\le 10^{-12}\)).

# requires: standalone snippet
from puremacro.dsge.shock_groups import shock_groups_decomposition

decomp = shock_groups_decomposition(
    model=m,
    data=observed_df,
    groups={
        "Supply": ["ea", "eb"],
        "Demand": ["eq", "ec"],
        "Monetary Policy": ["em"],
    }
)
fig = decomp.plot(variable="y")

docs.title: 4.3 Bayesian IRF Fan Charts & Prior Predictive Simulation
docs.text:
• bayesian_irf: Evaluates impulse responses across parameter draws from MCMC or SMC posterior chains, computing point-wise credible intervals (median, 68%, 90%, 95%) and generating fan charts (BayesianIRFResult).
  • prior_predictive: Samples parameters from prior distributions and computes unconditional moments and IRF distributions before observing empirical data, diagnosing prior model plausibility (PriorPredictiveResult).
  • Tunable qz_criterium: In models with unit roots or cointegrating vectors (such as growth models or monetary models without nominal anchors), the generalized Schur eigenvalue classification boundary can be tuned (\(\alpha = 1.0 + \varepsilon\)) to prevent spurious instability classifications.

docs.title: 5.1 Verification Engine & Metrics
docs.text:
The parity harness compares a model with caller-supplied Dynare decision rules or an oo_ mapping. It does not execute Dynare or read .mat files itself. Missing or malformed comparisons are UNAVAILABLE, never a pass. DR-only comparisons do not establish moment or shock-covariance parity. See current validation limits.

The automated test engine checks maximum absolute deviations:

\[\Delta_{max}(A, B) = \max_{i,j} |A_{ij} - B_{ij}|\] Metric Target Array Tolerance Threshold Steady state (\(ys\)) oo_.dr.ys \(\le 10^{-6}\) Cross state-shock (\(ghxu\)) oo_.dr.ghxu \(\le 10^{-4}\) Shock curvature (\(ghuu\)) oo_.dr.ghuu \(\le 10^{-4}\) First-order states (\(ghx\)) oo_.dr.ghx \(\le 10^{-6}\) (typically \(\le 10^{-12}\)) First-order shocks (\(ghu\)) oo_.dr.ghu \(\le 10^{-6}\) (typically \(\le 10^{-12}\)) Second-order states (\(ghxx\)) oo_.dr.ghxx \(\le 10^{-4}\) (typically \(\le 10^{-10}\)) Second-order risk (\(ghs2\)) oo_.dr.ghs2 \(\le 10^{-4}\) (typically \(\le 10^{-10}\)) Ergodic Means oo_.mean \(\le 10^{-5}\) Ergodic Variances oo_.var \(\le 10^{-5}\) Autocorrelations oo_.autocorr \(\le 10^{-5}\)

docs.title: 5.2 Python API
docs.text:
# requires: standalone snippet
import scipy.io

from puremacro.dsge.parity import verify_dynare_parity, run_parity_suite

# puremacro 4.0.0 reads no MATLAB files: load Dynare's oo_ yourself and pass
# the mapping. Everything downstream is unchanged.
oo = scipy.io.loadmat("sw07_results.mat", squeeze_me=True, struct_as_record=False)

# Single model verification
report = verify_dynare_parity(
    puremacro_model="sw07.mod",
    dynare_output=oo,
    order=2,
)
print(report.to_markdown())

# Suite verification across an entire directory
suite_report = run_parity_suite("models/", dynare_results={"sw07": oo}, order=2)
assert suite_report.passed

M_.Sigma_e is compared when the puremacro object declares a covariance (tolerance shock_cov, 1e-10, reported in details["covariance_status"]). By default, order-2 second moments follow stoch_simul(order=2) without pruning: the risk-corrected mean and first-order second moments. For a reference from stoch_simul(order=2, pruning), pass pruning=True: the comparison then uses the exact moments of the pruned solution, which reproduce Dynare 8's to 7e-14 on the five live models, autocorrelations included. Autocorrelation rows of zero-variance variables that are NaN on both sides are listed in details["moments_excluded"].

docs.title: 5.3 CLI availability
docs.text: puremacro-dynare parity deliberately exits with an error since 4.0.0: it has no supported way to receive a reference. Use verify_dynare_parity or run_parity_suite(..., dynare_results=...) from Python, as above. A directory without supplied references produces UNAVAILABLE entries, not passing models.

docs.title: 6. Runtime dependencies and portability
docs.text:
All Tier 3 components adhere strictly to the Pyodide four-package contract: - NumPy: Linear algebra, vectorization, array manipulation, eigenvalues, and pseudo-random numbers. - SciPy: Sparse linear systems (scipy.sparse.linalg.splu), special functions (erf, normcdf), and matrix factorizations (scipy.linalg.ordqz). - Pandas: Labeled Series and DataFrames for variables, dates, and scorecards. - Matplotlib: Presentation fan charts, shock decomposition bar graphs, and IRF visualizer.

No external solvers (SymPy, CasADi, JAX), parser generators (PLY, Lark, ANTLR), or compiled C/Fortran modules are required. Browser and accelerator execution require validation of the particular workload. Import checks do not establish runtime performance or cross-backend numerical identity.

docs.title: Independent higher-order reference benchmark (20 September 2026)
docs.text: Five source models were executed in Dynare 7.0 at orders two and three. The reproduction tools compare every unfolded tensor, risk correction, innovation covariance, simulated path and sample moments against frozen external outputs. This separate benchmark does not extend verify_dynare_parity beyond orders one and two. All ten exports completed before MATLAB crashed during process shutdown: the numerical comparisons pass, but the MATLAB process did not exit cleanly. The benchmark is not evidence for other models or runtimes.

docs.title: DSGE Frontier (Policy, DSGE-VAR & News)
docs.text: Español · English

docs.title: DSGE Frontier: Optimal Policy (Discretion vs Commitment), DSGE-VAR Hybrid Modeling, and Anticipated News Shocks
docs.text:
puremacro delivers three state-of-the-art computational frontiers for structural macroeconomic analysis:

  1. Optimal Policy Regimes (Discretion vs. Commitment): Solves Markov-perfect time-consistent discretionary policy via Dennis (2007) Riccati matrix iteration, alongside linear-quadratic (LQ) commitment via Lagrange multiplier augmentation and Klein (2000) QZ decomposition (the Ramsey plan from the steady state, whose law of motion is the timeless-perspective rule; section 1.3). Formalizes the quantification of Kydland-Prescott / Barro-Gordon inflation bias and stabilization bias.
  2. DSGE-VAR Hybrid Modeling (Del Negro & Schorfheide 2004): Bridges structural DSGE microfoundations with flexible vector autoregressions via an analytical Normal-Inverted-Wishart prior centered on theoretical cross-equation moments \(\Gamma_k(\theta)\). Provides closed-form evaluation of the log marginal data density \(\ln p(Y \mid \lambda, \theta)\), bounded hyperparameter optimization for \(\hat{\lambda} \in [\lambda_{\min}, \infty)\), and structural identification via the DSGE rotation matrix \(Q^*\).
  3. News & Anticipated Shocks Engine (Beaudry & Portier 2006; Schmitt-Grohé & Uribe 2012): Implements companion state-space augmentation for forward-looking announcements \(\epsilon_t = \eta_t^0 + \sum_{k=1}^H \eta_{t-k}^k\). Preserves Blanchard-Kahn saddle-path determinacy through nilpotent companion transition operators with zero eigenvalues, computes multi-lead impulse responses, and performs automated variance decompositions.

All algorithms are implemented in pure Python under the strict Pyodide four-package contract (numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib), requiring zero external solvers, zero C-extensions, and zero proprietary licenses.
