docs.title: Nonlinear transitions, domains and announcement dates
docs.text:
Puremacro can solve nonlinear deterministic boundary problems supplied as a supported .mod model or as Python equilibrium residuals. The equations are solved jointly across time; a prior perturbation solution is not required. This does not imply that every model has a solution, that the solution is unique, or that Newton iteration will find it from arbitrary starting values. The model must fit the supported timing and equation interfaces, and its boundary conditions, domains and information assumptions remain the caller's economic choices.

Entry point What it computes solve_perfect_foresight One finite deterministic boundary problem. solve_transition The same problem with explicit continuation, domain transforms, equation scales and optional horizon acceptance. solve_announced_path Realized segments of finite plans revised on specified information dates. extended_path Rolling plans with the current innovation realized and future innovations set to zero; this is not nonlinear integration over future risk.

These routines compute trajectories, not a global stochastic policy function. For that separate problem, see global equilibrium methods. The DSGE workflow guide compares the available methods and connects them to the teaching notebooks. For model loading and command support, see the nonlinear model guide and .mod inspection guide.

docs.title: The finite-horizon mathematical problem
docs.text:
Write the model with n endogenous variables and m exogenous inputs as

\[ f(y_{t+1},y_t,y_{t-1},\varepsilon_t;\theta,\bar y)=0, \qquad t=1,\ldots,T. \]

Each call returns n residuals. The unknown vector is \(Y=(y_1^\top,\ldots,y_T^\top)^\top\in\mathbb R^{nT}\). The initial lag and final lead are fixed:

\[ y_0=y_{\mathrm{init}},\qquad y_{T+1}=y_{\mathrm{end}}. \]

The stack contains T interior dates, with n*T equations and unknowns. The solver does not impose an extra equation saying y_T == y_end. A model without leads does not use the final boundary in its dynamic residuals; a model without lags does not use the initial boundary there. Supply a complete vector in declared variable order nevertheless. The equations determine which entries of that vector are economically relevant; the solver does not infer a new state/jump-variable boundary specification for the caller.

The residual callback order is exactly f(lead, current, lag, shock). In a .mod equation, the residual orientation is left-hand side minus right-hand side. The interface shown here has one lead, one current value and one lag; a model needing longer histories must be reduced to this form with explicit auxiliary states or supported parser transformations. This guide does not promise automatic support for every timing construct.

y_end is also the fixed reference \(\bar y\) for STEADY_STATE() within one solve. It is not replaced by the current iterate. A callback that explicitly declares a steady_state argument receives the same reference. An explicit terminal vector is a boundary assignment; it need not be a steady state merely because the argument is named y_end. The low-level alias y_ss has the same role. Bare .mod endval assignments and explicit terminal steady-state solves are distinct operations; see the model guide for command ordering.

docs.title: Array and date conventions
docs.text:
Object Convention y_init, y_end One physical value per endogenous variable. solve_transition also accepts mappings keyed by variable name. shocks Prefer shape (T, m); row 0 is date 1. For one shock, a length-T vector is also accepted. Zero shocks use shape (T, 0). Values are actual exogenous inputs in the equations, with no automatic logarithm, percentage conversion or standard-deviation scaling. initial_path Physical levels, shape (T, n), with no boundary rows. In continuation it initializes the baseline solve; accepted paths warm-start subsequent stages. Returned .path A DataFrame indexed 1,...,T, containing interior dates only. Horizon refinement can return more rows than the original shock path. terminal_error max(abs(y_T - y_end)); a descriptive distance, not an extra equilibrium residual or automatic proof of truncation accuracy.

solve_transition derives T from the supplied shock path. Do not pass periods, n_periods, exogenous_path, y_ss or surprise to this wrapper; they conflict with its explicit experiment. For the lower-level solve_perfect_foresight, pass periods=T explicitly: omitting it does not infer the horizon from shocks. That lower-level API also accepts a legacy T+2-row shock array and drops its first/last rows, or truncates other longer arrays. Exactly T rows avoids that ambiguity.

docs.title: Start from a nonlinear model
docs.text:
read_mod constructs a nonlinear specification without first solving a local approximation. The following small model keeps the timing visible. Run this guide's Python blocks in order in one session; later blocks reuse these imports and the linear example. English and Spanish use identical executable blocks. Plotting in the final block requires Matplotlib.

import numpy as np
from puremacro.dsge import read_mod, solve_perfect_foresight, solve_transition

model = read_mod("""
var x; varexo e;
model; x = 0.25*x(+1) + 0.4*x(-1) + e; end;
initval; x=0; e=0; end;
""")
shocks = np.r_[0.1, np.zeros(39)][:, None]
transition = solve_transition(
    model, y_init=[0.0], y_end=[0.0], shocks=shocks,
    horizon_tolerance=1e-8, compare_periods=20,
    max_periods=160, shock_tail=[0.0], linear_solver="krylov",
)
assert transition.converged, transition.summary()
assert transition.reason == "horizon_accepted"
path = transition.path
print(transition.summary())

The target is a date-1 innovation followed by zeros. The workflow solves that experiment and then checks that doubling the horizon has a sufficiently small effect on the first 20 dates. transition.path returns a copy; always inspect transition.converged before treating it as an accepted target.

docs.title: Direct sparse Newton or matrix-free Newton–Krylov
docs.text:
At a current trajectory define

\[ A_t=\frac{\partial f_t}{\partial y_{t+1}},\quad B_t=\frac{\partial f_t}{\partial y_t},\quad C_t=\frac{\partial f_t}{\partial y_{t-1}}. \]

For fixed boundaries, the stacked Jacobian and its action are

\[ J=\begin{bmatrix} B_1&A_1&&\\ C_2&B_2&A_2&\\ &\ddots&\ddots&\ddots\\ &&C_T&B_T \end{bmatrix},\qquad (Jv)_t=A_tv_{t+1}+B_tv_t+C_tv_{t-1}, \quad v_0=v_{T+1}=0. \]

Both backends seek a Newton direction from \(Jd=-F(Y)\) and use a line search. linear_solver="direct" assembles the sparse stacked matrix and solves the linear system directly. For a parsed model passed directly to solve_perfect_foresight, symbolic incidence limits stored entries to the structural pattern. Callback blocks, including transformed wrapper callbacks, may store a fuller per-date pattern.

linear_solver="krylov" applies the stacked Jacobian through products and uses LGMRES by default; restarted GMRES is an explicit option. It is useful when forming/factoring the full stack is costly, provided the linear iteration has an effective preconditioner. Matrix-free products do not make every storage cost small: per-date blocks and their factors can still be dense. Neither backend is guaranteed to be faster on every model.

method="auto" uses symbolic first derivatives for parsed models, preserving the fixed STEADY_STATE reference. For callbacks it probes complex-step compatibility and otherwise uses central differences. Supply jacobian_fn(lead,current,lag,shock) -> (A,B,C) to control the derivatives, as below. method="analytic" requires a parsed model or that callback. Explicit method="central" and "complex" remain available; complex-step requires the residual implementation to preserve complex perturbations and be suitable for that differentiation. An automatic probe is not a proof of that property.

def equilibrium(lead, current, lag, shock):
    return current - 0.25*lead - 0.4*lag - shock

def date_jacobian(lead, current, lag, shock):
    return np.array([[-0.25]]), np.array([[1.0]]), np.array([[-0.4]])

fixed_problem = dict(
    y_init=[0.0], y_end=[0.0], periods=len(shocks), shocks=shocks,
    variable_names=["x"], tol=1e-10,
)
direct = solve_perfect_foresight(model, **fixed_problem)
krylov = solve_perfect_foresight(
    equilibrium, jacobian_fn=date_jacobian,
    linear_solver="krylov", **fixed_problem,
)
assert direct.converged and krylov.converged
np.testing.assert_allclose(direct.path, krylov.path, atol=1e-9, rtol=0)
assert krylov.solver_diagnostics["jvp_method"] == "analytic"

docs.title: Preconditioners and supported combinations
docs.text:
The default Krylov preconditioner factors a block-tridiagonal system formed from fixed terminal-reference Jacobian blocks. Named preconditioners include steady_block_tridiagonal, steady_splu and current_block_tridiagonal; the last rebuilds from the current trajectory. See the stacked Newton guide for the full operator protocol, block-Jacobi options and linear residual diagnostics.

solve_transition and Krylov extended_path reuse the default steady factorization only if the horizon, block shapes, dtypes and numerical entries match exactly. Changing parameters, reference states or horizon can require a rebuild. reuse_preconditioner=False disables the cache. An explicit krylov_options["preconditioner"], including None, or an explicit time_block setting takes precedence over automatic reuse. The cache count reports its own builds; it does not count every factorization inside a user-supplied operator.

Requested combination Current behavior Direct + ordinary equations, domains/scales or MCP Supported. Direct + terminal policy, including explicit MCP mapping Supported; the terminal chain rule is included. Krylov + ordinary equations and domain/scale transforms Supported. Krylov + MCP bounds or mcp=True Rejected explicitly. Krylov + terminal_policy Rejected explicitly. Direct + any non-None krylov_options Rejected explicitly. terminal_jacobian without terminal_policy Rejected explicitly.

The high-level krylov_options keys are preconditioner, forcing, krylov_method, inner_m, outer_k, krylov_maxiter, side, max_log_move, time_block, progress and checkpoint. Other lower-level engine controls are not automatically accepted here. The chosen Krylov solver never silently switches the nonlinear problem to the direct backend. A block-Thomas preconditioner may use its documented SuperLU factorization fallback when a pivot is unsuitable; that is a preconditioner construction choice, not a switch of nonlinear solver.

docs.title: Continuation, baseline and solve budget
docs.text:
Continuation solves a family of explicitly stated experiments. For baseline inputs \((E^0,b^0,\theta^0)\) and target inputs \((E^1,b^1,\theta^1)\),

\[ E^\lambda=(1-\lambda)E^0+\lambda E^1,\qquad b^\lambda=(1-\lambda)b^0+\lambda b^1,\qquad \theta^\lambda=(1-\lambda)\theta^0+\lambda\theta^1. \]

The implementation copies endpoint values exactly at fractions zero and one. The initial lag y_init stays fixed. The terminal boundary and its STEADY_STATE reference follow b at each stage. A supplied terminal policy is kept as supplied; it is not silently recalibrated when parameters change.

The default baseline is zero shocks and baseline_end=y_init. This is a computational baseline, not an assertion that the initial state is a steady state. Supply baseline_shocks with the target path's shape and baseline_end when a different baseline is economically intended. The baseline itself must solve successfully. continuation=False requests one target solve directly.

For a NonlinearModel, baseline_params varies only the named, already calibrated parameters; others retain their target values. The source model's parameter dictionary is not mutated. No intermediate steady states are solved automatically. Supported parameter-dependent MCP tag bounds are resolved at each stage's calibration. User-supplied residual/derivative/terminal callbacks must remain consistent with the experiment they represent.

The starting increment is initial_step=0.25. A failed stage halves the increment; an accepted stage multiplies it by 1.5, capped at the remaining distance to one. min_step=1/1024 bounds reductions. max_iter applies to each numerical solve, whereas max_solves=40 counts the baseline, accepted and failed continuation attempts, and horizon refinements together. These are iteration and solve-count budgets, not wall-clock deadlines.

calibrated = read_mod("""
var x; parameters theta; theta=999;
model; x^3 = 1 + theta; end;
initval; x=1; end;
""")
parameter_path = solve_transition(
    calibrated, y_init=[1.0], y_end=[1.0], shocks=np.zeros((3, 0)),
    baseline_params={"theta": 0.0}, max_iter=4, max_solves=40, tol=1e-9,
)
assert parameter_path.converged, parameter_path.summary()
np.testing.assert_allclose(parameter_path.path["x"], 10.0, atol=1e-9)
assert parameter_path.continuation_history[-1]["fraction"] == 1.0
assert calibrated.parameter_values["theta"] == 999.0

limited = solve_transition(
    model, y_init=[0.0], y_end=[0.0], shocks=shocks, max_solves=1,
)
assert not limited.converged
assert limited.reason == "solve_budget_exhausted"

The cubic example has no exogenous variables, hence the (3, 0) shock array. Its exact target is x=10. The last check demonstrates that a solved baseline alone is never reported as target success. Continuation can help reach a root; it does not remove singularities, guarantee a branch is unique, or ensure that all possible baselines lead to the same target solution.

docs.title: Economic domains and residual scales
docs.text:
variable_bounds specifies open domains. With positive variable_scale[j]=s_j, the solver uses monotone coordinates:

Domain for y_j Physical value decoded from z_j Unbounded \(y_j=s_jz_j\) \(y_j>\ell_j\) \(y_j=\ell_j+\exp(s_jz_j)\) \(y_j<u_j\) \(y_j=u_j-\exp(-s_jz_j)\) \(\ell_j<y_j<u_j\) \(y_j=\ell_j+(u_j-\ell_j)/(1+\exp(-s_jz_j))\)

Boundary vectors, initial guesses and terminal-policy outputs must be strictly inside these domains. During transformed residual evaluations, overflowing or numerically saturated candidates are rejected before the equilibrium callback; no economic policy is clipped to a feasible value. This protects logarithms and powers defined only in the declared domain, but it cannot cure every ill-conditioned root.

equation_scale[i]=q_i>0 replaces row f_i by f_i/q_i. For an ordinary transition, acceptance requires both backend convergence and

\[ \max_{t,i}\left|f_i(y_{t+1},y_t,y_{t-1},\varepsilon_t)/q_i\right| \leq\texttt{tol}. \]

That explicit row-scaled check is stricter than merely trusting a backend flag whose residual test may also use a Jacobian magnitude scale. It does not use variable_scale as a substitute for economically meaningful equation units. Scales can be positive scalars, vectors or full mappings. A mapping follows residual row order through declared variable names; use a vector when variable names would obscure a different equation order.

def log_equation(lead, current, lag, shock):
    return 1000.0 * (np.log(current) - shock)

positive = solve_transition(
    log_equation, y_init=[1.0], y_end=[1.0],
    shocks=np.full(10, -3.0), variable_names=["c"],
    variable_bounds={"c": (0.0, None)},
    equation_scale=[1000.0], variable_scale=[2.0], tol=1e-9,
)
assert positive.converged, positive.summary()
np.testing.assert_allclose(positive.path["c"], np.exp(-3.0), rtol=1e-8)
assert positive.scaled_residual_norm <= 1e-9
physical_error = np.max(np.abs(1000.0*(np.log(positive.path["c"]) + 3.0)))
np.testing.assert_allclose(positive.solution.residual_norm, physical_error, atol=1e-12)

For an ordinary PerfectForesightResult inside transition.solution, residual_norm and initial_residual_norm retain original equation units; transition.scaled_residual_norm reports the row-scaled acceptance measure. For MCPResult, residuals and complementarity diagnostics remain in the transformed/scaled solver units, even though the returned path is decoded to physical levels. Check physical feasibility and complementarity independently when their economic tolerances matter.

An open domain cannot represent a constraint that should bind. Use MCP for that condition. If a variable has both a domain and a complementarity bound, the latter must lie strictly within its domain to have a finite transformed coordinate; a zero lower domain and a binding zero lower bound are incompatible.

docs.title: Horizon acceptance and permanent shock tails
docs.text:
A small stacked residual verifies a finite boundary problem. It does not establish that the chosen boundary adequately approximates an infinite horizon. With horizon_tolerance, the workflow first solves the exact target and then sets \(T'=\min(2T,\texttt{max_periods})\). It preserves the initial condition, shock prefix, target calibration and terminal policy/reference, extends the shock path explicitly, and warm-starts the longer solve.

For P=compare_periods, the acceptance statistic is

\[ \Delta_{T,T'}=\max_{1\leq t\leq P}\max_j \left|y^{T'}_{t,j}-y^T_{t,j}\right|. \]

This is an absolute difference in physical variable units. It is not divided by equation_scale or variable_scale. Choose its tolerance with the reported variables' units in mind. compare_periods cannot exceed the initial horizon; max_periods must exceed it. Refinement stops after the first accepted comparison, at the horizon cap, after a failed extended solve, or at the shared solve budget. The comparison establishes only the stated common-window check.

An explicit shock_tail is mandatory. It may be a scalar/row broadcastable to the extra dates, or a callable shock_tail(old_T, new_T) returning the extension. The arguments are horizon lengths, not one-based shock dates. No silent permanent-versus-transitory interpretation is imposed.

For example, if log productivity satisfies \(a_t=\rho a_{t-1}+u_t\), changing y_end alone does not hold productivity at a_star. From a_0=0, a permanent level a_star beginning at date 1 requires u_1=a_star, then u_t=(1-rho)*a_star. The same recurring innovation must be used in a refined tail:

productivity = read_mod("""
var a; varexo innovation; parameters rho; rho=0.9;
model; a = rho*a(-1) + innovation; end;
initval; a=0; innovation=0; end;
""")
rho, target_a, initial_horizon = 0.9, 0.2, 12
permanent_innovations = np.full((initial_horizon, 1), (1.0-rho)*target_a)
permanent_innovations[0, 0] = target_a
permanent = solve_transition(
    productivity, y_init=[0.0], y_end=[target_a],
    shocks=permanent_innovations, continuation=False,
    horizon_tolerance=1e-10, compare_periods=12, max_periods=48,
    shock_tail=[(1.0-rho)*target_a],
)
assert permanent.converged, permanent.summary()
np.testing.assert_allclose(permanent.path["a"], target_a, atol=1e-10)
assert permanent.horizon_history[-1]["accepted"]

horizon_history records old/new horizons, the comparison window, the maximum difference, tolerance and acceptance. terminal_error can remain positive in a valid finite solution and is not used as a replacement for this comparison.

docs.title: Announcements, surprises and belief revisions
docs.text:
In one perfect-foresight solve, the entire supplied shock path is known at the start. A nonzero shock at date 8 can therefore alter dates 1–7 through forward equations. A surprise revealed only at date 8 is a different information experiment, even if the realized exogenous array eventually looks the same.

ShockAnnouncement(date, shocks, y_end=None) records a new full-calendar belief path. The first announcement must occur at date 1; later dates must strictly increase within the same calendar. Every array has the same shape. Revisions may change current/future shocks and optionally the terminal boundary/reference, but all rows before the announcement date must equal previously realized shocks. If y_end is omitted, the previously announced boundary persists.

from puremacro.dsge import ShockAnnouncement, solve_announced_path

news = np.zeros((40, 1))
news[7, 0] = 0.1
anticipated = solve_announced_path(
    model, [ShockAnnouncement(1, news)], y_init=[0.0], y_end=[0.0],
)
surprise = solve_announced_path(
    model, [ShockAnnouncement(1, np.zeros_like(news)), ShockAnnouncement(8, news)],
    y_init=[0.0], y_end=[0.0],
)
assert anticipated.converged and surprise.converged
assert np.max(np.abs(anticipated.path.iloc[:7].to_numpy())) > 1e-4
np.testing.assert_allclose(surprise.path.iloc[:7], 0.0, atol=1e-12)
assert surprise.solver_diagnostics["completed_periods"] == 40

At announcement date d, the planner solves dates d,...,T, starting with the actual state from d-1, and implements only the segment before the next announcement. Future revisions are never revealed early. The remaining calendar shrinks; it is not silently replaced by a constant rolling horizon. A failed plan stops implementation and returns converged=False, the completed prefix, and per-announcement diagnostics. There is no single ex ante perfect-foresight audit context for the spliced realization.

solve_announced_path accepts the low-level perfect-foresight solver options, not the continuation/domain/horizon wrapper options. surprise, periods, n_periods, exogenous_path, y_ss and a single initial_path conflict with its dated plans and are rejected explicitly. Automatic horizon acceptance for this whole information calendar is not currently provided; compare explicitly constructed longer calendars if needed.

For repeated one-period surprises, simulate_surprise_shocks instead solves a fixed rolling horizon, realizes its first date, and repeats. Its default future shock baseline is zero. solve_perfect_foresight(..., surprise=True) dispatches to that rolling experiment. extended_path can supply or draw the current innovation and likewise sets future innovations to zero. These future paths are a certainty-equivalent approximation; nonlinear expectations are not obtained merely by substituting a mean innovation into nonlinear equations.

docs.title: Complementarity: variables, equation rows and signs
docs.text:
For a lower bound on variable j, explicit mapping (i,s) means

\[ y_{t,j}-\ell_j\geq0,\qquad s f_{t,i}\geq0,\qquad (y_{t,j}-\ell_j)s f_{t,i}=0,\qquad s\in\{-1,+1\}. \]

For an upper bound, the conditions use u_j-y_j >= 0 and s*f_i <= 0. With two finite bounds, s*f_i is nonnegative at the lower bound, zero in the interior and nonpositive at the upper bound. Other equation rows remain equalities. This is why an active constraint's original equality residual need not be zero.

mcp_bounds maps variable names or zero-based variable indices to (lower, upper); use None for an absent bound. mcp_equations maps those same keys to a zero-based residual row or (row, sign). An integer row alone means sign +1. An explicit mapping must cover exactly the bounded variables, with distinct equation rows. Equation order need not match variable order.

The supported source tag [mcp='r > lower'] means a lower bound on r, paired with the equation carrying the tag and its existing left-minus-right sign. Tags admit <, <=, > and >= with one variable and a finite bound expression depending only on calibrated parameters. The notation represents a closed MCP bound, not an open domain. Dynamic bounds, duplicate variable tags and arbitrary inequalities are not a general supported constraint language; two-sided bounds use the Python API.

bounded_model = read_mod("""
var x r; varexo e; parameters lower; lower=0;
model;
[mcp='r > lower'] r=e;
x=1-3*r;
end;
initval; x=1; r=0; e=0; end;
""")
bounded = solve_transition(
    bounded_model, y_init=[1.0, 0.0], y_end=[1.0, 0.0],
    shocks=-np.ones((5, 1)), mcp=True,
)
assert bounded.converged, bounded.summary()
np.testing.assert_allclose(bounded.path["r"], 0.0, atol=1e-8)

def reversed_residual(lead, current, lag, shock):
    x, r = current
    return np.array([shock[0]-r, x+3.0*r-1.0])

explicit = solve_perfect_foresight(
    reversed_residual, y_init=[1.0, 0.0], y_end=[1.0, 0.0],
    periods=5, shocks=-np.ones((5, 1)), variable_names=["x", "r"],
    mcp_bounds={"r": (0.0, None)}, mcp_equations={"r": (0, -1)},
)
assert explicit.converged
np.testing.assert_allclose(explicit.path, bounded.path, atol=1e-8)
gap = bounded.path["r"].to_numpy()
margin = gap + 1.0
assert np.min(gap) >= -1e-8 and np.min(margin) >= -1e-8
assert np.max(np.abs(np.hypot(gap, margin)-gap-margin)) < 1e-8

Here variable r is second, but its complementary equation is first. The tag implies mcp_equations={"r": (0, 1)}; the callback deliberately reverses that equation and therefore uses (0, -1). The final assertions check physical nonnegative gaps and a Fischer–Burmeister residual independently of the solver's flag.

Use mcp=True to activate supported model tags. Explicit nonempty bounds also select the native MCP solver. Without explicit mappings/tags, the older Python bound interface retains its loading-based row/sign heuristic; supplying the mapping is clearer when equations have economic sign restrictions. This is the native semismooth solver and does not claim equivalence to every Dynare complementarity algorithm or option. MCP remains direct-only.

docs.title: Terminal policies and the final Jacobian block
docs.text:
If a reliable terminal map g is available, terminal_policy(last_state) sets \(y_{T+1}=g(y_T)\). It must return a finite vector in the same variable order. y_end remains the fixed STEADY_STATE reference. The last diagonal block becomes

\[ \frac{d f_T}{d y_T}=B_T+A_T Dg(y_T). \]

Provide terminal_jacobian(last_state) as a square matrix, or let the direct solver differentiate the map centrally. With domains/scales, solve_transition accepts these callbacks in physical coordinates and composes their chain rule with the coordinate transformation.

For the linear example, a stable tail x_t=r^t*x_0 satisfies 0.25*r**2-r+0.4=0. Using its smaller root gives an exact tail for this specific shock-free linear model:

stable_root = (1.0 - np.sqrt(1.0 - 4.0*0.25*0.4)) / (2.0*0.25)
terminal = solve_perfect_foresight(
    model, y_init=[1.0], y_end=[0.0], periods=5, shocks=np.zeros((5, 1)),
    terminal_policy=lambda last: stable_root * last,
    terminal_jacobian=lambda last: np.array([[stable_root]]), tol=1e-10,
)
assert terminal.converged
np.testing.assert_allclose(terminal.path["x"], stable_root**np.arange(1, 6), atol=1e-10)

from puremacro.validation import audit_result
terminal_audit = audit_result(terminal, checks=["equations"])
assert np.max(np.abs(terminal_audit.maps["path_equations"])) < 1e-9

A local linear terminal map in a nonlinear model is an approximation whose adequacy still needs a horizon or economic check. Krylov rejects terminal policies. Ordinary retained path audits replay the policy and preserve the fixed reference; they also compare its original terminal input/output to detect changed callable state. Keep callbacks unchanged after solving. That replay is not a mathematical identity check over the whole policy domain. MCP paths need their own physical complementarity checks, as above.

docs.title: Diagnostics, failed runs and reporting
docs.text:
TransitionResult.converged requires the exact target and every requested horizon check. A retained solution is the last available numerical result; on failure it may be intermediate or failed. path is empty if no numerical result was retained. A converged inner solution alone does not establish wrapper success.

reason Interpretation target_solved Exact target accepted; no horizon check was requested. horizon_accepted Exact target and a requested common-window horizon comparison passed. baseline_failed The specified baseline did not pass numerical acceptance. target_failed A direct target attempt with continuation=False failed. continuation_step_exhausted Further reductions would violate min_step. solve_budget_exhausted The shared solve-count budget ended before completing all requested work. horizon_solve_failed An extended target problem failed numerically. horizon_budget_exhausted The maximum horizon was reached without the requested agreement.

continuation_history records each attempt's fraction, periods, parameters and acceptance. Completed numerical attempts include residuals, iterations and warnings; numerical exceptions retain an error record instead. Input contract errors are raised, rather than relabeled as successful partial results. solves, scaled_residual_norm and preconditioner_builds summarize the retained workflow; inspect the histories to distinguish a difficult equation solve from an inadequate horizon.

For ordinary solutions, solution.solver_diagnostics includes derivative/backend details and the wrapper's scales and original residual norm. Krylov's linear_history reports the returned direction's true_linear_residual, requested linear tolerance, iteration status, step and backtracking information. A positive inner iteration status is not itself nonlinear convergence; inspect the final result and residuals. extended_path.solver_diagnostics additionally records rolling solves and preconditioner builds/reuses.

Tables and plots expose the retained candidate; they do not override its status. to_frame() and to_dataframe() return copies. Markdown, LaTeX and Typst use the shared puremacro.reports formatting/escaping layer. plot(ax=..., show=False) respects caller axes and does not display a window by default. If no numerical solution was retained, plotting raises a clear error.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

assert transition.converged, transition.summary()
continuation_table = pd.DataFrame(transition.continuation_history)
horizon_table = pd.DataFrame(transition.horizon_history)
assert continuation_table.iloc[-1]["fraction"] == 1.0
assert bool(horizon_table.iloc[-1]["accepted"])
exported = transition.to_frame()
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(exported, transition.to_dataframe())
print(transition.to_markdown(head=3, digits=6))
assert r"\begin{tabular}" in transition.to_latex(head=3)
assert "#table(" in transition.to_typst(head=3)
figure, axes = plt.subplots()
assert transition.plot(ax=axes, show=False) is figure
plt.close(figure)

equation_audit = audit_result(transition.solution, checks=["equations"])
assert np.max(np.abs(equation_audit.maps["path_equations"])) < 1e-8

The ordinary equation audit checks the saved finite experiment independently of the convergence flag. Its small residual does not certify uniqueness, infinite-horizon accuracy or stochastic optimality. The numerical tests in tests/test_dsge_transition_workflows.py cover exact linear/stable-root paths, derivative agreement, continuation budgets and exact endpoints, domains/scales, information dates, MCP signs, terminal audits, preconditioner reuse and result exports. They establish those contracts on the tested cases, not universal convergence for arbitrary models.

docs.title: DSGE likelihood scores, HMC/NUTS and sequence-space HANK
docs.text: This guide explains capabilities introduced in the 3.x series and their current scope. Numerical parity is specific to the models, options and quantities checked in the validation status. The numerical core uses NumPy, SciPy, pandas and Matplotlib; browser execution has the limits described in the runtime guide.

docs.title: Capabilities and scope
docs.text:
Capability Supported workflow What to check Likelihood gradients Analytic Kalman score recursion and implicit decision-rule sensitivities for structural parameters in the supported first-order stationary likelihood. Structural derivative inputs may use finite differences. Compare the score with numerical derivatives of the same likelihood. Bayesian sampling Pure-Python HMC/NUTS with step-size and diagonal mass adaptation. Check chain mixing, divergences and effective sample sizes; speed depends on the model and posterior. HANK bridge Household blocks in .mod files connected through sequence-space Jacobians. Check the household backend and linear/nonlinear transition scope in the HANK guide.

log_posterior_and_gradient covers structural parameters declared by the model. Its analytic Kalman recursion does not imply an entirely symbolic parameter-to-likelihood derivative: structural Jacobian inputs may be finite-differenced. Noise scales, correlations, measurement equations, presamples and diffuse initialization require their own supported likelihood route. The estimation guide distinguishes analytic, user-supplied and numerical gradients, including fallback behavior.

OccBin solves piecewise-linear constrained paths. The development solve_pruned_occbin supports linear OccBin (including anticipated shocks) and slack second-order paths with one initial innovation; nonlinear binding episodes and nonlinear anticipated innovations are rejected. See the higher-order guide for these limits.

docs.title: Pillar 1: Kalman Likelihood Scores and Structural Sensitivities (\(\nabla_\theta \ln L\))
1.1 Motivation & Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
Estimating DSGE models via gradient-based optimizers (such as L-BFGS-B, SQP) or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo requires the gradient of the log-posterior: $\( abla_ heta \ln p( heta \mid Y) = abla_ heta \ln L(Y \mid heta) + abla_ heta \ln p( heta)\)$

One way to approximate the likelihood derivative is a central difference: $\( rac{\partial \ln L}{\partial heta_j} \approx rac{\ln L( heta + h e_j) - \ln L( heta - h e_j)}{2h}\)$

This requires two likelihood evaluations per parameter and a step-size choice. The score recursion differentiates the Kalman updates in a single forward sweep given state-space sensitivities. In the current implementation, those sensitivities can themselves contain finite-difference structural inputs; accuracy still needs an independent derivative check.

Consider a rational-expectations structural DSGE system around its deterministic steady state: $\(\mathbb{E}_t \left[ f(y_{t+1}, y_t, y_{t-1}, u_t; heta) ight] = 0\)$

Its first-order perturbation satisfies: $\(A_+( heta) y_{t+1} + A_0( heta) y_t + A_-( heta) y_{t-1} + B_u( heta) u_t = 0\)$

The unique stable recursive equilibrium law of motion is given by: $\(y_t = G( heta) y_{t-1} + N( heta) u_t\)$ where the state transition matrix \(G( heta)\) satisfies the quadratic matrix equation: $\(\mathcal{F}(G; heta) \equiv A_+( heta) G( heta)^2 + A_0( heta) G( heta) + A_-( heta) = 0\)$ and the innovation loading matrix \(N( heta)\) satisfies: $\((A_0( heta) + A_+( heta) G( heta)) N( heta) + B_u( heta) = 0\)$

docs.title: 1.2 The Generalized Sylvester Matrix Equation
docs.text:
Differentiating \(\mathcal{F}(G; \theta) = 0\) with respect to a scalar structural parameter \(\theta_j\) yields: $\((A_0 + A_+ G) \frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta_j} + A_+ \frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta_j} G = - \left( \frac{\partial A_+}{\partial \theta_j} G^2 + \frac{\partial A_0}{\partial \theta_j} G + \frac{\partial A_-}{\partial \theta_j} \right)\)$

This is a generalized Sylvester matrix equation of the canonical form: $\(\hat{A} X + B X C = D_j\)$ where: - \(\hat{A} = A_0 + A_+ G \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) - \(B = A_+ \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) - \(C = G \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) - \(D_j = - \left( \frac{\partial A_+}{\partial \theta_j} G^2 + \frac{\partial A_0}{\partial \theta_j} G + \frac{\partial A_-}{\partial \theta_j} \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\)

Because Blanchard-Kahn stability guarantees that all eigenvalues of \(C = G\) lie strictly inside the open unit circle, this generalized Sylvester system has a unique solution \(X = \frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta_j}\) for each parameter \(\theta_j\).

docs.title: Schur Triangular Back-Substitution Algorithm
docs.text:
Rather than solving \(K\) separate \(N^2 \times N^2\) Kronecker systems, puremacro computes the complex Schur decomposition of \(C\) once: $\(C = U_c T_c U_c^H\)$ where \(T_c\) is upper triangular and \(U_c\) is unitary.

Transforming \(\tilde{X} = X U_c\) and \(\tilde{D}_j = D_j U_c\), the Sylvester equation transforms to: $\(\hat{A} \tilde{X} + B \tilde{X} T_c = \tilde{D}_j\)$

Because \(T_c\) is upper triangular, column \(k\) of \(\tilde{X}\) decouples into: $\(\left( \hat{A} + (T_c)_{k, k} B \right) \tilde{X}_{:, k} = \tilde{D}_{:, k} - B \sum_{m < k} \tilde{X}_{:, m} (T_c)_{m, k}\)$

Each column \(k \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}\) is solved by back-substitution. The matrix \((\hat{A} + (T_c)_{k,k} B)\) is LU-factored once per column and reused across all \(K\) parameters simultaneously. The physical solution is recovered via \(X = \operatorname{Re}(\tilde{X} U_c^H)\).

Once \(\frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta_j}\) is known, differentiating \((A_0 + A_+ G) N + B_u = 0\) yields the exact innovation sensitivity: $\(\frac{\partial N}{\partial \theta_j} = - (A_0 + A_+ G)^{-1} \left[ \left(\frac{\partial A_0}{\partial \theta_j} + \frac{\partial A_+}{\partial \theta_j} G + A_+ \frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta_j}\right) N + \frac{\partial B_u}{\partial \theta_j} \right]\)$

docs.title: 1.3 State-Space Sensitivities & Lyapunov Initialization
docs.text:
The structural decision rules map directly into the standard linear state-space system: $\(\alpha_{t+1} = T(\theta) \alpha_t + c(\theta) + R(\theta) \eta_{t+1}, \quad \eta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q(\theta))\)$ $\(y_t = Z(\theta) \alpha_t + d(\theta) + \epsilon_t, \quad \epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, H(\theta))\)$

The unconditional stationary covariance \(P_0(\theta)\) satisfies the discrete Lyapunov equation: $\(P_0 = T P_0 T^\top + R Q R^\top\)$

Differentiating with respect to \(\theta_j\) yields the discrete Lyapunov equation for \(\frac{\partial P_0}{\partial \theta_j}\): $\(\frac{\partial P_0}{\partial \theta_j} - T \frac{\partial P_0}{\partial \theta_j} T^\top = \frac{\partial T}{\partial \theta_j} P_0 T^\top + T P_0 \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial \theta_j}\right)^\top + \frac{\partial (R Q R^\top)}{\partial \theta_j}\)$ which puremacro solves directly via scipy.linalg.solve_discrete_lyapunov.

docs.title: 1.4 Single-Pass Forward Kalman Score Recursion
docs.text:
Given observed data \(y_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n_y}\), the forecast errors \(v_t = y_t - Z a_{t|t-1} - d\) and error covariances \(F_t = Z P_{t|t-1} Z^\top + H\) determine the Gaussian log-likelihood: $\(\ln L(Y \mid \theta) = -\frac{T_{obs} n_y \ln(2\pi)}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=1}^{T_{obs}} \left( \ln |F_t| + v_t^\top F_t^{-1} v_t \right)\)$

Given the state-space sensitivities, the score vector \(\nabla_\theta \ln L\) is computed in a single forward sweep: $\(\frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \theta_j} = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=1}^{T_{obs}} \left[ \operatorname{tr}\left( F_t^{-1} \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial \theta_j} \right) + 2 v_t^\top F_t^{-1} \frac{\partial v_t}{\partial \theta_j} - (F_t^{-1} v_t)^\top \frac{\partial F_t}{\partial \theta_j} (F_t^{-1} v_t) \right]\)$

During each forward step \(t\), state sensitivities \(\frac{\partial a_{t|t-1}}{\partial \theta_j}\) and covariance sensitivities \(\frac{\partial P_{t|t-1}}{\partial \theta_j}\) are updated alongside the standard Kalman equations: $\(\frac{\partial v_t}{\partial \theta_j} = -\frac{\partial Z}{\partial \theta_j} a_{t|t-1} - Z \frac{\partial a_{t|t-1}}{\partial \theta_j} - \frac{\partial d}{\partial \theta_j}\)$ $\(\frac{\partial F_t}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \theta_j} P_{t|t-1} Z^\top + Z \frac{\partial P_{t|t-1}}{\partial \theta_j} Z^\top + Z P_{t|t-1} \left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial \theta_j}\right)^\top + \frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta_j}\)$

With Kalman gain \(K_t = T P_{t|t-1} Z^\top F_t^{-1}\) and closed-loop transition \(L_t = T - K_t Z\), the Joseph-stabilized covariance sensitivity is propagated forward: $\(\frac{\partial P_{t+1|t}}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{\partial L_t}{\partial \theta_j} P_{t|t-1} L_t^\top + L_t \frac{\partial P_{t|t-1}}{\partial \theta_j} L_t^\top + L_t P_{t|t-1} \left(\frac{\partial L_t}{\partial \theta_j}\right)^\top + \frac{\partial K_t}{\partial \theta_j} H K_t^\top + K_t \frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta_j} K_t^\top + K_t H \left(\frac{\partial K_t}{\partial \theta_j}\right)^\top + \frac{\partial (R Q R^\top)}{\partial \theta_j}\)$

This recurrence maintains numerical positive semi-definiteness and symmetry without requiring gradient tape storage.

docs.title: 1.5 Python Code Example: Evaluating Analytic Likelihood Gradients
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from puremacro.dsge import load_mod
from puremacro.dsge.observation import make_state_space_from_varobs
from puremacro.dsge._gradients import (
    build_state_space_sensitivities,
    kalman_score,
    ScoreDiagnosticsResult,
)

MOD_CODE = """
var y c a;
varexo e_a;
parameters beta sigma rho_a;
beta = 0.99;
sigma = 1.0;
rho_a = 0.8;

model;
  c = c(+1) - (1/sigma)*y;
  y = c + a;
  a = rho_a * a(-1) + e_a;
end;

steady_state_model;
  y = 0; c = 0; a = 0;
end;

shocks;
  var e_a; stderr 0.2;
end;

varobs y;
"""

# 1. Parse and solve model
model = load_mod(MOD_CODE)
varobs = ["y"]
param_names = ["sigma", "rho_a"]

# 2. Simulate observed series
rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
y_sim = rng.normal(0, 0.5, size=(100, 1))

# 3. Construct state space and parameter sensitivities
ssm = make_state_space_from_varobs(model, varobs)
sens = build_state_space_sensitivities(model, varobs, param_names)

# 4. Evaluate exact log-likelihood and score in a single forward pass
loglik, score = kalman_score(y_sim, ssm, sens)

# 5. Format and inspect score diagnostics
res = ScoreDiagnosticsResult(
    loglik=loglik,
    gradient=score,
    param_names=tuple(param_names),
    elapsed_sec=0.002,
)

print(f"Exact Log-Likelihood: {res.loglik:.4f}")
print(res.to_markdown())

docs.title: 2.1 The No-U-Turn Sampler Algorithm
docs.text:
Standard Random-Walk Metropolis-Hastings (RWMH) explores high-dimensional posteriors via Brownian diffusion: the distance traversed scales as \(\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})\), resulting in poor exploration, strong autocorrelations, and low Effective Sample Sizes (\(ESS < 2\%\)).

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) transforms posterior sampling into Hamiltonian mechanics. It augments the parameter state \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^K\) with continuous momentum vectors \(p \sim \mathcal{N}(0, M)\), defining total Hamiltonian energy: $\(H(\theta, p) = V(\theta) + K(p) = - \ln p(\theta \mid Y) + \frac{1}{2} p^\top M^{-1} p\)$ where \(M^{-1}\) is a positive-definite inverse mass matrix.

The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) (Hoffman & Gelman 2014; Betancourt 2017) eliminates the requirement to hand-tune the trajectory length \(L\) by recursively building binary leapfrog trees and stopping as soon as the trajectory begins to fold back on itself.

docs.title: 2.2 Symplectic Leapfrog Integrator
docs.text:
Phase space trajectories \((\theta(t), p(t))\) are integrated using the velocity Verlet symplectic scheme: $\(\tilde{p} = p + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \nabla_\theta \ln p(\theta \mid Y)\)$ $\(\theta' = \theta + \epsilon M^{-1} \tilde{p}\)$ $\(p' = \tilde{p} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \nabla_\theta \ln p(\theta' \mid Y)\)$

Symplectic leapfrog integration exactly preserves phase space volume (Liouville's theorem) and exhibits bounded energy fluctuations \(\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)\) without secular energy drift.

docs.title: 2.3 Generalized U-Turn Condition & Divergence Detection
docs.text:
At recursion depth \(j\), the trajectory doubles forward (\(v = +1\)) or backward (\(v = -1\)) with equal probability. Let \(\theta^-\) and \(\theta^+\) denote the extreme left and right parameter coordinates of the sub-tree, and \(p^-, p^+\) denote the momenta at those endpoints.

The recursive tree expansion stops immediately when either endpoint turns back towards the opposite end (Betancourt 2017): $\(( \theta^+ - \theta^- )^\top M^{-1} p^+ < 0 \quad \text{or} \quad ( \theta^+ - \theta^- )^\top M^{-1} p^- < 0\)$

Furthermore, if numerical error causes Hamiltonian divergence: $\(H(\theta', p') - H(\theta, p) > \Delta_{max} \quad (\Delta_{max} = 1000)\)$ the trajectory is immediately flagged as a divergence, signaling regions of extreme posterior curvature or boundary violations.

docs.title: 2.4 Hoffman-Gelman Dual Averaging Step-Size Adaptation
docs.text: During the warmup phase, step size \(\epsilon\) is adapted to attain a target acceptance probability \(\delta^* = 0.80\) using Nesterov dual averaging: $\(H_m = \left( 1 - \frac{1}{m + t_0} \right) H_{m-1} + \frac{1}{m + t_0} (\delta^* - \alpha_m)\)$ $\(\ln \epsilon_{m+1} = \mu - \frac{\sqrt{m}}{\gamma} H_m, \quad \ln \bar{\epsilon}_{m+1} = m^{-\kappa} \ln \epsilon_{m+1} + (1 - m^{-\kappa}) \ln \bar{\epsilon}_m\)$ with default hyperparameters \(\gamma = 0.05\), \(t_0 = 10.0\), \(\kappa = 0.75\), and \(\mu = \ln(10 \epsilon_0)\).

docs.title: 2.5 Welford Online Covariance Adaptation with Stan Shrinkage
docs.text:
Parameter scales and correlations vary widely in DSGE estimation (e.g., standard deviation of shocks vs. habit persistence). puremacro implements online sample variance adaptation using Welford's algorithm: $\(\bar{\theta}_m = \bar{\theta}_{m-1} + \frac{\theta_m - \bar{\theta}_{m-1}}{m}, \quad M_2^{(m)} = M_2^{(m-1)} + (\theta_m - \bar{\theta}_{m-1})(\theta_m - \bar{\theta}_m)\)$

To ensure stability, puremacro organizes warmup into Stan-style staged windows: 1. Initial Fast Buffer (75 draws): Step size adapts while mass matrix remains fixed. 2. Doubling Slow Windows (25, 50, 100, 200 draws): Diagonal mass matrix \(M^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(\widehat{\sigma}^2_1, \dots, \widehat{\sigma}^2_K)\) updates at the end of each window, regularized with prior shrinkage: $\(\widehat{\Sigma}_{reg} = w S + (1 - w) \Sigma_{prior}, \quad w = \frac{m}{m + 5}\)$ 3. Final Fast Buffer (50 draws): Step size settles while metric is frozen.

docs.title: 2.6 Comprehensive MCMC Diagnostics
docs.text: Every NUTS run produces an audited set of diagnostics: - Split-\(\hat{R}\) (Gelman-Rubin on half-chains, not rank-normalized): Splits each chain in half to detect both within-chain non-stationarity and between-chain lack of mixing; values \(< 1.05\) indicate convergence. - Bulk Effective Sample Size (\(ESS_{bulk}\)): Measures estimation accuracy for posterior means and medians via Geyer's initial monotone sequence (single-chain ESS summed over chains; not rank-normalized, so it is not the multi-chain bulk ESS of Vehtari, Gelman, Simpson, Carpenter and Bürkner 2021, Bayesian Analysis 16(2)). - Tail Effective Sample Size (\(ESS_{tail}\)): Evaluates sampling quality in the tails (5% and 95% quantiles). - Energy Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information (\(E\text{-}BFMI\)): $\(E\text{-}BFMI = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^N (E_t - E_{t-1})^2}{(N-1) \operatorname{Var}(E)}\)$ Values \(< 0.3\) warn of poor momentum energy exploration.

docs.title: 2.7 Python Code Example: DSGE Estimation via NUTS
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from puremacro.dsge import load_mod

MOD_CODE = """
var y c a;
varexo e_a;
parameters beta sigma rho_a;
beta = 0.99;
sigma = 1.0;
rho_a = 0.8;

model;
  c = c(+1) - (1/sigma)*y;
  y = c + a;
  a = rho_a * a(-1) + e_a;
end;

steady_state_model;
  y = 0; c = 0; a = 0;
end;

varobs y;
estimated_params;
  sigma, gamma_pdf, 1.0, 0.25;
  rho_a, beta_pdf, 0.7, 0.15;
end;
"""

# 1. Load DSGE model
model = load_mod(MOD_CODE)

# 2. Generate sample data
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
data = pd.DataFrame({"y": rng.normal(0, 0.5, size=80)})

# 3. Estimate this first-order model using pure-Python NUTS
res = model.estimate(
    data=data,
    method="nuts",
    n_draws=300,
    n_chains=2,
    burn_in=150,
    seed=42,
)

# 4. Posterior summary and convergence diagnostics
print(res.summary())
print("Divergences:", res.diagnostics["n_divergences"])
print("Step Sizes:", res.diagnostics["step_sizes"])

# 5. Energy diagnostics & figure exports
stats, fig, ax = res.energy_diagnostics()
print(f"Mean E-BFMI: {stats['mean_ebfmi']:.3f} (Passed: {stats['passed']})")

# Export to clean Markdown table
print(res.to_markdown())

docs.title: Pillar 3: HANK Sequence-Space Bridge in .mod Files
3.1 The Representative-Agent Wall & Sequence Space
docs.text:
Standard DSGE models assume a representative household whose Euler equation pins down aggregate consumption. Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) models replace this fictional agent with a continuum of households facing uninsurable idiosyncratic income risk and borrowing constraints.

In state-space representations, solving HANK models requires carrying the infinite-dimensional wealth distribution \(D_t(a, s)\) as a state variable, causing the curse of dimensionality.

puremacro 3.0.0 breaks this barrier by integrating the Sequence-Space Jacobian (SSJ) method of Auclert, Bardóczy, Rognlie & Straub (2021, Econometrica) directly into .mod files.

docs.title: 3.2 The hetagent_block Syntax
docs.text:
To declare a heterogeneous agent sector in a .mod file, puremacro introduces hetagent_block:

var Y C r pi i;
varexo eps_m;

parameters beta gamma r_ss phi_pi kappa;
beta = 0.985;
gamma = 1.0;
r_ss = 0.01;
phi_pi = 1.5;
kappa = 0.1;

hetagent_block;
  model = one_asset_hank;
  n_a = 50;
  a_max = 30.0;
  borrowing_limit = 0.0;
  grid = hyperbolic;
end;

model;
  Y = C;
  pi = beta * pi(+1) + kappa * Y;
  i = r_ss + phi_pi * pi + eps_m;
  r = i - pi(+1);
end;

The model; block is parsed and kept on HANKModel.dag for inspection, but it is not solved: every household backend is closed by the built-in New Keynesian Phillips curve \(\pi_t = \beta \pi_{t+1} + \kappa Y_t\) and Taylor rule \(i_t = \phi_\pi \pi_t + \varepsilon_{m,t}\) (ex-ante real rate \(r_t = i_t - \pi_{t+1}\); the two-asset household adds \(dr^a_t = \alpha_{ab}\, dr^b_t\)) evaluated on the declared beta, kappa, phi_pi (and alpha_ab) parameters, and the only shock is the monetary path magnitude * rho**t; the shock argument only labels the result (shock_name, plus a transition_paths column holding the monetary path when the name is a declared varexo); it never selects a different shock. Change the parameters, not the equations, to change the closure.

docs.title: Supported hetagent_block Attributes
docs.text:
• model: Sector template name (one_asset_hank or custom identifier).
  • n_a: Number of wealth grid points (default: 100).
  • a_max: Upper bound of asset grid (default: 50.0).
  • borrowing_limit: Hard borrowing constraint (default: 0.0).
  • grid: Asset grid spacing (hyperbolic or exponential).

docs.title: 3.3 Stationary Distribution \(\mathcal{D}^*(a)\) & Marginal Propensity to Consume
docs.text: Upon initialization, the microeconomic household problem is solved in steady state: 1. Endogenous Grid Method (EGM): Solves backwards for optimal policy rules \(c^*(a, s)\) and savings \(a^*(a, s)\) given steady-state interest rate \(r_{ss}\) and wage \(w_{ss}\). 2. Invariant Markov Distribution: Pushes forward transition probabilities until the stationary distribution \(\mathcal{D}^*(a, s)\) converges: $\(\mathcal{D}^* = \Pi^\top \mathcal{D}^*\)$ 3. MPC Schedule: Evaluates local marginal propensities to consume \(MPC(a) = \frac{\partial c(a)}{\partial a}\) across wealth tiers, capturing the high MPC of hand-to-mouth households.

docs.title: 3.4 The Fake-News Algorithm for Sequence-Space Jacobians
docs.text:
To couple household behavior with the aggregate DSGE equations, puremacro computes the intertemporal sequence-space Jacobians: $\(\mathcal{J}_{C, r} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \mathbf{r}} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T}, \quad \mathcal{J}_{C, Y} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \mathbf{Y}} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times T}\)$

The Fake-News Algorithm evaluates these \(T \times T\) matrices in \(\mathcal{O}(T^2)\) time rather than \(\mathcal{O}(T^3)\): 1. Define fake-news matrix \(\mathcal{F}_{s, t} = \mathbb{E}_s [ c_{t} ] - \mathbb{E}_{s-1} [ c_{t} ]\), representing the update to consumption at date \(t\) upon receiving news at date \(s\) about a shock at date 0. 2. Exploit the time-invariance of Markov transition matrices after date \(s\): $\(\mathcal{J}_{t, s} = \sum_{k=0}^{\min(t, s)} \mathcal{F}_{t-k, s-k}\)$

docs.title: 3.5 General Equilibrium Solvers: Linear & Nonlinear Broyden
docs.text: Aggregate market clearing over the horizon \(T\) forms the sequence-space system: $\(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{r}, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \equiv \mathbf{Y} - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{0}\)$

docs.title: Linear Sequence-Space Solver
docs.text: Differentiating around steady state yields: $\((\mathbf{I} - \mathcal{J}_{C, Y}) d\mathbf{Y} - \mathcal{J}_{C, r} d\mathbf{r} = 0\)$ Combining with the built-in aggregate Taylor rule and Phillips curve (the model; block is not read) produces a linear system solved in a single block matrix operation in \(< 0.05\) s.

docs.title: Nonlinear Broyden Solver
docs.text: For large MIT shocks where borrowing constraints bind asymmetrically, simulate(..., nonlinear=True) activates the Broyden quasi-Newton solver with Sherman-Morrison rank-1 updates: $\(B_{k+1} = B_k + \frac{(\Delta \mathbf{U}_k - B_k \Delta \mathbf{H}_k) (\Delta \mathbf{U}_k^\top B_k)}{\Delta \mathbf{U}_k^\top B_k \Delta \mathbf{H}_k}\)$ combined with an Armijo backtracking line search, guaranteeing convergence without recomputing microeconomic Jacobians at each iteration. nonlinear=True is implemented for the built-in one-asset household only: a two-asset hetagent_block (assets = 2) and any household_model bridge raise NotImplementedError, and their linear sequence-space transition (nonlinear=False) stays available.

docs.title: 3.6 Python Code Example: Solving a HANK .mod Model
docs.text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from puremacro.dsge.hank import load_hank_mod, solve_hank_bridge

HANK_MOD = """
var Y C r pi i;
varexo eps_m;

parameters beta gamma r_ss phi_pi kappa;
beta = 0.985;
gamma = 1.0;
r_ss = 0.01;
phi_pi = 1.5;
kappa = 0.1;

hetagent_block;
  model = one_asset_hank;
  n_a = 50;
  a_max = 30.0;
  borrowing_limit = 0.0;
  grid = hyperbolic;
end;

model;
  Y = C;
  pi = beta * pi(+1) + kappa * Y;
  i = r_ss + phi_pi * pi + eps_m;
  r = i - pi(+1);
end;
"""

# 1. Parse and initialize HANK model from .mod specification
model = load_hank_mod(HANK_MOD)
print("Stationary Steady State:", model.steady_state)

# 2. Inspect Fake-News Jacobians
jacobians = model.compute_jacobians(T=40)
print("J_C_r Shape:", jacobians["J_C_r"].shape)
print("Impact MPC (dC_0 / dY_0):", jacobians["J_C_Y"][0, 0])

# 3. Simulate an expansionary monetary policy shock (-25 bps)
# Linear Sequence-Space IRF
res_linear = model.simulate(
    shock="eps_m",
    magnitude=-0.0025,
    rho=0.5,
    horizon=30,
    nonlinear=False,
)

# Nonlinear Broyden Transition IRF

    shock="eps_m",
    magnitude=-0.0025,
    rho=0.5,
    horizon=30,
    nonlinear=True,
)

# 4. Display results summary table
print(res_linear.summary())

# 5. One-liner shortcut API
res_bridge = solve_hank_bridge(
    HANK_MOD,
    shock="eps_m",
    magnitude=-0.0025,
    horizon=30,
)

docs.title: Conclusion & Next Steps
docs.text:
These workflows provide: - Analytic Kalman score recursions with explicitly scoped structural sensitivities. - Automated, pure-Python Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for high-dimensional Bayesian DSGE posteriors without C++ dependencies. - Sequence-space HANK bridges through supported hetagent_block declarations.

To explore further: - View the Dynare estimation guide at dsge_estimation.md. - Explore nonlinear sequence-space theory at hank_nonlinear.md. - Inspect high-order perturbation options at dsge_higher_order.md.

docs.title: DSGE workflows: one model, several solution methods
docs.text:
Puremacro 5.7 separates the economic equations from the method used to solve them. Start with read_mod for a supported Dynare .mod file, or with NonlinearModel.from_equations for Python residuals. Then choose a steady state, a local stochastic approximation, a deterministic transition, or an explicitly mapped global policy problem. Reading a model does not silently select or solve one of these problems.

The guides below are intended to be read together. Their Python examples run in page order and are exercised by the documentation tests.

Your task Guide Main interface Declare equations, inspect timing, migrate a .mod workflow Nonlinear models and ordered commands read_mod, NonlinearModel, execute_mod_commands Solve a large deterministic change, news announcement, or constrained path Transitions and announcements solve_transition, solve_announced_path Compare local orders, solve a stochastic policy, or check approximation error Global policies and local accuracy EquilibriumProblem, solve_time_iteration, audit_policy Inspect syntax and command support before solving Model inspection inspect_mod, command-support reports Understand the existing local solution and simulation machinery Higher orders and constraints local perturbation, pruning, OccBin 
flowchart TD
    A[".mod file or Python equilibrium equations"] --> B["NonlinearModel: timing, calibration, named residuals"]
    B --> C["Checked steady state"]
    B --> D["Known exogenous path and boundary conditions"]
    C --> E["Local stochastic approximation: orders 1–3"]
    D --> F["Nonlinear deterministic transition"]
    B --> G["Explicit states, controls, transition, domain and quadrature"]
    G --> H["Global stochastic policy"]
    E --> I["Independent equilibrium and feasibility checks"]
    F --> I
    H --> I

docs.title: Choose the mathematical problem first
docs.text:
A typical model is written as

\[ E_t F(y_{t+1},y_t,y_{t-1},\varepsilon_t;\theta)=0. \]

The syntax alone does not identify which unknowns you want to solve for. In particular, a nonlinear perfect-foresight path is not a stochastic global policy, even when both use the same equilibrium equations.

Problem Unknown Information and boundaries What the result describes Steady state A constant endogenous vector Fixed calibration and exogenous values One static equilibrium candidate checked in the original equations Local perturbation Taylor coefficients of a policy near a reference equilibrium Shock covariance, timing, local determinacy and differentiability A local approximation; higher orders can include risk terms Perfect foresight Every endogenous value along a finite path A fully known exogenous path, inherited state and terminal closure One deterministic equilibrium path Announced-path experiment A sequence of conditional deterministic plans Explicit announcement dates and the full path believed at each date Realized values stitched from successive information sets Global time iteration A control policy over a declared state domain A state transition, shock integration rule and admissibility conditions An approximation over that domain, with finite numerical accuracy evidence

Setting future shocks to their means in a nonlinear model generally does not evaluate its conditional expectations. Preserve the expected marginal-utility Euler equation when moving between deterministic and stochastic exercises. For example, with log utility and gross return \(R_{t+1}\), use \(1/c_t=\beta E_t[R_{t+1}/c_{t+1}]\). Multiplying by random future consumption inside an expectation changes the stochastic equation. The revised MAV neoclassical and RBC examples use the expected marginal-return formulation.

docs.title: A reproducible modeling sequence
docs.text:
1. Declare and inspect. Give equations meaningful names, retain variable and innovation order, and inspect leads and lags. Keep economic units explicit. A timing error can produce a numerically small residual for the wrong model.
  2. Check the reference equilibrium. Solve model.steady(...) at the intended exogenous values and inspect the original residuals. An analytical declaration is a useful seed; it is not itself a convergence certificate.
  3. Define the experiment. For a path, specify inherited and terminal values, shock dates and the tail beyond the initial horizon. For a policy, declare state/control mappings, domain, quadrature and feasible choices explicitly.
  4. Solve with a finite budget. Select a backend and tolerances that suit the structure. Continuation can help reach a difficult target; grid refinement can improve an approximation. Neither removes the need for a stopping rule.
  5. Audit beyond the stopping rule. Re-evaluate economic residuals and constraints. Compare path horizons or policies on points not used to fit them. Increase integration accuracy separately from interpolation accuracy.
  6. Save the experiment. Retain calibration, equation/source hashes, solver options, boundaries, shock paths, grids, quadrature and audit points alongside the result. Table exports are convenient summaries; they do not contain all the information needed to rerun a calculation.

docs.title: Read accuracy reports in layers
docs.text:
Evidence Useful conclusion What remains to check Solver reports convergence Its implemented stopping rule was met Original equation units, feasibility and boundary sensitivity Small equilibrium residuals on a finite path That truncated boundary problem is satisfied to the reported tolerance A longer horizon, the terminal policy and alternative equilibrium branches Small time-iteration update Successive fitted policies changed little Off-grid Euler/KKT errors and quadrature accuracy Small off-grid errors The sampled equations are accurate on those points under that integration rule Other states, domain exits, rare shocks and richer integration Stable successive grids or horizons The reported comparison changed little Global existence, uniqueness and the economic adequacy of the model

Scaled residuals and complementarity functions have different interpretations from raw Euler residuals. Read the units in the method-specific report. A bound that keeps consumption positive is a numerical domain restriction; a borrowing constraint that can bind requires the corresponding economic inequality and complementarity condition.

docs.title: Follow the MAV teaching sequence
docs.text:
The bilingual course guide pins T02_A–D, their helpers and their model files to v5.7.1. The original 72-notebook edition remains available at course-2026A-5.5.0.

Lesson What to reproduce Independent check to notice T02_A: neoclassical growth Callback and .mod stacking; direct/Krylov paths; permanent changes; announcements; local/global comparisons Path agreement, 80/160-period comparison, off-grid policy audit with richer quadrature T02_B: RBC First-, second- and third-order stochastic rules with correctly specified Euler expectations Common audit points and separation of a risky steady state from an ergodic mean T02_C: New Keynesian Local solutions and model frictions Conditioning diagnostics alongside the existing determinacy checks T02_D: constraints and uncertainty Irreversible investment, nonlinear transitions and stochastic volatility Original nonlinear residuals, complementarity and horizon sensitivity

For local execution use Python 3.12 or later for these course notebooks, even though the library supports Python 3.11+. Use a fresh virtual environment and the same interpreter to install dependencies and start Jupyter:

git clone --branch v5.7.1 --depth 1 https://github.com/jalonso1979/puremacro.git puremacro-5.7.1
cd puremacro-5.7.1
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[notebooks]" jupyterlab
cd curso/notebooks
python -m jupyterlab

On Windows PowerShell, replace the activation command with ./.venv/Scripts/Activate.ps1. Keep _dsge_labs.py, modelos/ and data_curso/ beside the notebooks. If an older package was already imported, restart the kernel after installation. Execute cells in order; do not mix the 5.5.0 course environment with the updated DSGE lessons.

The execution record identifies notebook and runtime inputs, cell execution and saved figures. Local execution and the headless Pyodide smoke suite are distinct checks; neither certifies every Colab, Juno or browser notebook session.

docs.title: Compatibility and practical limits
docs.text:
Puremacro provides a documented subset of Dynare syntax and command semantics. Use the compatibility table, not the presence of a familiar command name, to decide whether a file is supported. The Dynare manual is the reference for Dynare itself; it is not a promise that every option runs in Puremacro. Unsupported commands and options in the ordered execution workflow fail explicitly.

The global interface deliberately requires an economic mapping from residuals to states, controls and transitions. This avoids guessing which variables are predetermined, what information is available when choices are made, or which equations are inequalities. The parser does not infer a general Bellman problem.

Smooth residuals, a well-posed finite boundary problem and a reasonable initial guess are still relevant for Newton methods. Nonexistence, indeterminacy, singularities, discontinuities and multiple equilibria need explicit analysis. No available backend solves models of every kind or proves global uniqueness. For failure-specific next steps, see the troubleshooting sections in the model, transition and policy guides.

docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Real-data published replication
docs.text: This study extends the research workflows with an original-paper specification and its original data. It asks whether puremacro reproduces a specified published result.

docs.title: Romer–Romer (2010): original baseline tax response
docs.text:
python -m puremacro.examples.romer_romer_2010_replication --output research_output/rr2010

This study checks one baseline result in Romer and Romer (2010), The Macroeconomic Effects of Tax Changes. The original workbook and EXOGERNR.RAT specification come from the authors' data archive. Their hashes and the derived data/reference hashes are retained.

from puremacro.replication import estimate_rr2010_baseline

replication = estimate_rr2010_baseline()
print(replication.to_frame().loc[10])
# Preserve the complete response covariance when using these empirical targets.
targets = replication.to_moment_targets()
print(targets.labels)

For 1950Q1–2007Q4, the baseline regression explains 100 * delta log(real GDP) with a constant and contemporaneous through twelve lags of 100 * (DEFIC + LONGR) / NOMGDP. Cumulative sums of the thirteen tax coefficients give the response of the GDP level to a tax increase equal to one percent of GDP. Positive tax shocks mean tax increases.

The original specification uses conventional OLS covariance with the residual degrees-of-freedom adjustment. Cumulative-response covariance applies the same linear cumulative-sum transformation to the full coefficient covariance. HAC and local projections can be useful extensions, but they change this published specification.

Two different comparisons are reported:

  1. Numerical parity: all coefficients, covariance entries and cumulative responses against a frozen independent-software run that does not import puremacro. Tolerances allow numerical roundoff.
  2. Published evidence: the horizon-ten trough, GDP response -3.08 and t statistic -3.53, reported on printed page 781. Only published rounding justifies the looser tolerance here; it is not used for software parity.

The original data give a horizon-ten response of -3.0808127631 and t statistic -3.5249960750. Software parity passes, and the response and trough horizon reproduce the printed results. The t statistic misses the -3.53 rounding interval by 0.000003925. An independent read of the authors' RATS databanks corroborates this value. Its source is unresolved; neither intermediate rounding nor a wider tolerance is used to force agreement. The published case and application therefore report FAIL, with a nonzero command exit status. This is a verified discrepancy, not a claim that all published targets agree.

The scope is this original-data baseline. It does not reproduce every robustness exercise or independently establish the narrative exclusion assumption. The earlier regression.romer_romer_tax_multiplier_ols gallery case is a modified horizon-eight LP with a different sample and revised data; its coarse headline comparison is explicitly labeled as such.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
The application runs offline with packaged numerical inputs and reference evidence. The exported report includes data/model definitions, sample and units, estimates, uncertainty diagnostics and figures. Source conversion and independent reference regeneration are development steps, distinct from the offline runtime. Reference software is not a runtime dependency.

Use the structural bridge guide for covariance conventions and the benchmark guide for provenance, strict comparisons and negative controls.
