docs.title: Local language models: iPad, Mac, Windows, Linux and Colab
docs.text:
puremacro.llm runs a small language model on your own device, with no API key and no network after a one-time download. complete(prompt) returns the model's answer, choosing the engine on its own: MLX, llama.cpp, Ollama or an OpenAI-compatible server. Every answer is stored in a completion cache that does not depend on the device or the engine, so an answer computed once, on a Mac, is read back on an iPad, on Windows, in Colab, or in the browser, where no model runs at all. The narrative LLM features (score_llm, llm_prob_kernel) go through the same entry point.

# requires: a local LLM engine (mlx-lm, llama-cpp-python, or a running Ollama / OpenAI-compatible server)
import puremacro.llm as llm

print(llm.complete("In one sentence, what is a local projection?", max_tokens=64))
print(llm.chat([{"role": "system", "content": "Answer in Spanish."},
                {"role": "user", "content": "What is a Taylor rule?"}], max_tokens=128))

puremacro.llm is new after puremacro 4.8.1 (see the CHANGELOG, Unreleased): a release that includes it is needed. import puremacro.llm imports no inference package and opens no connection; each engine is imported only when it is used.

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
Platform Engine You install The model comes from iPad, Juno app MLX; llama.cpp as backup the Juno app; puremacro through Juno's package manager Hugging Face, downloaded by mlx-lm on first use and kept in the app's container Mac (Apple silicon) MLX, else Ollama pip install "puremacro[local-llm]", or the Ollama app the same, or ollama pull qwen3:4b Windows, Linux Ollama, or llamafile the Ollama installer, or one llamafile run as a local server the Ollama tag, or the GGUF inside the llamafile Colab llama.cpp on the GPU, or Ollama inside the notebook nothing; a setup cell does it a GGUF file from Hugging Face Browser, JupyterLite none nothing the shipped cache only

engine="auto" (the default) takes the first available of: mlx (when mlx and mlx_lm can be imported), llamacpp (when llama_cpp can be imported), Ollama on http://localhost:11434, then OpenAI-compatible servers on http://localhost:8080 (llamafile, llama-server) and http://localhost:1234 (LM Studio). What is installed decides, never the operating system or the processor family, which is why MLX is chosen on the iPad. A server counts as available when its model list (/api/tags or /v1/models) answers with JSON within three seconds. Pass engine="mlx", "llamacpp", "ollama" or "openai" to name one.

What has been checked, as of 2026-10-12:

  • On a Mac (M3 Pro), with the Qwen3 1.7B model: MLX, llama-cpp-python (built from source with Metal) and llama-cpp-python's OpenAI-compatible server all answered with no thinking left in the text, for the index prompt and the event-extraction prompt (whose answers write "sign": +1, which score_llm now parses).
  • Ollama: the request is in place ("think": false) but has not yet been run against a pulled Qwen3 model.
  • iPad (Juno app, iPad Pro M4, 16 GB): mlx, mlx_lm, llama_cpp and huggingface_hub import and Hugging Face is reachable; a completion through Juno's mlx-lm build is not yet verified on device.
  • Colab: the llama.cpp CUDA wheel and the in-notebook Ollama recipes below are not yet verified on device.

docs.title: Install per platform
docs.text:
iPad. Install the Juno app and, in it, puremacro through Juno's package manager (Juno has no pip). Juno ships MLX and mlx-lm, so nothing else is needed. The first completion downloads the model; see On the iPad.

Mac. Either the Python engines:

pip install "puremacro[local-llm]"     # llama-cpp-python, huggingface_hub, and mlx-lm on Apple silicon

or the Ollama app (https://ollama.com), then ollama pull qwen3:4b. MLX is the one puremacro picks when both are present. The extra installs mlx-lm on Apple silicon only; on an Intel Mac it installs llama-cpp-python and huggingface_hub, and Ollama works there too. The [local-llm] extra builds llama-cpp-python from source, which needs the Xcode command-line tools. Do not use the prebuilt Metal wheel of llama-cpp-python 0.3.36 from the project's extra index: as of 2026-10-12 it is corrupt (half of its files fail their CRC check). To build llama.cpp with Metal explicitly:

CMAKE_ARGS="-DGGML_METAL=on" pip install llama-cpp-python --no-binary llama-cpp-python

If that build fails, skip llama.cpp: pip install puremacro mlx-lm is enough for MLX, and Ollama needs no Python package at all.

Windows and Linux. Install Ollama (https://ollama.com) and run ollama pull qwen3:4b. Or download a llamafile and run it as a local server; it listens on port 8080 with an OpenAI-compatible API, which engine="auto" finds. pip install "puremacro[local-llm]" also works where llama-cpp-python builds (a C compiler and CMake are needed).

Colab. Choose a GPU runtime (Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU), then paste into one code cell:

# requires: Colab with a GPU runtime (not yet verified on device)
%pip install -q --only-binary=llama-cpp-python llama-cpp-python --extra-index-url https://abetlen.github.io/llama-cpp-python/whl/cu124
%pip install -q huggingface_hub puremacro

The CUDA wheel is about 1.8 GB; --only-binary makes the cell fail fast instead of starting a long CPU-only build. The engine offloads every layer to the GPU (n_gpu_layers=-1). The other route is Ollama inside the notebook. First install what its Linux install script needs, apt-get -qq update; apt-get -qq install -y zstd pciutils lshw (zstd because newer Ollama Linux bundles are .tar.zst archives, pciutils and lshw for the script's GPU detection); then run curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh, start ollama serve in the background and run ollama pull qwen3:4b; engine="auto" then finds it on port 11434.

Browser (JupyterLite, juno.sh). No engine runs under Pyodide. Ship a cache (see The cache and how to ship one) and use cache mode. Pyodide 0.28 adds sqlite3 only on request: run await pyodide.loadPackage('sqlite3') before importing puremacro.

docs.title: The model ladder
docs.text:
One reference model for everything, qwen3-4b: shipped caches are built with it, and default names it. All three rungs are Apache-2.0.

Alias Tier name Parameters Memory, approx. Minimum budget Licence Picked automatically qwen3-1.7b small 1.7 B 2.0 GB 3 GB apache-2.0 below a 5 GB budget qwen3-4b default 4 B 3.5 GB 5 GB apache-2.0 from 5 GB up qwen3-8b large 8 B 6.0 GB 10 GB apache-2.0 never; ask for it by name

What each engine loads (puremacro.llm.resolve_model_id(alias, engine)):

Alias MLX (Hugging Face) llama.cpp (repository, file) Ollama tag qwen3-1.7b mlx-community/Qwen3-1.7B-4bit ggml-org/Qwen3-1.7B-GGUF, Qwen3-1.7B-Q4_K_M.gguf qwen3:1.7b qwen3-4b mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-4bit Qwen/Qwen3-4B-GGUF, Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf qwen3:4b qwen3-8b mlx-community/Qwen3-8B-4bit Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF, Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf qwen3:8b

The downloads are about 1.0, 2.3 and 4.6 GB for MLX, and about 1.3, 2.5 and 5 GB for the GGUF files and the Ollama tags. OpenAI-compatible servers receive the alias itself as model ("qwen3-4b"); llamafile and llama-server answer with the model they were started with.

  • The budget (device_budget_gb()) is the memory a model may use: the working set MLX recommends for the GPU when mlx is installed, else 60 % of physical memory, else an assumed 8 GB. pick_model() turns it into a model; check_fits refuses a model whose minimum budget the device does not reach, and complete() then raises ModelTooLarge (with alias, suggested and budget_gb) before any engine is looked for. A cached answer is served whatever the device. The budget is the local device's even when PUREMACRO_LLM_BASE_URL or base_url= names another machine: a registry alias above it is refused before that server is asked; the engine's own model id (qwen3:8b) bypasses the check, at the cost of a different cache key and no thinking switch.
  • Names. model= takes a tier name, an alias, or an engine's own id (an Ollama tag, a .gguf path, a Hugging Face repository), which reaches the engine unchanged. Such an id has no entry in the model registry, so it is not checked against the budget and is not treated as a thinking model: the engine gets no thinking switch and no extra tokens (see Thinking), and only strip_thinking cleans the answer. Use the alias (qwen3-4b, not qwen3:4b) to get the switch. PUREMACRO_LLM_MODEL changes what default means, and nothing else.
  • Thinking. The Qwen3 models think before they answer. The engines switch that off (MLX and llama.cpp through the chat template, Ollama with "think": false, OpenAI-compatible servers with chat_template_kwargs and a /no_think suffix), and strip_thinking removes any <think>…</think> block that still comes back. A thinking model gets 8 tokens beyond max_tokens at the engine, room for the empty think block it may open with.
  • The models of 4.8.1 stay under their names, for code that uses them: qwen2.5-3b-instruct (licence qwen-research), gemma2-2b (gemma), llama3.2-3b (llama3.2) and phi3.5 (mit). They are never picked automatically.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
The mode argument, else the environment variable PUREMACRO_LLM_MODE, else auto (puremacro.llm.current_mode() says which applies):

Mode Reads the cache Runs a model Writes the cache On a cache miss auto yes on a miss yes (non-empty answers) checks the budget, finds an engine, runs the model cache yes never no raises CacheMiss off no always no (the cache is not used)

In cache mode no engine is constructed, no socket is opened and no model is loaded. A cache that cannot be read at all (no sqlite3, a file that is not a cache, such as a Git LFS pointer) raises CacheUnavailable, a kind of CacheMiss whose reason says why. off mode neither opens nor creates a cache file. With no engine available, auto and off raise LocalLLMUnavailable with install instructions.

The narrative features follow the mode:

  • LocalBackend (for score_llm) and LocalProvider (for llm_prob_kernel) take model="default", engine="auto", base_url=None, timeout=120.0 and mode=None, look for no engine when they are built, and send every call through puremacro.llm.complete. So a corpus scored once is scored again with no engine installed.
  • get_default_backend() and get_default_provider() print one status line:
[puremacro] local LLM: mode=cache engine=cache model=qwen3-4b

In cache mode they return the local object without probing anything. In auto and off modes they ask puremacro.llm.engines.available_engines(base_url=…); when no engine (or not the one named) is listed, they print the install hint, report engine=mock and return MockBackend (zero events) or MockProvider, so demos always run. - In cache mode score_llm raises CacheMiss (or CacheUnavailable) for a record the cache does not hold, instead of dropping it: a corpus that was not scored ahead of time fails loudly rather than returning a shorter list. ModelTooLarge propagates too. Other failures of one record's call (a timeout, say) are still counted as malformed and the loop goes on. - OllamaBackend() and OllamaProvider() default to the alias qwen3-4b: the server receives its tag qwen3:4b, and the cache rows are those of LocalBackend("default"). An explicit tag, OllamaBackend("qwen3:4b"), reaches the server unchanged and then keys the cache on the tag, so its rows are not shared with the alias. Nor is it known to think: the request goes without "think": false and without the 8 extra tokens, and only strip_thinking cleans the answer. Keep the alias to get the switch.

from puremacro.narrative.scoring import get_default_backend

backend = get_default_backend(mode="cache")   # probes nothing; prints the status line
print(type(backend).__name__, backend.model)  # LocalBackend qwen3-4b

docs.title: The cache and how to ship one
docs.text:
One SQLite file, ~/.cache/puremacro/llm_cache.sqlite, or the file named by PUREMACRO_LLM_CACHE. A row is keyed (format v1) on the canonical alias (qwen3-4b, never an engine's id), the prompt and system prompt as you wrote them (before any chat template), max_tokens, temperature (to three decimals) and json_mode. The engine is recorded for provenance only, so a row written by MLX answers the same call made through llama.cpp or Ollama. The key function is fixed for the life of the format; its golden value is pinned by the tests: cache_key("qwen3-4b", "hola", max_tokens=8, temperature=0.0, json_mode=False) is c630a581ab2b323492ac1db08bfc8b8f5a72655db00282142eb5762eacccb586.

To ship one: run the notebooks or scripts once in auto mode on a machine with the reference model, export the rows, and hand over the file. On the receiving side, point PUREMACRO_LLM_CACHE at it and set PUREMACRO_LLM_MODE=cache, or merge it into your own cache. A cache on a read-only volume still serves hits.

from puremacro.llm import CacheMiss, CacheRow, CompletionCache, cache_key, complete, open_cache
from puremacro.llm.cache import prompt_sha256

# A stand-in for a cache built on a machine that runs the model: one row written by hand
built = CompletionCache("built_on_a_mac.sqlite")
prompt = "Does 'the outlook remains highly uncertain' express uncertainty? Answer yes or no."
key = cache_key("qwen3-4b", prompt, max_tokens=8, temperature=0.0, json_mode=False)
built.set(CacheRow(key, "qwen3-4b", prompt_sha256(prompt), 8, 0.0, False, "yes",
                   engine="mlx", engine_model_id="mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-4bit"))

# Ship the rows of the reference model in a file of their own
print(built.export("course_cache.sqlite", model="qwen3-4b"))   # 1 row copied

# Read it anywhere, with no engine installed: cache mode never loads a model
shipped = CompletionCache("course_cache.sqlite")
print(complete(prompt, model="qwen3-4b", max_tokens=8, mode="cache", cache=shipped))   # yes
try:
    complete("A prompt nobody ran", model="qwen3-4b", max_tokens=8, mode="cache", cache=shipped)
except CacheMiss as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__, exc.model)                        # CacheMiss qwen3-4b
print(shipped.stats()["by_model"])                              # {'qwen3-4b': 1}

# Two-tier cache: check student_cache first, fall back to course_cache (read-only), write only to student_cache
two_tier = open_cache(["student_cache.sqlite", "course_cache.sqlite"])
print(complete(prompt, model="qwen3-4b", max_tokens=8, mode="cache", cache=two_tier))  # yes

# Or add the shipped rows to a cache of your own (rows it already has are kept)
print(CompletionCache("my_cache.sqlite").merge("course_cache.sqlite"))   # 1
  • open_cache([student_cache, course_cache]) (or CompletionCache(student_cache, fallback_paths=[course_cache])) opens a two-tier cache: lookups check student_cache first and then course_cache in read-only mode without creating or modifying course_cache, while new completions are written only to student_cache.
  • export(dest, *, model=None, since=None) copies rows into another file, creating it; since="2026-10-01" keeps rows created on or after that date (UTC). merge(src) adds the rows of another file that this one lacks. Both return the number of rows added and raise if they cannot do their work; stats() gives rows, by_model, bytes and path (plus fallback_paths when fallback tiers are configured).
  • A cache hit needs the same call: the same alias, the same prompt, max_tokens, temperature and json_mode. PUREMACRO_LLM_MODEL changes the alias that default stands for, and an explicit Ollama tag keys rows under the tag.
  • A cache that cannot be written (a read-only directory, a corrupt file) never stops a completion: answers are recomputed instead, and one warning per file says why.
  • llm_prob_kernel keeps its own score cache in front of this one (~/.cache/puremacro/llm_scores.sqlite, or PUREMACRO_LLM_SCORES_CACHE). Shipping the completion cache is enough: a score missing there falls through to the completion cache.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Effect PUREMACRO_LLM_MODE auto, cache or off when no mode= is given; blank counts as unset, anything else raises ValueError PUREMACRO_LLM_MODEL what default means: a tier name, an alias or an engine's own id; small, large and explicit aliases are not affected PUREMACRO_LLM_CACHE the completion cache file (default ~/.cache/puremacro/llm_cache.sqlite) PUREMACRO_LLM_FALLBACK_CACHE read-only fallback completion cache path(s) consulted when a key is missing in PUREMACRO_LLM_CACHE PUREMACRO_LLM_BASE_URL one server to use instead of the three default local ones, tried as Ollama and then as OpenAI-compatible PUREMACRO_LLM_SCORES_CACHE the score cache of llm_prob_kernel (default ~/.cache/puremacro/llm_scores.sqlite) PUREMACRO_LLM_BUDGET spend removes the call cap (max_calls) of llm_prob_kernel HF_HUB_OFFLINE 1 makes llama.cpp load a downloaded GGUF file from the Hugging Face cache with no network

A server URL, from base_url= or PUREMACRO_LLM_BASE_URL, loses its trailing slashes and then one trailing /v1. So http://localhost:1234/v1, the form LM Studio and OpenAI clients document, names the same server as http://localhost:1234.

docs.title: On the iPad
docs.text:
• Keep Juno in front while a model downloads and while a corpus is scored. iPadOS suspends an app in the background, and a download or a scoring loop stops with it. Scoring runs are short; split a long corpus into pieces, and the cache keeps every answer already computed.
  • Models persist in the app's container. The first completion downloads the model from Hugging Face (about 2.3 GB for qwen3-4b with MLX, about 1 GB for qwen3-1.7b) into the app's container, where later sessions find it: the download happens once.
  • The budget. On an iPad Pro M4 with 16 GB, MLX recommends a working set of about 11 GB, so pick_model() chooses qwen3-4b, and qwen3-8b fits when asked for by name. Devices with less memory fall to qwen3-1.7b, whose answers can differ from those of the reference model that shipped caches are built with.
  • Compute is smaller. A float32 matrix product (2048 × 2048) ran at 117 GFLOPS through MLX on the iPad Pro M4, against 430 on an M3 Pro Mac. Expect slower generation than on a Mac, and prefer the shipped cache for anything long.
  • The browser is not the app. The Pyodide kernel of juno.sh (JupyterLite) runs no engine; there, use cache mode. See also the runtime guide.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
report() says what this machine offers a local model: host, device, memory, the budget, the engines, the model pick_model would choose, the cache file and the mode. It prints nothing, creates no cache file and, with probe_servers=False or in cache mode, probes no server.

import puremacro.llm as llm

print(llm.report(probe_servers=False))

On a Mac with mlx-lm and llama-cpp-python installed it reads like this (an example: the numbers depend on the machine and the cache):

puremacro.llm
  host    : cpython 3.13.12 (arm64)
  device  : workstation
  memory  : 36,864 MB
  budget  : 28.08 GB for a model
  engines : mlx, llamacpp (servers not probed)
  model   : qwen3-4b (about 3.5 GB)
  cache   : ~/.cache/puremacro/llm_cache.sqlite (1,204 rows, 2,457,600 bytes)
  mode    : auto (the cache, then a local model, whose answer is stored)
Symptom Cause and remedy LocalLLMUnavailable no engine can serve the model: install one (see above) or use cache mode with a shipped cache engines : none nothing installed was found; for a server, check that it answers at /api/tags or /v1/models CacheMiss in cache mode the shipped cache lacks this exact call; compare the alias, max_tokens, temperature and json_mode with the call that built it CacheUnavailable the cache cannot be read here; its reason says why (in Pyodide, load sqlite3 first; a Git LFS pointer needs git lfs pull) ModelTooLarge the model needs more memory than the budget; use the suggested model, or small HTTP 404 from Ollama the model was never pulled: run ollama pull qwen3:4b engine=mock in the status line get_default_backend / get_default_provider found no engine and returned the mock the first call is slow the model is being downloaded and loaded; later calls reuse it

docs.title: Long national accounts panel
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: The long national accounts panel
docs.text:
qna_panel gives you the OECD's quarterly national accounts, which for most of Europe begin in 1995. qna_long_panel extends that spine backwards, per country, by ratio-splicing archived national vintages onto it.

from puremacro.fetch import qna_long_panel

long, seams = qna_long_panel(["ESP", "JPN"], return_seams=True)

long.loc["ESP"].index.min()   # 1970-01-01   (OECD: 1995-01-01)
long.loc["JPN"].index.min()   # 1955-04-01   (OECD: 1994-01-01)

The column schema is exactly qna_panel's, so qna_identity, qna_rebase and qna_contributions work unchanged. Alongside each value column sits a src_<column> recording which vintage produced each quarter.

country reaches gain sources Spain 1970Q1 +100 quarters INE base-1995 tables (JSON API) + the base-1986 workbook Japan 1955Q2 +155 quarters Cabinet Office 93SNA and 68SNA archived releases

docs.title: What a ratio splice does, and does not, preserve
docs.text:
The only thing worth keeping from an abandoned vintage is its growth rates. Its levels are expressed in a base and a methodology that were later replaced, so carrying them over unchanged would put a step in the series at the seam. The older segment is therefore rescaled by the ratio between the two vintages over their overlap, and only then used to extend the newer one backwards.

A useful consequence: any constant factor is absorbed exactly and silently. Japan's ESRI files are in billions of yen at annual rates while the OECD spine is in millions per quarter — a factor of 250 — and nothing has to special-case it. Rebasings and currency redenominations behave the same way.

docs.title: The ratio's stability is the test
docs.text:
What a rescaling cannot absorb is a ratio that drifts across the overlap. That means the two vintages disagree about growth itself, not merely about level, and the spliced level then depends on which quarter you happened to anchor to — a result about your arbitrary choice rather than about the economy.

So drift is measured and reported per column:

seams[~seams.stable][["code", "column", "older", "overlap_n", "ratio_drift"]]

The answer differs by column, and only the seam table will tell you:

  • Spain — GDP and household consumption hold steady across both seams (0.9–1.3% drift). Capital formation does not: 5.1% drift, with the ratio ranging 1.04–1.39 across 76 overlapping quarters. Spanish GDP back to 1970 is defensible; Spanish investment back to 1970 is indicative at best.
  • Japan — everything holds except government consumption at the 68SNA seam (5.3%), which is unsurprising: 68SNA defined the government sector differently.

Nine of twenty-eight seams are unstable. qna_long_panel warns and names the worst; drop_unstable=True blanks those quarters instead if you would rather have a gap than a number you might not notice is shaky.

docs.title: The identity does not close, on purpose
docs.text:
Columns are spliced independently, each keeping its own source's growth rates, so C + G + I + X − M no longer equals spliced GDP:

from puremacro.fetch import long_panel_residual
(long_panel_residual(long) / long["gdp"]).abs().mean()   # ~0.33%

Forcing it to zero — by splicing GDP and component shares and rebuilding levels — would produce a tidier panel that no agency ever published, and would have buried the investment problem above inside whichever series was designated the residual. Measuring the gap is the more useful answer.

Within each source vintage the identity closes exactly, which is what validated the column mappings in the first place — including the discovery that Spanish cons_hh must be households plus NPISH to match the OECD's S1M sector.

docs.title: What is refused
docs.text:
Three situations raise rather than returning a number:

  • no overlap — there is nothing to estimate a ratio from, and concatenating two segments puts an unmeasured step in the series;
  • fewer than four overlapping quarters — the ratio cannot be told apart from a one-off revision;
  • a definitional break — a change in what is being measured rather than a revision of it.

Germany is the standing example. Its pre-1991 nominal accounts cover West Germany; rescaling those onto unified Germany would fabricate an East German economy back to 1970. ratio_splice refuses unless the caller passes allow_definitional_break=True and takes responsibility. Germany can reach 1970 in volumes, because the Bundesbank has already done that linking officially over the 1991 annual average and publishes the result (BBNZ1 Q.DE.Y.H.*.L).

docs.title: Splicing many sources at once
docs.text:
splice_sources applies the same rules to a long frame with columns code, date, variable, value, source, one row per observation, from as many sources as you have. to_long builds that frame from any (code, date) wide panel. Add a source column and stack the panels:

from puremacro.fetch.longpanel import splice_sources, to_long

long = pd.concat([to_long(qna).assign(source="oecd"),
                  to_long(old).assign(source="archive")])
panel, provenance, seams = splice_sources(long, {"oecd": 0, "archive": 1})

For every (code, variable), the best-ranked source with at least min_obs observations is the primary. Its values are never changed and its gaps are never filled. Older sources only extend it backwards. Each one is rescaled by the mean ratio over the first min_overlap common dates, and a units change such as millions against billions shows up as pow10. Variables declared as rate or ratio in kinds are appended unscaled, but only when the gap at the seam is within rate_tol. seams keeps one row per attempt, including rejected ones. provenance says which source is the primary for each series and which sources extended it.

docs.title: Why only two countries
docs.text:
Because only two archived sources were measured to reach further back than the OECD already does. Seven candidates buy zero quarters, and the reasons are kept in the code rather than lost:

from puremacro.fetch import LONG_PANEL_KNOWN_GAPS
LONG_PANEL_KNOWN_GAPS["MEX"]
  • Eurostat publishes the same numbers as the OECD — the splice ratio is 1.0 — beats it for no country, is shorter for Denmark (1995 vs 1990) and Switzerland (1995 vs 1980), and has no United Kingdom row at all, where the OECD has the UK from 1960.
  • IMF ties the OECD on seven of eight economies checked and is 12 quarters shorter on the United States.
  • INEGI serves nothing before 1993 and is identical to the OECD after dividing by four. IBGE ties the OECD at 1996Q1 — a hard floor across all seven candidate tables.
  • CEPALSTAT's Mexican 1980–92 join has a ratio drifting 0.754–0.837 across the overlap, which is exactly the condition this module refuses to call a splice.

"We checked and it buys nothing" is a different statement from "we did not check", and the difference is worth keeping.

docs.title: Local Projections
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Local Projections (LP)
docs.text:
Local Projections (Jordà 2005) estimate impulse response functions by running a sequence of direct predictive regressions for each horizon \(h = 0, 1, \dots, H\):

\[y_{t+h} - y_{t-1} = \alpha_h + \beta_h x_t + \gamma_h' w_t + \sum_{l=1}^p \Gamma_{h,l} w_{t-l} + \varepsilon_{t+h}\]

where \(x_t\) is a structural shock or policy variable, \(w_t\) contains control variables (which enter contemporaneously and with \(p\) lags, together with \(p\) lags of \(y_t\) and \(x_t\)), and \(\beta_h\) traces out the impulse response function at horizon \(h\).

In contrast to Structural VARs, which iterate forward a one-step-ahead linear model, Local Projections: - Do not compound specification errors across horizons. - Naturally accommodate non-linearities, asymmetric regimes, and state-dependent effects. - Support flexible inference via Newey-West HAC or Driscoll-Kraay standard errors without requiring stationary companion matrices.

In puremacro 2.0, all local projection estimators return a unified LPResult object that behaves as a pandas DataFrame while exposing one-call plotting (.plot()) and publication-grade export methods (.to_latex(), .to_typst(), .to_markdown()).

The code blocks on this page build on each other: run them in order and the whole page executes verbatim.

docs.title: Quickstart: Single-Series LP-HAC
docs.text:
To estimate impulse responses with Newey-West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from puremacro.lp import lp_hac

# Synthetic dataset: response of output to a policy shock
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
T = 200
shock = rng.standard_normal(T)
output = np.cumsum(0.6 * shock + 0.4 * rng.standard_normal(T))
df = pd.DataFrame({"gdp": output, "shock": shock})

# Estimate LP up to horizon 12 with 4 lags of controls and 90% CI
res = lp_hac(df, y="gdp", x="shock", horizon=12, lags=4, ci=0.90)

# 1. Print structured summary (with significance flags)
print(res.summary())

# 2. Inspect point estimates and standard errors
print(res[["h", "beta", "se", "lo", "hi"]].head())

# 3. Plot IRF with confidence bands in 1 line
res.plot(title="Response of GDP to Structural Shock")

docs.title: The LPResult Object
docs.text:
The returned res is an LPResult (subclassing pd.DataFrame). You can treat it as a standard DataFrame or use its specialized econometric attributes:

Property / Method Description res.point Point estimates \(\hat{\beta}_h\) as a NumPy array of shape (H+1,) res.se HAC standard errors \(\hat{\text{se}}(\hat{\beta}_h)\) of shape (H+1,) (all-NaN for band-only estimators such as lp_quantile) res.ci_lower Lower confidence bound \(\hat{\beta}_h - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \hat{\text{se}}\) res.ci_upper Upper confidence bound \(\hat{\beta}_h + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \hat{\text{se}}\) res.t_stat \(\hat{\beta}_h / \hat{\text{se}}\) (NaN where no SE is available) res.horizons Array of horizons evaluated [0, 1, ..., H] res.labels [] for single-coefficient results; ['H', 'L'] / ['pos', 'neg'] for regime or sign results res.plot() Renders an impulse response plot with shaded confidence bands (one line and band per regime for regime results, one line per quantile for lp_quantile) res.summary() Formatted tabular summary string with significance flags: *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.10 (two-sided normal z-test); for band-only estimators a single * marks bands that exclude zero res.to_markdown() Renders table formatted for Quarto, GitHub, or Obsidian res.to_latex() Generates a clean \begin{tabular} for LaTeX / Overleaf res.to_typst() Generates a #table(...) block for modern Typst documents

For regime or sign results (lp_state_dep, lp_state_dep_iv, lp_asymmetric, lp_garch_state) the table carries one coefficient per label (beta_H/beta_L, beta_pos/beta_neg) and res.point, res.se, res.ci_lower, res.ci_upper and res.t_stat return a DataFrame indexed by h with one column per label.

docs.title: Instrumental Variable Local Projections (lp_iv)
docs.text:
When the policy intervention \(x_t\) is endogenous (for example, policy interest rates reacting contemporaneously to economic shocks), standard OLS local projections suffer from omitted-variable bias.

lp_iv implements Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) local projections using an external instrument \(z_t\) (such as high-frequency monetary surprises or narrative tax changes):

\[\text{Stage 1: } x_t = \pi_{0,h} + \pi_{1,h} z_t + \text{controls} + v_{t,h}$$ $$\text{Stage 2: } y_{t+h} - y_{t-1} = \alpha_h + \beta_h \hat{x}_t + \text{controls} + \varepsilon_{t+h}\]

The block below first extends the synthetic dataset with the illustrative columns used in the rest of this page (an endogenous policy rate driven by a high-frequency surprise, two controls, government spending driven by a military-news instrument, and an unemployment rate in percent):

from puremacro.lp import lp_iv

# Illustrative columns for the remaining examples (synthetic, seeded above)
df["hf_monetary_surprise"] = rng.standard_normal(T)
df["fedfunds"] = 0.7 * df["hf_monetary_surprise"] + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(T)
df["inflation"] = rng.standard_normal(T)
df["commodity_prices"] = rng.standard_normal(T)
df["military_news"] = rng.standard_normal(T)
df["gov_spending"] = 0.6 * df["military_news"] + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(T)
df["unemployment_rate"] = 6.0 + 1.5 * rng.standard_normal(T)   # percent

res_iv = lp_iv(
    df,
    y="gdp",
    x="fedfunds",
    z="hf_monetary_surprise",
    controls=["inflation", "commodity_prices"],
    horizon=16,
    lags=4,
    ci=0.90,
)

# First-stage F statistics across horizons
print("First stage F:", res_iv["first_stage_f"].values)
res_iv.plot(title="LP-IV: Monetary Transmission via External Instrument")

docs.title: Weak-instrument diagnostics (3.4.0)
docs.text:
z accepts a sequence as well as a single name, and every LP-IV row now carries the Montiel Olea & Pflueger (2013) effective F-statistic alongside its critical values:

Column Meaning first_stage_f With one instrument, the squared first-stage t-statistic (unchanged from 3.3.0). With two or more, it equals mop_f, because a robust joint Wald F is the only sensible scalar there mop_f The MOP effective F, \(\hat{\pi}' (Z'Z) \hat{\pi} \; / \; \operatorname{tr}\!\big((Z'Z)^{-1} \hat{\Omega}_{zz}\big)\), with the same Newey-West bandwidth \(L = h + 1\) as the horizon's HAC errors mop_cv_10, mop_cv_20 Critical values at the 5% level for 10% and 20% worst-case Nagar bias

The critical values are computed from the MOP closed form rather than read off a table:

\[\text{cv}(K, \tau, \alpha) = \frac{\chi^2_{K, \, 1-\alpha}(K / \tau)}{K}\]

the \(1 - \alpha\) quantile of a non-central \(\chi^2\) with \(K\) degrees of freedom and non-centrality \(K / \tau\), divided by \(K\). For a single instrument at \(\alpha = 0.05\) this reproduces the published MOP values 23.11 (\(\tau = 10\%\)) and 15.06 (\(\tau = 20\%\)) — and 37.42 at 5%, 12.04 at 30%:

from puremacro.lp.iv import mop_critical_values   # not re-exported at puremacro.lp

mop_critical_values(1)                  # (23.10851121160664, 15.061552535779715)
mop_critical_values(1, tau=(0.05, 0.30))  # (37.417561545697716, 12.045036998377999)
mop_critical_values(2)                  # (19.294343449962533, 12.172075007359934)

For \(K \ge 2\) the full MOP critical value is data dependent (it replaces \(K\) by an effective degrees of freedom estimated from the first-stage HAC covariance). What mop_cv_10 / mop_cv_20 report is the \(W = I\) reduction, which is exact for \(K = 1\) and a reference point otherwise.

docs.title: Anderson-Rubin confidence sets
docs.text:
anderson_rubin=True (alias weak_iv_robust=True) adds ar_lo, ar_hi and ar_set_type. The set \(\{\beta_0 : AR(\beta_0) \le \chi^2_{K,\,1-\alpha}\}\) is inverted in closed form — the limit \(AR(\pm\infty)\) decides whether the tails are rejected, and the endpoints are Brent roots of \(AR - \text{cv}\) — rather than being read off a fixed grid, so an interval far from the 2SLS point estimate is not silently truncated:

ar_set_type The set is Read it as bounded \([\,\)ar_lo, ar_hi\(\,]\) the usual interval; the instruments identify \(\beta\) unbounded_rays \((-\infty,\) ar_hi\(\,] \cup [\,\)ar_lo\(, \infty)\), with ar_lo > ar_hi weak identification: a bounded interval does not exist all_real \((-\infty, \infty)\); ar_lo = \(-\infty\), ar_hi = \(+\infty\) the instruments say nothing about \(\beta\) empty \(\varnothing\); both bounds NaN every candidate is rejected — normally a misspecified or over-identified model 
# Two instruments for one endogenous regressor
df["hf_surprise_2"] = 0.4 * df["hf_monetary_surprise"] + 0.6 * rng.standard_normal(T)
df["fedfunds2"] = (0.5 * df["hf_monetary_surprise"] + 0.5 * df["hf_surprise_2"]
                   + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(T))

res_weak = lp_iv(
    df,
    y="gdp",
    x="fedfunds2",
    z=["hf_monetary_surprise", "hf_surprise_2"],
    controls=["inflation"],
    horizon=4,
    lags=4,
    ci=0.90,
    weak_iv_robust=True,
)

print(res_weak[["h", "beta", "mop_f", "mop_cv_10", "ar_lo", "ar_hi", "ar_set_type"]].round(4))
#    h    beta     mop_f  mop_cv_10   ar_lo   ar_hi ar_set_type
# h
# 0  0  0.0115  238.0877    19.2943 -0.0967  0.1123     bounded
# 1  1  0.1049  229.4756    19.2943 -0.0479  0.2764     bounded
# 2  2  0.1415  228.8576    19.2943 -0.0408  0.3303     bounded
# 3  3  0.0729  228.2393    19.2943 -0.1292  0.2407     bounded
# 4  4  0.0952  233.6795    19.2943 -0.1213  0.2832     bounded

Lag-augmented LP-IV is the same surface under a different variance estimator. la_lp gained z=, anderson_rubin= and weak_iv_robust=, and la_lp_iv is the instrument-first spelling of the same estimator (res.method == "la_lp_iv"); both are exported from puremacro.lp:

from puremacro.lp import la_lp_iv

res_la = la_lp_iv(
    df, y="gdp", x="fedfunds", z="hf_monetary_surprise",
    horizon=4, lags=4, ci=0.90, weak_iv_robust=True,
)

Lag augmentation (Montiel Olea & Plagborg-Møller 2021, Econometrica 89(4), 1789–1823) controls for one more lag of every series than the non-augmented LP needs. The regression scores are then serially uncorrelated, so the plain Eicker-Huber-White (HC0) standard error is valid at every horizon, uniformly over the persistence of the data (their §2.1 and Proposition 1). MOPM prove this for OLS local projections; la_lp_iv carries it over to LP-IV and uses White — not HAC — everywhere: in the second stage, in mop_f, and in the AR set (lags = 0 is the zero-lag Bartlett case). first_stage_f there equals mop_f for any number of instruments.

Lag count. la_lp and la_lp_iv include p_aug = n_lags + extra_lags lags of x and y and control_lags lags of each control (default p_aug), with the same p_aug at every horizon. The default extra_lags=1 is MOPM's single extra lag: in a VAR(p) their LP controls for p lags of all the series, one more than the p − 1 lags that the LP representation needs (§4.1, p. 20), so n_lags = p − 1 reproduces their specification exactly. A larger n_lags is the conservative choice, and MOPM note that it has no asymptotic efficiency cost (§6, p. 28). No source recommends p + h lags. The lag specification is recorded on the result:

from puremacro.lp import la_lp

res_ols = la_lp(df, y="gdp", x="fedfunds", horizon=8, lags=4, ci=0.90)
print(res_ols.attrs["extra_lags"], res_ols.attrs["p_aug"])
# 1 5

Changed after 4.3.0. The default used to be extra_lags = max(horizons) lags at every horizon. The estimate at a given h therefore depended on the largest horizon requested, horizons=[0] got no augmentation, and controls got only n_lags lags. To reproduce old results exactly, pass extra_lags=max(horizons), control_lags=n_lags.

Clustering is not supported. Neither lp_iv nor la_lp_iv takes a cluster= argument, and no weak-instrument statistic on this page is cluster-robust: the variance is Newey-West HAC in lp_iv and White in la_lp_iv. Cluster-robust panel inference lives in panel_lp / panel_lp_dk (§ Panel Local Projections), which do not compute mop_f or AR sets. puremacro.inference.weak_iv.olea_pflueger_f accepts a cluster= array, but that is a standalone first-stage statistic, not part of the LP-IV pipeline.

docs.title: State-Dependent Local Projections (lp_state_dep)
docs.text:
Macroeconomic transmission often differs across economic regimes (e.g. recessions vs. expansions, or high vs. low debt regimes). lp_state_dep partitions responses based on a state variable \(s_t\):

\[y_{t+h} - y_{t-1} = \alpha_h + F(s_t) \beta_h^H x_t + (1 - F(s_t)) \beta_h^L x_t + \text{controls} + \varepsilon_{t+h}\]

where \(F(s_t) \in [0, 1]\) is the high-regime weight.

docs.title: Smooth Logistic vs. Sharp Threshold
docs.text:
• Sharp Threshold (transition="threshold"): \(F(s_t) = \mathbb{I}\{s_t > c\}\). Observations are discretely partitioned into high and low regimes.
  • Smooth Transition (transition="logistic", default): \(F(s_t) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\gamma (s_t - c) / \sigma_s)}\), where \(\sigma_s\) is the sample standard deviation of the state, so \(\gamma > 0\) is the speed of transition in standard deviations of \(s_t\) (Auerbach & Gorodnichenko 2012 use \(\gamma = 1.5\) on a standardized state).

The cutoff \(c\) is the threshold argument on the raw scale of the state variable: threshold=6.5 on an unemployment rate in percent means 6.5 %. The default threshold=None splits at the sample mean of the state (the standardized-zero convention of Auerbach-Gorodnichenko). A cutoff that leaves every observation in one regime raises a ValueError naming the state's range instead of a singular regression.

from puremacro.lp import lp_state_dep

# Smooth transition around 6.5 % unemployment (state_var= is an alias of state=)
res_state = lp_state_dep(
    df,
    y="gdp",
    x="gov_spending",
    state="unemployment_rate",
    transition="logistic",
    gamma=3.0,
    threshold=6.5,
    horizon=12,
    lags=2,
    ci=0.90,
)

print(res_state[["h", "beta_H", "se_H", "beta_L", "se_L"]].head())
print(res_state.summary())              # one row per horizon and regime, with flags
print(res_state.point.head())           # DataFrame with columns H and L
res_state.plot(title="Spending multiplier: high vs low unemployment")

docs.title: State-Dependent LP-IV (lp_state_dep_iv)
docs.text:
Following Ramey & Zubairy (2018, JPE), evaluating state-dependent government spending multipliers requires instrumenting the interaction terms to identify state-specific causal effects:

\[\text{Endogenous: } [F(s_t) x_t, \; (1 - F(s_t)) x_t]$$ $$\text{Instruments: } [F(s_t) z_t, \; (1 - F(s_t)) z_t]\]

lp_state_dep_iv estimates both first-stage regressions, checks regime-specific instrument relevance via first-stage F statistics, and computes second-stage multipliers with HAC inference. threshold and gamma follow exactly the lp_state_dep conventions above:

from puremacro.lp import lp_state_dep_iv

res_rz = lp_state_dep_iv(
    df,
    y="gdp",
    x="gov_spending",
    z="military_news",
    state="unemployment_rate",
    threshold=6.5,          # 6.5 % unemployment, raw scale of the state
    transition="threshold", # Or 'logistic'
    horizon=16,
    lags=4,
    ci=0.90,
)

# Inspect high-slack vs low-slack multipliers and first-stage F stats
print(res_rz[["h", "beta_H", "first_stage_f_H", "beta_L", "first_stage_f_L"]])

# Export the multipliers table directly to LaTeX for your manuscript
latex_table = res_rz.to_latex()

docs.title: Panel Local Projections (panel_lp & panel_lp_dk)
docs.text:
For cross-country or regional panel datasets, puremacro provides two-way fixed-effects panel local projections with cluster-robust (panel_lp) or Driscoll-Kraay (1998) standard errors (panel_lp_dk, or panel_lp(..., cov_type="driscoll-kraay")) robust to cross-sectional spatial correlation and arbitrary serial correlation.

The panel can be a long-form frame whose entity and time identifiers are columns (unit_col= / time_col=), or a frame already indexed by an (entity, time) MultiIndex whose level names are given by entity_level= / time_level=:

from puremacro.lp import panel_lp, panel_lp_dk

# Long-form panel: one row per (country, date)
countries = [f"C{i}" for i in range(8)]
dates = list(pd.period_range("2000Q1", periods=60, freq="Q"))
panel_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "country": np.repeat(countries, len(dates)),
    "date": dates * len(countries),
})
panel_df["credit_shock"] = rng.standard_normal(len(panel_df))
panel_df["real_gdp"] = 0.5 * panel_df["credit_shock"] + rng.standard_normal(len(panel_df))

res_panel = panel_lp_dk(
    panel_df,
    y="real_gdp",
    x="credit_shock",
    unit_col="country",
    time_col="date",
    horizon=12,
    lags=2,
)
res_panel.plot(title="Panel LP: Credit Shock Response (Driscoll-Kraay SEs)")

# Same estimates from a frame already indexed by (country, date)
res_indexed = panel_lp_dk(
    panel_df.set_index(["country", "date"]),
    y="real_gdp", x="credit_shock",
    entity_level="country", time_level="date",
    horizon=12, lags=2,
)
assert np.allclose(res_panel.point, res_indexed.point)

# Cluster-robust SEs by entity, or Driscoll-Kraay through cov_type
res_cluster = panel_lp(panel_df, y="real_gdp", x="credit_shock",
                       unit_col="country", time_col="date", horizon=12, lags=2)
res_dk = panel_lp(panel_df, y="real_gdp", x="credit_shock",
                  unit_col="country", time_col="date", horizon=12, lags=2,
                  cov_type="driscoll-kraay")
assert np.allclose(res_dk.se, res_panel.se)

docs.title: Automatic Row-Order Invariance
docs.text: In puremacro, all panel LP estimators sort the panel index (unit, time) before applying time shifts. Even if your input DataFrame contains unsorted rows, puremacro ensures bit-identical numerical results and guards against positional lag leakage.

docs.title: Standardized Signatures & Parameter Aliases
docs.text:
Every estimator exported by puremacro.lp (including lp_state_dep and lp_did) accepts the modern keyword-only arguments below in addition to the legacy names:

Modern Parameter Accepted Legacy Alias Default Description lags n_lags 2 — except la_lp and smooth_lp (4) and lp_did (0) Number of lag controls included in the projection (for lp_did: lagged outcome changes \(\Delta y_{i,t-k}\) added as controls) horizon horizons 20, i.e. \(h = 0 \dots 20\) — except lp_iv_lewbel and lp_did (12) Max projection horizon (computes \(h = 0 \dots H\)) ci alpha 0.90 — except smooth_lp (0.95) Confidence interval coverage (e.g. ci=0.95 \(\leftrightarrow\) alpha=0.05)

ci and alpha must be probabilities in \((0, 1)\): passing a percentage by mistake (ci=90) or alpha=1.5 raises a ValueError instead of silently producing NaN bands. lp_state_dep additionally accepts state_var= as an alias of state=.

docs.title: Comparison: Local Projections vs. SVAR
docs.text: Feature Local Projections (puremacro.lp) Structural VAR (puremacro.var) Underlying Philosophy Direct multi-step regression Iterated 1-step linear model Persistence Assumption Robust to non-stationary persistence Sensitive to unit roots in companion matrix State Dependence Built-in via interaction terms (\(F(s_t) x_t\)) Requires non-linear TVP/Threshold VAR Efficiency at Long Horizons Higher variance at large \(H\) More efficient if VAR is correctly specified Data Requirements Long time series needed for high \(H\) Moderate samples suffice

docs.title: Multichain MCMC diagnostics
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Multichain MCMC diagnostics
docs.text:
Puremacro provides rank-normalized split R-hat, multichain bulk/tail effective sample size (ESS), and a Monte Carlo standard error for the posterior mean. They require only NumPy and SciPy. NUTSResult.summary() uses them automatically; the stored posterior draws and sampler algorithm are unchanged.

import numpy as np
from puremacro.mcmc import rank_normalized_rhat, multichain_ess, mcse_mean

chains = np.random.default_rng(12).normal(size=(4, 1000))
print(rank_normalized_rhat(chains))
print(multichain_ess(chains, method="bulk"))
print(multichain_ess(chains, method="tail"))
print(mcse_mean(chains))

Supply independently initialized post-warmup chains for one parameter, with shape (chains, draws). Do not stack unrelated parameters as if they were chains, or concatenate chains before computing ESS. The input is not modified.

docs.title: What each statistic measures
docs.text:
Statistic Calculation and interpretation rank_normalized_rhat Split each chain, pool average ranks, transform with normal quantiles, and take the larger R-hat of those scores and the folded scores. Folding helps reveal scale differences between chains. multichain_ess(..., method="bulk") Rank-normalized split-chain ESS, combining within-chain autocovariances with between-chain variation before Geyer's truncation. multichain_ess(..., method="tail") The smaller ESS of indicators below the pooled 5th and 95th percentiles. tail_probability changes these symmetric probabilities. multichain_ess(..., method="mean") Split-chain ESS of the untransformed draws, for inference about a finite-variance posterior mean. mcse_mean Pooled sample standard deviation divided by the square root of mean ESS. This is simulation error, not posterior parameter uncertainty.

Rank scores use Blom's (rank - 3/8)/(S + 1/4). Odd-length chains drop their central draw when split. Tail thresholds use all supplied draws before the indicators are split. ESS can exceed the retained count for negatively autocorrelated chains; the finite-sample cap is S*log10(S).

R-hat requires at least two original chains and four draws per chain. ESS accepts one chain, with the same minimum length, but cannot then test agreement between independent chains. Short, nonfinite or globally constant input yields NaN; different constant chains give infinite R-hat. If a tail indicator is constant, its evidence is unavailable and the reported tail ESS is NaN. This last policy is deliberately more explicit than assigning nominal ESS to a constant indicator.

Values near one for R-hat and large ESS are useful screening evidence. They do not prove global exploration, identify an economic model, or compensate for a wrong likelihood. Examine divergences, energy diagnostics, traces, parameter regions and the log posterior as well. Mean MCSE requires finite posterior variance and appropriate Markov-chain limit conditions; rank normalization does not make the mean of a Cauchy posterior well defined.

docs.title: Migration from 5.5.0
docs.text: Previously, the NUTS helpers called “bulk” and “tail” ESS summed separate-chain ESS estimates and did not penalize chains trapped in different regions. They now use the multichain definitions above. NUTS summary r_hat now uses the rank-normalized/folded statistic, and mcse_mean is an additional column. One-chain R-hat is NaN. Summary attributes identify the diagnostic methods. The classic gelman_rubin and single-chain effective_sample_size APIs remain available. compute_split_rhat retains its classical split definition, but constant/invalid draws no longer produce an artificial success value of one; the energy helper likewise returns NaN for a constant trace.

docs.title: Independent verification
docs.text:
The offline regression fixture records an actual ArviZ 0.22.0 run on eight stored input arrays, with input hashes, package versions and a source hash. Finite informative comparisons use relative tolerance 2e-11 for ESS and MCSE, and 2e-12 for R-hat. The discrete-tie case's constant upper-tail indicator is an explicitly tested policy difference, with the original ArviZ reference retained unchanged. ArviZ is used only to regenerate development fixtures and is not a dependency of Puremacro.

These methods follow Vehtari et al. (2021). The independent software implementation is ArviZ 0.22.0 diagnostics.

docs.title: Source registry & survey microdata
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Data sources registry and survey microdata
docs.text:
Two pieces sit on top of the existing fetchers:

  • puremacro.fetch.registry: one table of every source puremacro can reach (series, panels, real-time vintages, microdata and the narrative text connectors), with what each one needs before you call it.
  • puremacro.fetch.micro: household and person surveys fetched through public APIs or download files, returned with their survey design so that every estimate comes with a design-based standard error.

docs.title: The registry
docs.text:
The registry describes; it does not wrap. Existing fetchers keep their own signatures, and an entry records where the callable lives, whether it needs a key, the terms, and whether results may be redistributed. Importing it pulls in no network code, so it also works in the browser.

from puremacro.fetch import registry

micro = registry.sources("micro")
print(micro[["id", "auth", "credential", "redistributable"]])
print(registry.sources()["kind"].value_counts())   # series, panel, vintage, micro, text
print(registry.info("fed.scf").terms_url)

auth is one of none, key_optional, key, registration (a free account with terms accepted per collection), approval (a reviewed project proposal) or unaudited. The narrative text connectors are listed as unaudited and not redistributable: their terms have not been reviewed one by one, so check a source's own terms before republishing its text. registry.load(id) imports and returns the fetcher; registry.register(SourceInfo(...)) adds your own.

docs.title: Microdata providers
docs.text:
function survey variance design fetch_acs_pums(year, variables, ...) Census American Community Survey PUMS (1- or 5-year), persons or households 80 successive-difference replicate weights fetch_cps_basic(year, month, variables, ...) Census Current Population Survey, basic monthly weights only (no published replicates) fetch_scf(year, variables, ...) Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, summary extract five implicates, 999 bootstrap replicate weights, Rubin's rules fetch_enigh(year, variables, ...) INEGI ENIGH (Mexico), 2016 onwards strata and PSUs, Taylor linearisation

The Census API needs a free key: store it as described in Credentials (service census) rather than passing it in code. Keys never reach the cache file names, the manifest or error messages. The SCF and ENIGH need no key.

# requires: network (Census API key)
from puremacro.fetch.micro import fetch_acs_pums

acs = fetch_acs_pums(2023, ["AGEP", "WAGP", "SEX"], geography="state:11",
                     where={"AGEP": (25, 64)})
acs.mean("WAGP", by="SEX")          # estimate, se, n per group

# requires: network (federalreserve.gov)
from puremacro.fetch.micro import fetch_scf

scf = fetch_scf(2025, ["networth", "income", "age"])
scf.quantile("networth", 0.5)                  # published: $215,900
scf.ratio("networth", "income", q=0.5)         # median wealth / median income
scf.gini("networth"), scf.top_share("networth", 0.01)

Downloads go through the shared HTTP cache, so a second call is offline.

docs.title: Facts worth knowing before you estimate
docs.text:
• Not-applicable codes. Census codes such as WAGP == -1 (persons under 15) or ESR == 0 are set to NaN by default, read from the endpoint's own codebook, so they do not enter means and totals as values. na_to_nan=False keeps the raw codes and frame.codebook lists every labelled code. CPS sends some earnings codes with implied decimals (-1 arrives as -0.01); those are handled too.
  • SCF dollars. The Fed publishes every wave of the summary extract in the dollars of the latest survey. With the 2025 release (October 2026) the 2022 levels rose by 9.0%; ratios, shares and the Gini are unaffected.
  • SCF implicates. The SCF imputes missing answers five times. Each household has five rows; estimates average over implicates and the standard error adds the between-implicate variance (Rubin's rules) to the sampling variance from the replicates on implicate 1, as the Fed's documentation prescribes.
  • ENIGH has no replicate weights. Means, totals and quantiles use Taylor linearisation with the ultimate-cluster variance; ratio, gini and top_share raise NotImplementedError there rather than return an estimate without its standard error.

docs.title: Estimating from a MicroFrame
docs.text:
Every provider returns a MicroFrame: the records, a SurveyDesign that says which columns are weights and how to turn replicates into variances, and the query that produced them. The estimators mean, total, quantile, share, ratio, gini and top_share all return the estimate, its standard error, the unweighted n and the number of implicates, optionally by groups.

The block below builds a frame by hand so it runs offline; a fetched frame behaves the same way.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from puremacro.fetch.micro import MicroFrame, SurveyDesign

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
w = rng.uniform(50, 150, n)
records = pd.DataFrame({"PWGTP": w, "WAGP": rng.lognormal(10.5, 0.8, n),
                        "SEX": rng.integers(1, 3, n)})
replicates = pd.DataFrame(w[:, None] * rng.uniform(0.7, 1.3, (n, 80)),
                          columns=[f"PWGTP{r}" for r in range(1, 81)])
frame = MicroFrame(pd.concat([records, replicates], axis=1),
                   SurveyDesign.acs_pums(), unit="person",
                   source="synthetic", vintage="demo")

print(frame.mean("WAGP", by="SEX"))
print(frame.quantile("WAGP", 0.5))
print(frame.gini("WAGP"))
print(frame.top_share("WAGP", 0.10))

SurveyDesign(...) describes any other survey: a main weight, replicate weights with their method ("sdr", "bootstrap", "jk1", ...), scale and centring, or strata and PSUs for method="taylor".

docs.title: Worked example: an Aiyagari economy against the SCF
docs.text:
python -m puremacro.examples.scf_aiyagari --output results/

The script fetches one SCF wave, estimates wealth-to-income ratios and concentration moments with replicate standard errors, calibrates the discount factor of a dp Aiyagari model (solved by EGM) to one ratio, carries the target's sampling error into beta by the delta method, and sets the untargeted moments against the data. On SCF 2025, with beta calibrated to median wealth over median income:

moment SCF (se) model (se) median wealth / median income 2.628 (0.077) targeted mean wealth / mean income 8.518 (0.175) 3.912 (0.101) Gini 0.824 (0.004) 0.591 (0.001) top 1% share 0.313 (0.009) 0.063 (0.000) top 10% share 0.721 (0.007) 0.379 (0.001) bottom 50% share 0.021 (0.001) 0.088 (0.001)

beta = 0.952 (se 0.002), r = 4.08%, K/Y = 2.98. The gap at the top is the known failure of the one-asset model with earnings risk and a borrowing limit; nothing in the example is tuned to close it. Targeting the mean ratio instead is not possible with beta < 1: the model reaches at most 7.55, with r < 0.

docs.title: Sequence-Space HANK
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Sequence-Space HANK
docs.text:
puremacro.models is the structural side of the package: models you solve for a steady state and then push along a transition path, with no compiler, no MEX toolchain and no Dynare in the loop. Everything on this page is offline — none of it touches the network.

from puremacro.models import solve_hank_sequence_space

res = solve_hank_sequence_space(T=40, n_a=100, beta=0.985, r_ss=0.01,
                                phi_pi=1.5, kappa=0.1,
                                shock_magnitude=0.0025, shock_rho=0.7)
print(res.summary())

That is a 25bp contractionary monetary shock in a one-asset heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian economy, and it returns in 0.21 s.

docs.title: What the package ships
docs.text:
module import path what it solves hank_sequence_space puremacro.models one-asset HANK: EGM steady state, exact \(\mathcal{O}(T^2)\) Fake News algorithm, targeted fiscal transfers, and GE transition by one T x T linear solve monetary_transmission puremacro.models HANK vs. RANK monetary policy and balance-sheet transmission with Kaplan-Moll-Violante decomposition dmp_regime_dependent puremacro.models representative-firm DMP, Hall sticky wages, regime-dependent vacancy cost and TFP bump nested_dmp (package) puremacro.models.nested_dmp heterogeneous-firm DMP with Bayesian beliefs about the policy rule: steady state, perfect-foresight IRF, IRF-matching estimation, recursive stochastic solve, welfare sweep smm puremacro.models.smm moment loader and objective for estimating dmp_regime_dependent against local-projection IRFs

For the HANK vs. RANK monetary transmission simulator and its browser lab (curso/site/labs/), see Monetary Transmission Simulator: HANK vs. RANK.
