docs.title: Quantitative Spatial Economics and Gravity Trade General Equilibrium
docs.text:
puremacro.trade and puremacro.spatial implement two general equilibrium frameworks for international trade and economic geography: 1. The multi-country, multi-sector Ricardian trade model with input-output linkages, intermediate goods, and tariffs developed by Caliendo and Parro (2015, Review of Economic Studies), solved via Exact Hat Algebra (puremacro.trade.CaliendoParroModel). 2. The continuous geographic spatial equilibrium model with labor mobility, agglomeration externalities, and congestion forces developed by Allen and Arkolakis (2014, Quarterly Journal of Economics) (puremacro.spatial.AllenArkolakisModel).

Both conform strictly to the pure Python / Pyodide runtime contract (zero C++ dependencies, pure NumPy/SciPy/Pandas/Matplotlib), enabling rapid counterfactual policy evaluations—such as tariff changes and retaliation, regional transport infrastructure investments, and localized environmental shocks. The full multi-country, multi-sector trade CGE on input-output tables (calibrate_trade_model, solve_trade_equilibrium) is documented in consistent trade accounting; its bundled data are described in section 7.

docs.title: 1.1 Caliendo-Parro (2015) Multi-Sector Ricardian Trade with I-O Linkages
docs.text:
Consider a global economy with \(N\) countries (\(n, i = 1, \dots, N\)) and \(J\) sectors (\(j, k = 1, \dots, J\)). Production in country \(n\) and sector \(j\) combines labor \(L_{n, j}\) with intermediate inputs from all sectors \(k = 1, \dots, J\) under constant returns to scale:

\[Y_n^j = z_n^j \left( L_n^j \right)^{\gamma_n^j} \prod_{k=1}^J \left( M_n^{j, k} \right)^{\gamma_n^{j, k}}\]

where \(\gamma_n^j > 0\) is the value-added share, \(\gamma_n^{j, k} \ge 0\) is the cost share of intermediate input \(k\) in producing good \(j\), and cost shares sum to unity:

\[\gamma_n^j + \sum_{k=1}^J \gamma_n^{j, k} = 1, \quad \forall n, j\]

Cost minimization implies unit cost of the input bundle:

\[c_n^j = \Upsilon_n^j w_n^{\gamma_n^j} \prod_{k=1}^J \left( P_n^k \right)^{\gamma_n^{j, k}}\]

where \(w_n\) is the competitive wage in country \(n\), \(P_n^k\) is the composite price index of sector \(k\), and \(\Upsilon_n^j\) is a constant.

docs.title: 1.2 Exact Hat Algebra Formulation
docs.text:
Following the Exact Hat Algebra methodology of Dekle, Eaton, and Kortum (2007) extended by Caliendo and Parro (2015), counterfactual changes are expressed in proportional changes \(\hat{x} \equiv x' / x\). This allows researchers to solve for counterfactual equilibria directly from observed baseline trade shares \(\pi_{ni}^j\) and input-output matrices without estimating unobserved fundamentals (such as technology levels \(T_n^j\) or bilateral baseline iceberg frictions \(d_{ni}^j\)).

Given a counterfactual gross tariff change \(\hat{\tau}_{ni}^j \equiv (1 + t_{ni}'^j) / (1 + t_{ni}^j)\):

  1. Unit Cost Changes: $\(\hat{c}_n^j = \hat{w}_n^{\gamma_n^j} \prod_{k=1}^J \left( \hat{P}_n^k \right)^{\gamma_n^{j, k}}\)$
  2. Bilateral Trade Share Changes (Eaton-Kortum Gravity): $\(\hat{\pi}_{ni}^j = \left( \frac{\hat{c}_i^j \hat{\tau}_{ni}^j}{\hat{P}_n^j} \right)^{-\theta_j}\)$ where \(\theta_j > 0\) is the sector-specific trade elasticity.
  3. Sectoral Price Index Changes: $\(\hat{P}_n^j = \left( \sum_{i=1}^N \pi_{ni}^j \left( \hat{c}_i^j \hat{\tau}_{ni}^j \right)^{-\theta_j} \right)^{-\frac{1}{\theta_j}}\)$
  4. Expenditures & Goods Market Clearing: Counterfactual sectoral expenditures \(X_n'^j\) and gross output \(Y_n'^j\) solve the global Leontief input-output balance: $\(X_n'^j = \alpha_n^j I_n' + \sum_{k=1}^J \gamma_n^{k, j} Y_n'^k, \quad Y_n'^j = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\pi_{in}'^j}{\tau_{in}'^j} X_i'^j\)$ where \(I_n' = w_n' L_n + R_n' + D_n'\) is national income comprising labor income, tariff revenues \(R_n'\), and trade deficits \(D_n'\).
  5. Labor Market Clearing & Wage Tatonnement: Wages \(\hat{w}_n\) are updated iteratively until excess labor demand satisfies: $\(\left| \sum_{j=1}^J \gamma_n^j Y_n'^j - w_n' L_n \right| < \text{tol}\)$
  6. Real Income & Welfare Changes: $\(\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_n = \frac{\hat{I}_n}{\hat{P}_n}, \quad \text{where} \quad \hat{P}_n = \prod_{j=1}^J \left( \hat{P}_n^j \right)^{\alpha_n^j}\)$

docs.title: 1.3 Allen-Arkolakis (2014) Geographic Gravity Model with Labor Mobility
docs.text: Allen and Arkolakis (2014) formulate a continuous spatial general equilibrium model over \(N\) geographical regions where workers freely migrate until real utility is equalized everywhere.

docs.title: Trade Flows and Market Access
docs.text:
Bilateral trade between origin \(i\) and destination \(j\) satisfies gravity:

\[\pi_{ij} = \frac{\left( \frac{w_i \tau_{ij}}{A_i} \right)^{-\theta}}{\sum_{k=1}^N \left( \frac{w_k \tau_{kj}}{A_k} \right)^{-\theta}} = \frac{\left( \frac{w_i \tau_{ij}}{A_i} \right)^{-\theta}}{P_j^{-\theta}}\]

where \(\tau_{ij} \ge 1\) are iceberg trade costs (\(\tau_{ii} = 1\)), \(\theta = \sigma - 1\) is the trade elasticity, and \(P_j\) is the Consumer Market Access index:

\[P_j^{-\theta} = \text{CMA}_j = \sum_{i=1}^N \tau_{ij}^{-\theta} \left( \frac{w_i}{A_i} \right)^{-\theta}\]

Firm Market Access (\(\text{FMA}_i\)) captures export demand:

\[\text{FMA}_i = \sum_{j=1}^N \tau_{ij}^{-\theta} P_j^\theta w_j L_j\]

Goods market clearing equates regional labor income to total sales:

\[w_i L_i = \sum_{j=1}^N \pi_{ij} w_j L_j = \left( \frac{w_i}{A_i} \right)^{-\theta} \text{FMA}_i\]

docs.title: 1.4 Agglomeration, Congestion, and Spatial Equilibrium
docs.text:
Worker utility in location \(i\) depends on real wages, local amenities \(a_i\), and endogenous population \(L_i\):

\[u_i = a_i \frac{w_i}{P_i}\]

Endogenous productivity and amenities incorporate spillover forces: - Productivity Agglomeration: \(A_i = \bar{A}_i L_i^\alpha\), where \(\alpha > 0\) reflects Marshallian external scale economies. - Amenity Congestion: \(a_i = \bar{a}_i L_i^\beta\), where \(\beta < 0\) captures housing supply inelasticity, commuting congestion, and pollution.

docs.title: Spatial Utility Equalization
docs.text:
Free labor mobility equalizes utility across all populated regions:

\[u_i = \bar{u}, \quad \forall i \quad \implies \quad L_i = \bar{L} \frac{\left( \frac{w_i \bar{a}_i}{P_i} \right)^{-\frac{1}{\beta}}}{\sum_k \left( \frac{w_k \bar{a}_k}{P_k} \right)^{-\frac{1}{\beta}}}\]

docs.title: Uniqueness Theorem
docs.text:
Allen and Arkolakis (2014, Theorem 2) prove that the spatial general equilibrium is unique and strictly stable if and only if congestion forces dominate agglomeration spillovers:

\[\alpha + \beta \le \frac{\theta}{1 + \theta} \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha \le \frac{1}{\theta}\]

AllenArkolakisModel.is_unique verifies this condition automatically during initialization.

docs.title: 2. Methodological & Model Options
docs.text: Dimension Caliendo-Parro (2015) Allen-Arkolakis (2014) Core Economic Mechanism Multi-sector trade with input-output linkages & tariffs Spatial labor mobility with agglomeration & congestion Solving Approach Exact Hat Algebra on observable trade shares Contraction mapping fixed point on \((w_i, L_i)\) Endogenous Margins Sectoral prices, wages, expenditure shares Population distribution, wages, market access Labor Mobility Immobile across countries; mobile across sectors Free continuous spatial mobility across regions Primary Use Cases Free trade agreements, tariff changes, retaliation High-speed rail, highway corridors, climate shocks Convergence Rate 10–30 iterations (\(< 0.01\) s) 20–50 iterations (\(< 0.005\) s)

docs.title: 2.1 Hardware backends (backend=, 3.4.0)
docs.text:
The Allen-Arkolakis fixed-point solver accepts a backend keyword — "numpy" (the default), "mlx" (Apple Silicon) or "cupy" (NVIDIA); with the model aa_model of section 4:

aa_res = aa_model.solve_equilibrium(backend="mlx")
cf_res = aa_model.solve_counterfactual(trade_costs_new=tau_new, backend="mlx")

Three properties are worth knowing before you reach for one:

  • NumPy is the oracle. Every accelerated path is checked against the NumPy reference, never the other way round. numpy is always available and keeps the Pyodide contract intact.
  • tol still means tol. Metal has no float64, so the MLX contraction in AllenArkolakisModel runs in float32 down to a 1e-6 floor; the result is then polished with the float64 NumPy contraction warm-started at the device solution, so converged refers to the tol you asked for.
  • Failure is loud and non-fatal. A backend that is not installed, an array namespace that will not import, or an exception on the device each emit a RuntimeWarning and fall back to NumPy. An accelerated result that did not converge is never returned either: AllenArkolakisModel finishes the device solution with the float64 NumPy contraction above — no warning, because converged is then the NumPy verdict at your tol.
from puremacro._backend import available_backends
available_backends()          # ('numpy', 'numba', 'mlx') on this machine

CaliendoParroModel and the trade CGE solve_trade_equilibrium run on NumPy only (solve_trade_equilibrium(..., backend=...) accepts "numpy" and raises NotImplementedError for anything else). GPU tariff counterfactuals — batched Jacobians, homotopy continuation, and the optional torch / mlx solvers of puremacro.trade.gpu — are a separate surface documented in docs/trade_gpu.md.

docs.title: 1. Caliendo-Parro 3-Country, 2-Sector Economy
docs.text:
• Countries: three stylized economies HOM, FOR and ROW with hand-set trade shares (no data).
  • Sectors: Manufacturing (tradable, \(\theta = 5.0\)) and Services (non-tradable, \(\theta = 4.0\)).
  • Value added share: \(\gamma_n^j = 0.50\); input-output share: \(\gamma_n^{j, k} = 0.25\).
  • Initial tariffs: baseline free trade \(\tau_{ni}^j = 1.0\).

docs.title: 2. Allen-Arkolakis 4-City US Geography
docs.text:
• Cities: New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, Houston (with actual latitude/longitude coordinates).
  • Trade elasticity: \(\theta = 4.0\).
  • Agglomeration elasticity: \(\alpha = 0.08\); congestion elasticity: \(\beta = -0.35\).
  • Iceberg costs: parametrized via Haversine great-circle distances: \(\tau_{ij} = 1.0 + \delta \cdot d_{ij}^\gamma\).

docs.title: 4. Runnable Worked Examples
docs.text:
The following scripts simulate a \(25\%\) bilateral tariff shock in Caliendo-Parro and evaluate a transport infrastructure investment in Allen-Arkolakis:

import numpy as np
from puremacro.trade import CaliendoParroModel

# 3-Country, 2-Sector Caliendo-Parro Trade Economy with Tariffs (hand-set shares)
N, J = 3, 2
trade_shares = np.zeros((J, N, N))
trade_shares[0] = np.array([
    [0.60, 0.20, 0.20],
    [0.20, 0.60, 0.20],
    [0.20, 0.20, 0.60],
])
trade_shares[1] = np.eye(N)  # Non-tradables

cp_model = CaliendoParroModel(
    trade_shares=trade_shares,
    gamma_va=np.full((N, J), 0.50),
    gamma_io=np.full((N, J, J), 0.25),
    alpha=np.full((N, J), 0.50),
    theta=np.array([5.0, 4.0]),
    labor_income=np.array([100.0, 100.0, 100.0]),
    nontradables=[1],
    country_codes=["HOM", "FOR", "ROW"],
    sector_codes=["Manufactures", "Services"],
)

# Simulate a 25% tariff by HOM on manufactures from FOR
cp_res = cp_model.simulate_tariff_shock("HOM", "FOR", sector="Manufactures", tariff_rate=0.25)
assert cp_res.converged
assert len(cp_res.welfare_pct) == 3
print(f"Caliendo-Parro HOM welfare change: {cp_res.welfare_pct[0]:+.2f}%")

import numpy as np
from puremacro.spatial import AllenArkolakisModel

# 4-City Allen-Arkolakis Spatial GE Model with Labor Mobility
coords = np.array([
    [40.7128, -74.0060],  # NYC
    [34.0522, -118.2437], # LA
    [41.8781, -87.6298],  # Chicago
    [29.7604, -95.3698],  # Houston
])
names = ["NYC", "LA", "CHI", "HOU"]

aa_model = AllenArkolakisModel.from_coordinates(
    coords,
    region_names=names,
    theta=4.0,
    alpha=0.08,
    beta=-0.35,
    total_population=100.0,
)
aa_res = aa_model.solve_equilibrium()
assert aa_res.converged
assert np.isclose(np.sum(aa_res.population), 100.0)

# Simulate Regional Transport Infrastructure Shock (20% bilateral cost reduction between NYC and Chicago)
infra_res = aa_model.simulate_infrastructure_shock("NYC", "CHI", cost_reduction=0.20)
assert infra_res.converged

print(f"Allen-Arkolakis population in NYC: {aa_res.population[0]:.2f}, LA: {aa_res.population[1]:.2f}")
print(f"Infrastructure welfare change: {infra_res.welfare_pct:+.2f}%")

docs.title: CaliendoParroResult
docs.text:
• res.w_hat: Gross change in nominal wages \(\hat{w}_n\).
  • res.P_index_hat: Gross change in consumer price indices \(\hat{P}_n\).
  • res.real_wage_hat: Gross change in real wages \(\hat{w}_n / \hat{P}_n\).
  • res.welfare_pct: Percentage change in national welfare \((\widehat{\mathcal{W}}_n - 1) \times 100\).
  • res.tariff_revenue_prime: Counterfactual tariff revenues by country.
  • res.summary() -> pd.DataFrame: Country-level summary of welfare, wages, prices, and revenues.
  • res.sector_summary() -> pd.DataFrame: Country-by-sector breakdown of gross outputs and prices.
  • res.to_frame(), res.to_markdown(), res.to_latex(), res.to_typst(): Publication serialization formats.
  • res.plot(kind="welfare") -> matplotlib.figure.Figure: Bar chart of country welfare impacts.

docs.title: AllenArkolakisResult
docs.text:
• res.wages: Equilibrium regional nominal wages \(w_i\).
  • res.population: Spatial population distribution \(L_i\), strictly conserving \(\sum L_i = \bar{L}\).
  • res.price_index: Spatial CES price index \(P_i\).
  • res.real_wages: Spatial real wages \(w_i / P_i\).
  • res.welfare: Equalized spatial utility level \(\bar{u}\).
  • res.consumer_market_access: Regional consumer market access index \(\text{CMA}_i\).
  • res.firm_market_access: Regional firm export market access index \(\text{FMA}_i\).
  • res.welfare_pct: Counterfactual percentage utility change \((\bar{u}' / \bar{u} - 1) \times 100\).
  • res.summary() -> pd.DataFrame: Regional summary table.
  • res.plot(kind="spatial") -> matplotlib.figure.Figure: Geographic scatter plot sized by population and colored by real wages.

docs.title: 7. Bundled calibration data and attribution
docs.text:
One OECD Inter-Country Input-Output table ships inside the package, so load_icio_data() needs no file outside your installation: the OECD ICIO tables, 2023 edition, reference year 2019, in current million USD, aggregated to the 19 G20 member countries plus ROW (the other economies of the OECD tables) and to the 20 ISIC Rev.4 sections A to T, with final uses C (final consumption), I (gross capital formation) and Cx (residents' direct purchases abroad). The grouping is the published ISIC section structure and the country rule is stated in the data notice; value added is split 2/3 labour, 1/3 capital, because the OECD tables do not split it.

from puremacro.trade import calibrate_trade_model
from puremacro.trade.data import load_icio_data

icio = load_icio_data(return_structured=True)      # the bundled 2019 table
print(icio.matrix.shape, icio.country_codes[:3], icio.sector_codes[:3])   # (403, 460)
calib = calibrate_trade_model(icio.matrix, country_codes=icio.country_codes,
                              sector_codes=icio.sector_codes)
print(calib.nc, calib.ns)                          # 20 countries, 20 sectors

The table is an adaptation of OECD data, redistributed under the OECD terms of use, which permit reuse and adaptation with attribution. If you publish results computed from it, credit the OECD: "OECD (2023), OECD Inter-Country Input-Output Tables, http://oe.cd/icio", not puremacro; the OECD is not affiliated with this project and does not endorse it, and the opinions expressed in work built on this adaptation should not be reported as the official views of the OECD or of its member countries. puremacro's MIT licence covers its own code, not this third-party data.

The table is rebuilt byte for byte from the public release with python tools/build_icio_isic.py --download, which downloads the OECD archive into $PUREMACRO_OECD_ICIO_DIR (default ~/.cache/puremacro/oecd_icio) and refuses a source file whose MD5 is not the registered one; a copy already on disk can be passed with --source. Other years, editions or groupings go through the native readers of puremacro.trade.mrio and puremacro.trade.data (load_oecd_icio_granular, load_figaro, ...). To solve full-size tables use solve_trade_equilibrium(calib, method="equilibrated_newton"), which runs Newton on the row/column-equilibrated Jacobian and, on failure, names in metadata the country whose price-level direction has become singular. The full notice, including the source and bundled-file digests, the concordance and the build record, is in puremacro/trade/_datafiles/SOURCES.md, which is installed with the package.

docs.title: Empirical-to-structural estimation
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: From empirical moments to structural parameters
docs.text:
puremacro.structural fits a callable structural model to empirical moment estimates, keeping their full covariance, labels, units and research metadata. It connects existing empirical estimates to a model; it does not supply a new economic model or identify one merely by optimizing it.

The covariance contract is Cov(empirical moment estimators). For example, the diagonal contains the squared standard errors of estimated impulse responses, and the off-diagonals contain covariance between those estimates. Do not pass the covariance of raw observations or a covariance multiplied by sample size. fit_structural never applies a sample-size multiplier.

docs.title: A complete small example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from puremacro.structural import MomentTargets, fit_structural

h = np.arange(4)
empirical_irf = np.array([0.80, 0.61, 0.47, 0.34])
covariance = 0.01 * 0.5 ** np.abs(h[:, None] - h[None, :])
targets = MomentTargets.from_irf(
    empirical_irf,
    covariance=covariance,
    response="output",
    shock="monetary",
    units="percent per 25bp tightening",
    metadata={"sample": "illustrative", "shock_size": 25, "shock_unit": "bp"},
)

# This reduced example has a closed-form model response. A DSGE, VFI or
# HANK model wrapper can return its selected moments through the same API.
def moments_at(theta):
    impact, persistence = theta
    return impact * persistence ** h

result = fit_structural(
    moments_at, targets, [0.7, 0.7],
    parameter_names=("impact", "persistence"),
    bounds=[(0, None), (0, 0.99)],
    moment_labels=targets.labels,
)
print(result.summary())
print(result.moment_fit())
print(result.to_latex())

This is synthetic input, not an empirical monetary-policy estimate. Model responses must use the same variables, horizon frequency, cumulative/level convention, transformation and shock normalization as the targets. The adapter records these choices; it does not infer or reconcile them.

docs.title: Constructing and combining targets
docs.text:
Entry point Contract MomentTargets(values, covariance, labels, units=..., metadata=...) One-dimensional values, full square covariance, unique string labels. MomentTargets.from_frame(frame, covariance=...) Columns label, estimate, unit; index labels and unspecified units are fallback choices. Column names can be changed with label=, value=, unit=. MomentTargets.from_irf(irf, covariance=..., response=..., shock=..., units=...) One selected response to one shock: a vector or an LP table with h and beta. Select a VAR tensor slice explicitly first. MomentTargets.from_draws(draws, values=..., labels=...) Rows are joint sampling/bootstrap replicates, columns are moments. Sample covariance uses ddof=1 without division by the number of replicates. targets.select(labels) Subsets/reorders both the moment vector and covariance axes. targets.rescale(factors, units=...) Applies D m and D S D' together. Metadata records the previous units and scaling. targets.stack(other, cross_covariance=...) Explicit cross block in the two label orders. Alternatively use assume_independent=True, which records that assumption.

Pointwise IRF bands and standard errors do not determine a joint covariance. For bootstrap targets, reestimate all moments on each valid joint replicate, retaining the dependence across horizons and responses. Posterior draws and independently resampled horizons are not automatically valid inputs to from_draws. The supplied values remain the original point estimates. There is no automatic removal of failed/nonfinite replicates.

Labeled pandas inputs must have exactly the declared order. Plain arrays are positional: the caller guarantees their order. A model returning a pandas Series is checked against target labels on every evaluation. An optional moment_labels= declaration catches a mismatched model order before fitting.

Target arrays are copied and made read-only. Mapping/list/array metadata is copied and frozen; from_frame and from_irf preserve table attributes. Stacking preserves both component metadata records, including separate samples and shock normalizations. A stack does not make incompatible units compatible.

docs.title: Joint local-projection covariance
docs.text:
lp_moment_targets estimates the empirical responses and their joint covariance directly from a regularly spaced time-series table:

from puremacro.structural import lp_moment_targets

import pandas as pd
# Synthetic, already-transformed data for a runnable API illustration.
rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
data = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(160, 3)),
                    columns=["output", "inflation", "monetary_innovation"],
                    index=pd.period_range("1980Q1", periods=160, freq="Q"))
empirical = lp_moment_targets(
    data,
    responses=("output", "inflation"),
    shock="monetary_innovation",
    horizons=(0, 1, 2, 3),
    response_units={"output": "log points", "inflation": "percentage points"},
    shock_unit="percentage points",
    frequency="Q",
    lags=2,
    bandwidth=4,
    shock_size=0.25,
)

frequency is a pandas alias: a PeriodIndex takes period aliases ("Q", "M", "Y"), while a DatetimeIndex accepts both the pandas 2 ("Q", "M", "Y") and the pandas 3 ("QE", "ME", "YE", which need pandas 2.2 or later, or "QS"/"MS"/"YS") offset spellings, compared at the index's own resolution; an unrecognised alias raises a ValueError that names the index kind.

Like lp_hac, the dependent variable is y[t+h] - y[t-1]. The design includes the contemporaneous shock, response/shock lags, and any declared controls both contemporaneously and at each lag. A structural response must match that convention. Moment order is response first, then the supplied horizon order; labels are response:shock:h=H.

Coefficient influence contributions from all regressions are aligned on the original time grid, with zeros outside their estimation windows. Applying a single Bartlett HAC kernel to that matrix retains cross-horizon and cross-response covariance. The default bandwidth is max(horizons)+1, an explicit heuristic; no small-sample correction is applied. This estimator requires an exogenous shock conditional on the controls and regular time-series HAC conditions. It is neither LP-IV nor inference robust to weak identification. The covariance may be singular when too many moments are included; the subsequent fit will refuse it.

Inputs must be finite and their index unique/increasing. Datetime/Period indices are checked against frequency; other indices rely on the caller's explicit frequency declaration. The function does not drop missing periods or infer percentage conversions from variable names. Metadata retains the sample, frequency, per-moment observation counts, transformation, bandwidth, units and shock magnitude.

docs.title: Criterion and local covariance
docs.text:
Let S denote the supplied covariance, r(theta) = m(theta) - m_hat, and G = dm/dtheta. The implementation minimizes

\[ Q(\theta)=r(\theta)' W r(\theta), \qquad W=S^{-1}\text{ by default}. \]

Writing S = D L L' D, with D containing target standard errors and L the Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix, the weighted residual is L^{-1} D^{-1} r. Standardizing before factorization makes the covariance checks insensitive to different moment units. The reported objective is the full quadratic criterion using the original weights.

The optimizer uses coordinates centered at theta0, scaled by the initial weighted Jacobian, and adaptive Jacobian trust-region scaling. It also divides all residuals by one common sampling-uncertainty scale. This preserves relative weights and the minimizer while preventing parameter units, large offsets or arbitrary scalar multiples of custom weights from causing premature numerical convergence. These internal normalizations do not change the reported objective or parameter covariance.

For a fixed supplied positive-definite weight=W, the covariance is

\[ A=(G'WG)^{-1}G'W,\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\hat\theta)=A S A'. \]

With optimal weighting this reduces to (G' S^{-1} G)^{-1}. The implementation uses the SVD of the weighted Jacobian and covariance factors, avoiding an explicit inverse of its normal equations. It never estimates a residual variance or rescales the supplied covariance by fit quality.

These are local, correctly specified minimum-distance formulas; regular asymptotic inference requires a consistent moment covariance and full-rank interior identification. See Newey and McFadden (1994), Sections 3.1, 4.1 and 5.2, for the minimum-distance framework, and Section 9.5 for the overidentification result. Original chapter.

jac(theta) may supply the unweighted moments-by-parameters Jacobian. Otherwise the bridge uses second-order finite differences, with one-sided stencils near parameter bounds. This does not implement missing derivatives through heterogeneous-agent distributions or general equilibrium. Stochastic, nonsmooth, or grid-discontinuous model moments need a different inference design; fixing a simulation seed alone does not eliminate simulation error. Optimization uses a local trust-region reflective solve and does not establish a global optimum. SciPy least_squares reference.

docs.title: Acceptance and identification diagnostics
docs.text:
result.success is numerical optimizer success. result.inference_valid means the local numerical checks permit the stated conditional formulas. Neither asserts that the economic model is correct.

Normal standard errors and intervals are returned as NaN, with a warning and named diagnostic reasons, if the optimizer fails, the weighted Jacobian lacks column rank, its condition number exceeds condition_limit, any parameter is at/near a bound, or an interior solution fails a numerical first-order condition (nonstationary_solution). The latter checks the residual projection onto the local weighted Jacobian's column space; overidentified models may retain residuals orthogonal to that space. The result retains estimates, moment residuals and optimizer information for inspection. Rank uses s_i > rank_rtol * s_max (default rank_rtol=1e-10); the default condition limit is 1e8. Conditioning depends on the supplied parameter units. This is a numerical diagnostic, not a statistical test of weak identification; full local rank also does not establish global identification.

Covariances and weights must be finite, symmetric and positive semidefinite as data; fitting additionally requires numerically positive-definite factorizations. Singular covariances are refused rather than inverted with a pseudoinverse. No ridge, eigenvalue clipping or automatic moment deletion is performed. Redundant targets can be explicitly removed with select, with the economic reason for the selection recorded by the researcher.

Model nonfinite outputs, incompatible dimensions and invalid derivatives raise errors. Failed economic solves should likewise raise in moments_at; the bridge does not convert an invalid solve into a moment vector or a penalty.

docs.title: Overidentification and held-out moments
docs.text:
For q > p, the minimized criterion has the usual asymptotic chi-square reference with q-p degrees of freedom only under the relevant regular correct-specification conditions and optimal weighting. To request it, set assume_correct_specification=True. This records an assumption, not a test that the assumption holds. j_statistic and j_pvalue stay NaN for custom weights, exact/underidentification, or failed numerical inference checks. The criterion is always available as objective; j_df is max(q-p, 0).

unused = MomentTargets([0.2], [[0.02]], ("output_later",), targets.units[0])
checked = fit_structural(
    moments_at, targets, [0.7, 0.7],
    bounds=[(0, None), (0, 0.99)],
    held_out=unused,
    held_out_moments_at=lambda theta: [theta[0] * theta[1] ** 6],
)
print(checked.moment_fit(held_out=True))

Held-out labels must be distinct from fitted labels. Their comparison never affects the objective. It reports targets, target standard errors, model predictions and residuals, with no p-value or predictive interval: uncertainty in fitted parameters and cross-covariance with held-out estimates have not been supplied. Holding out moments from the same sample does not imply statistical independence.

docs.title: Evidence and limits
docs.text: tests/test_structural_bridge.py checks a closed-form correlated GLS solution and covariance, arbitrary-weight sandwich covariance, the correctly scaled J statistic, exact nonlinear impulse-response recovery, mixed-unit invariance, adapters and named failure cases. These are analytical and software checks. They do not constitute an empirical model replication or establish nominal coverage for every estimator producing targets. HA distribution derivatives, weak-identification-robust confidence sets, simulation-noise corrections, global search and inference under misspecification remain outside this bridge.

docs.title: Reproducible studies and scenarios
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Reproducible studies and comparisons
docs.text: puremacro.study records one explicit statistical study: selected inputs, transformations, units, identification assumptions, estimator settings, results, diagnostics, dependency versions and checksums. It reuses the existing LP and recursive VAR estimators, report formatters and portable runtime frame codec. It does not infer a causal interpretation or certify an economic model.

docs.title: Run and compare local projections
docs.text:
This complete offline example uses synthetic observations. Its exogeneity assumption is declared for illustration; the workflow does not establish it.

from dataclasses import replace
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from puremacro.study import (
    VariableSpec, StudySpec, run_study, compare_studies,
    save_study, load_study,
)

rng = np.random.default_rng(173)
observations = rng.normal(size=(240, 3))
for t in range(1, len(observations)):
    observations[t] += 0.4 * observations[t - 1]
data = pd.DataFrame(
    observations,
    columns=["shock", "output", "price"],
    index=pd.period_range("1960Q1", periods=240, freq="Q"),
)
data.attrs = {"source": "synthetic demonstration", "data_seed": 173}

spec = StudySpec(
    name="LP, two lags", method="lp",
    variables=(
        VariableSpec("shock", "percentage points"),
        VariableSpec("output", "index points"),
        VariableSpec("price", "index points"),
    ),
    responses=("output",), shock="shock", controls=("price",),
    frequency="Q", identification="observed_exogenous",
    lags=2, horizon=8, shock_size=0.25, ci=0.90,
)
baseline = run_study(data, spec)
alternative = run_study(data, replace(spec, name="LP, four lags", lags=4))
comparison = compare_studies(baseline, alternative)
print(comparison.to_frame())
print(baseline.audits)

# A new directory only: existing results are not overwritten.
baseline.write_report("study_output/lp_two_lags")
# Or retain the complete record in memory, including in a browser kernel.
payload = save_study(baseline)
restored = load_study(payload)
assert restored.manifest == baseline.manifest

write_report writes Markdown, LaTeX, Typst and CSV tables, manifest.json, and the lossless study.pmstudy archive. Markdown and the manifest include methods, assumptions, effective samples and audit limits. CSV is a presentation format; use the archive to preserve index types and supported DataFrame.attrs. to_json() contains the manifest and output tables, not the input frames. Both StudyResult and StudyComparison are frozen records; returned frames and manifest dictionaries are independent copies.

docs.title: State the transformations, units and time grid
docs.text:
Every input column needs a VariableSpec. Available transformations are identity, log, diff, and logdiff; scale multiplies the transformed series. The declared unit describes that final quantity. For example, VariableSpec("output", "percent log growth", "logdiff", 100) computes 100 * diff(log(output)). The caller supplies positive output levels. There is no variable-name heuristic for percent conversion or annualization.

The input index must be a unique, increasing, consecutive PeriodIndex or DatetimeIndex. frequency="Q" describes quarterly periods; for timestamp indices use the corresponding calendar offset, such as "QS" or "MS". Quarter/month-end aliases accept the supported pandas spelling. A missing period or nonfinite value is an error; time is never compressed by dropping missing rows. Extra undeclared columns are errors too.

sample_start and sample_end, if supplied, must identify observations on that grid. Selection precedes transformation. Differencing removes exactly the first selected observation from every series; it does not borrow a value from outside the selected sample. The archive retains the selected raw inputs, not rows outside the requested sample. Source, vintage and retrieval notes can be stored in data.attrs; unsupported metadata objects raise an error instead of being silently discarded.

docs.title: Understand the estimator contracts
docs.text:
Setting method="lp" method="var_cholesky" Identification observed_exogenous: the observed shock is exogenous conditional on regressors, as an assumption recursive: declared contemporaneous recursive ordering Response at horizon h y[t+h] - y[t-1] Level impulse response at h Shock size Multiple of the observed shock's transformed unit Named shock variable's impact in its transformed unit lags=p Lags 1–p of the individual response, shock and controls; contemporaneous controls and a constant Lags 1–p of every ordered variable and a constant; p ≥ 1 Effective sample First shock date is max(1,p); last is T-h-1 Dates p through T−1 for the fitted VAR Uncertainty Pointwise normal HAC intervals; Bartlett bandwidth h+1 Optional residual bootstrap pointwise percentile intervals

Horizons are inclusive: horizon=8 returns 0 through 8. LP responses have different estimation windows by horizon. Changing lags can also change fitted observations. n_obs is reported per result, and effective_by_horizon in the manifest records the shock/regressor dates. Identical raw and transformed input windows do not imply identical fitted observations.

LP response, shock and control names must be distinct. With multiple responses, each LP uses its own response lags; other responses are not silently inserted as controls. n_boot must be zero for LP. For VAR, ordering contains every variable exactly once and controls is empty:

recursive = replace(
    spec, name="Recursive VAR", method="var_cholesky",
    identification="recursive", controls=(),
    ordering=("price", "shock", "output"), n_boot=199, seed=71,
)
var_result = run_study(data, recursive)

The VAR normalizes the entire response by shock_size / P[k,k], where P is the point estimate's Cholesky factor and k is the shock's ordered position. Bootstrap intervals use this fixed normalization: they do not renormalize every draw to the same impact. Negative shocks reverse interval endpoints correctly. n_boot=0 omits interval columns; it does not fabricate zero-width bands. Failed bootstrap draws and estimated VAR instability remain visible in the audit table. Nonfinite exported estimates or intervals raise an error.

compare_studies accepts at least two uniquely named studies with matching method, identification, ordering, horizon, variable definitions, response convention, shock size and units, and identical raw/transformed data and metadata. Lags, confidence level, seed and bootstrap count may differ and are recorded. Mixed LP/VAR comparisons are rejected: an observed exogenous shock with a cumulative response is not automatically the same estimand as a recursively identified innovation with a level response. The API does not add a cosmetic overlay that conceals this difference.

docs.title: Preserve and reload evidence safely
docs.text:
save_study(result, "study.pmstudy") writes a new file; save_study(result) returns bytes. load_study(path_or_bytes, max_bytes=64 * 1024 * 1024) validates the exact archive inventory, schema, frame and manifest SHA-256 checksums, units, sample counts and finite numerical values. ZIP expansion and NPY array shapes are bounded before decoding. It uses JSON and the version-2 runtime NPZ codec, including supported frame metadata. It neither extracts archive paths nor unpickles objects, imports callbacks or executes an estimator. No Parquet engine, cloud account or network connection is required.

Checksums detect changed content; they do not authenticate authors or prove the correctness of a deliberately rehashed result. Seeds and numerical package versions are retained. Bitwise rerun equality is expected only within the same numerical environment; different BLAS libraries or package versions can change floating-point results. The diagnostic statuses are passed, failed, not_checked and unsupported; identification remains not_checked.

docs.title: Record an evaluated model or scenario
docs.text:
ScenarioSpec, ScenarioResult and record_scenario record existing DSGE, dynamic-programming, HANK, structural-fit or static scenario outputs. They do not run a second solver. Source is inert text; parameters, evaluated outputs, input tables, audit statuses and optional evidence frames are retained.

The following illustrates an explicitly calibrated response path, without claiming that its parameters were estimated from the example observations:

from puremacro.study import ScenarioSpec, record_scenario

scenario_spec = ScenarioSpec(
    name="Calibrated response illustration", model="declared geometric response",
    variables=spec.variables, responses=spec.responses, shock=spec.shock,
    frequency=spec.frequency, identification=spec.identification,
    response_convention="y[t+h]-y[t-1]",
    horizon=spec.horizon, shock_size=spec.shock_size,
)
outputs = pd.DataFrame({
    "response": ["output"] * (spec.horizon + 1),
    "horizon": range(spec.horizon + 1),
    "estimate": [0.1 * 0.7**h for h in range(spec.horizon + 1)],
})
scenario = record_scenario(
    outputs, scenario_spec,
    inputs=baseline.inputs, transformed_inputs=baseline.data,
    model_source="response[h] = 0.1 * persistence**h; pre-shock baseline = 0",
    parameters={"persistence": 0.7, "impact": 0.1},
    audits=pd.DataFrame([{
        "check": "economic_identification", "status": "not_checked",
        "detail": "External shock equivalence is assumed for this illustration.",
    }]),
    provenance={"purpose": "calibrated illustration; parameters not estimated"},
)
overlay = compare_studies(
    baseline, scenario,
    comparison_note="Assume the model innovation maps to the declared observed "
                    "exogenous shock and the same pre-shock baseline; illustrative only.",
)
scenario.write_report("study_output/calibrated_response")

Outputs contain exactly response, horizon, estimate, in response-major order and horizons 0..H. Units are supplied by variables. Audit tables have check, status, detail; failed, unsupported or not-checked rows are retained. parameters contains finite real scalars; evidence={"name": dataframe} can store general calibration matrices, actual full joint moment covariance, fit/held-out targets, distribution/state paths or separate draw records. The recorder never constructs a covariance from marginal LP bands.

inputs may be a static model/calibration table. transformed_inputs is mandatory when variable definitions declare a nonidentity transform or scale; the recorder does not infer or recompute model data transformations. For a static input-output scenario, horizon=0, frequency="annual_static", identification="calibrated_input_output_scenario" and response_convention="static_level_change" are honest explicit labels. No empirical date index is required for a standalone scenario.

Any comparison containing scenarios requires comparison_note. It also checks exact shock/response units and transformations, shock size, identification, frequency, horizon and response convention, and identical raw/transformed input snapshots. A note cannot override an inconsistent contract. These checks verify declared comparability; they do not prove economic equivalence. Scenario tables do not fabricate empirical observation counts or confidence intervals.

save_study/load_study distinguish empirical and scenario archive tags. Scenario reports additionally include model_source.txt; lossless evidence and provenance remain inside the archive. Unsupported frame structures, such as named MultiIndex column levels or subclass-specific result attributes, are rejected if the runtime codec cannot preserve them. Convert deliberately to a plain table and retain coordinate definitions in provenance. All numeric evidence must be finite; retain failed-draw status separately instead of hiding or replacing failed numerical output.

This workflow does not automate IV identification, structural estimation or model/scenario selection. To construct correlated empirical targets and fit a model callback, use the existing structural bridge and research workflows, then record their actual outputs.

docs.title: Runnable workflow templates
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Runnable study and scenario templates
docs.text:
These examples require Puremacro 5.6.0 and run offline with its standard dependencies. They connect data or model declarations, estimation or solution, diagnostics, and a portable report archive. They demonstrate methods and their assumptions; they do not reproduce a published causal policy finding.

The executed English notebook 69 and its editable source walk through all three experiments with figures, audits, archive checks and exercises. They require Python 3.11+, Puremacro 5.6.0 and _nbstyle.py beside the notebook.

python -m puremacro.examples.study_workflows --output study_output
# Or select --workflow mexico, household or tariff.

The output directory must be new. Each subdirectory contains Markdown, LaTeX, Typst, CSV, a manifest and study.pmstudy. Model scenarios also retain their source as inert text. The archive includes the original inputs and named evidence frames; study recording explains the integrity checks.

docs.title: Mexican interest rates and inflation
docs.text:
run_mexico uses the already frozen course snapshots of OECD observations distributed by FRED: three-month interbank interest rates and year-on-year CPI inflation. The packaged manifest records the source URLs, units and exact input hashes. The original retrieval date was not recorded; these are not real-time vintages. The common monthly window is explicitly January 2000–December 2023. No interior missing month is deleted or interpolated.

These OECD observations distributed by FRED are third-party data outside the code's MIT license. Cite OECD and retain attribution when sharing. The packaged manifest preserves source URLs, hashes, citations and OECD reuse terms.

The recursive VAR uses six lags, orders inflation before the rate, and reports horizons 0–18 after a 0.25 percentage-point increase in the annualized rate. Inflation is already year-on-year growth; no further log/difference/annualization is applied. The ordering assumes inflation does not respond within the month to the identified rate innovation. This is an identifying restriction; the result is not an external-instrument or narrative-surprise estimate. The small two-variable system omits other potentially relevant information and allows a price puzzle. The 199 seeded residual-bootstrap draws use the fixed normalization described in the study guide. No structural HANK parameters are silently fitted to this VAR.

from puremacro.examples.study_workflows import run_mexico

result = run_mexico(n_boot=199)
print(result.to_frame().head())
print(result.audits)

docs.title: A household transfer written as a dynamic program
docs.text:
run_household loads the saving model from DP .mod declarations, solves EGM, then evaluates a nonlinear 40-quarter transition from the stationary distribution. A date-0 transfer of 0.05 consumption units per household is externally funded. Prices and earnings risk stay fixed; there is no government financing or general equilibrium response. This is an illustrative calibration, not a survey fit.

The report gives changes in consumption and entering assets, subtracting the zero-shock path under identical terminal values. It retains both paths, the transfer, initial distribution, policies, shock transition matrix, parameters and stationary audit. Assets cannot jump on impact; subsequently, consumption plus next-period assets exhaust current resources. Tests check this identity. The audit preserves any grid/boundary failures; a small solve tolerance is not a grid-accuracy certificate. Use the explicit refinement API when changing grids or horizons. For survey calibration see the existing SCF Aiyagari example.

from puremacro.examples.study_workflows import run_household

scenario = run_household(amount=0.05, horizon=40, n_a=100)
print(scenario.to_frame().head())
print(scenario.audits)

docs.title: Tariffs through a production network
docs.text:
run_tariff aggregates the bundled OECD ICIO 2023 edition, reference year 2019 to USA/Mexico/rest and resources/manufacturing/other industries (including utilities, construction and services). Every original economy and activity belongs to a group; all intermediate, final-use and value-added totals are conserved. Source hashes, grouping maps and the calibration table are archived. Cite OECD (2023), OECD Inter-Country Input-Output Tables, OECD ICIO. The bundled-data attribution and adaptation terms in puremacro/trade/_datafiles/SOURCES.md also apply to redistributed outputs.

The illustrative scenario is a 5% US tariff on Mexican manufactures, with lump-sum duty rebates and fixed foreign saving in numeraire units. The USA resources producer price is fixed at one. Value added is split two-thirds labor, one-third capital by assumption. The existing accounting guide states the technology, fiscal and closure conventions. Results are changes in gross output at baseline prices, not GDP, welfare or a policy forecast. Both equilibria must converge; their named accounting checks, full physical-equation residuals, prices and outputs are retained. The equation maximum mixes native units (quantities, relative prices, factors and nominal budgets); it is not a single monetary amount. Parameter uncertainty and alternative closures are not estimated.

from puremacro.examples.study_workflows import run_tariff

tariff = run_tariff(rate=0.05)
print(tariff.to_frame())

The empirical study and model scenarios stay separate. Comparing model and empirical responses requires matching frequency, units, shock interpretation, response convention and input sample, plus an explicit economic rationale.

docs.title: Running Anywhere (iPad / browser)
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Running anywhere: iPad, Juno, and the browser
docs.text: puremacro's numerical core is pure numpy + scipy + pandas + matplotlib, which is what makes it importable on an iPad. Importable is not the same as usable. Four things a workstation provides silently are missing on a tablet, and this page is about closing that gap rather than restating the promise.

docs.title: Start here: what can this machine do?
docs.text:
from puremacro import runtime
print(runtime.report())

puremacro runtime
  host       : pyodide 3.12.7 (wasm32)
  device     : tablet
  network    : js-fetch (call runtime.enable_browser_network())
  parquet    : unavailable -> use puremacro.runtime.store / pocket
  threads    : no (1 cpu, unknown)
  writable fs: yes
  backends   : numpy

Detection is heuristic by necessity — no Python API answers "am I inside Juno?" — so it reads sys.platform, the iOS sandbox path (/var/mobile/), and the browser user agent, and every field can be pinned when it guesses wrong:

variable effect PUREMACRO_HOST cpython / pyodide / unknown PUREMACRO_DEVICE workstation / tablet / browser / unknown PUREMACRO_SOCKETS force the socket verdict PUREMACRO_PARQUET force the parquet verdict PUREMACRO_THREADS force the threads verdict

runtime.capabilities() returns the same information as a frozen dataclass, and records which fields came from an override in .overridden.

docs.title: 1. There are no sockets
docs.text:
Under Pyodide there is no TCP stack, so requests and urllib both fail and every puremacro.fetch.* call dies — even though the estimator core imported perfectly. The browser can still make requests; it just does them in JavaScript. One call reroutes the whole existing fetch layer over that:

# requires: a Pyodide / browser kernel with network access
from puremacro import runtime
from puremacro.fetch import fetch_xrate_monthly

runtime.enable_browser_network()
fx = fetch_xrate_monthly(["MEX"])

Nothing in fetch or narrative.sources is modified. The switch replaces the two chokepoints those modules already funnel through: the urllib call in puremacro._http and the requests module object in puremacro.fetch._http. runtime.disable_browser_network() puts both back.

Two browser limits are worth knowing before you depend on this:

  • CORS. The browser refuses cross-origin responses without Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Some public statistical endpoints send it; many WAF-fronted government sites do not. A blocked request raises TransportError naming CORS as the likely cause. Pass proxy= to route through a CORS proxy you control.
  • No timeouts, no custom User-Agent. A synchronous XMLHttpRequest on the main thread cannot set either, so both are accepted and ignored rather than raising — which also means the WAF-bypass user-agent trick in narrative/sources/RETRY_POLICY.md §7 does not work in a browser.

docs.title: 2. There may be no pyarrow
docs.text:
pyarrow is an optional extra (puremacro[io]), and only recent Pyodide distributions (314.x) include it, so on older kernels such as Pyodide 0.28 every parquet path (cache, fetch.labor*, shock_atlas, build_panel) is unreachable. numpy's own .npz container has no such problem — it is zlib plus a header, implemented in numpy itself.

runtime.store is a DataFrame ⇄ npz codec built on that: one array per column plus a JSON schema recording dtypes, index structure and column labels, so a frame survives the round trip with its index intact. It handles PeriodIndex, tz-aware datetimes, Categorical, pandas nullable extension dtypes and MultiIndex, and refuses to pickle arbitrary objects rather than writing an archive that will not load elsewhere. On a 5,000×8 quarterly panel it is also smaller than parquet (310 KB vs 409 KB).

Above it sits puremacro.pocket: pack data where the network and pyarrow are, open it where they are not.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from puremacro import pocket

# A frame to ship (in practice: the panel you just fetched on the workstation)
panel = pd.DataFrame(
    {"USA": [1.0, 1.2, 1.1], "DEU": [0.8, 0.9, 1.0]},
    index=pd.period_range("2025Q1", periods=3, freq="Q"),
)

# workstation, online
pocket.pack(panel, "g7.pmz", source="OECD QNA", vintage="2026-08-19")

# iPad, airplane mode
cart = pocket.load("g7.pmz")
panel = cart.frame()          # sha256-checked on read
cart.provenance.vintage       # '2026-08-19'
print(cart.summary())

A .pmz is a plain zip: a JSON manifest plus one npz per frame, both stdlib or numpy, so it opens without puremacro installed at all. pocket.snapshot(fn, *args, path=...) runs a call and records the reproducing expression in the manifest. And because getting a file onto an iPad is often more friction than the analysis, a cartridge also travels as text:

blob = pocket.to_base64("g7.pmz")     # paste into a message, a note, an email
pocket.from_base64(blob, "g7.pmz")    # on the other machine

Cartridges are a transport format, not a trust boundary: the checksums detect corruption in transit, and nothing more.

docs.title: 3. The app gets suspended
docs.text:
iPadOS stops a backgrounded app. A four-minute bootstrap does not survive someone answering a message, and neither does a Metropolis-Hastings chain or a Krusell-Smith solve. The tablet is not so much slow as interruptible, and an ordinary estimator call is one opaque block that either finishes or is lost.

import numpy as np
from puremacro import longrun

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Y = rng.standard_normal((120, 2))          # your VAR data

def one_draw(i):
    """One bootstrap replication: returns whatever you want the bands of."""
    idx = np.random.default_rng(i).integers(0, len(Y), len(Y))
    return Y[idx].mean(axis=0)

job = longrun.bootstrap(one_draw, 2000, checkpoint="irf.ckpt")
job.run(seconds=30)     # 240/2000 · 12% · ~220s of compute left
job.run(seconds=30)     # ... and again, in a later session
bands = np.percentile(job.result(), [5, 95], axis=0)

Draw i always uses default_rng([seed, i]), so results are invariant to chunk size and to how many sessions the job took — a run resumed across five sittings is bit-identical to one that went straight through. That is what makes a resumed run publishable rather than merely finished. job.result() raises unless the job is complete, so a half-run bootstrap cannot be mistaken for a full one, and a checkpoint carries a fingerprint of the job that wrote it and refuses to be resumed by a different one.

Checkpoints are plain npz loaded with allow_pickle=False, so a job started on the iPad can be finished on the workstation.

docs.title: 4. Compute is smaller
docs.text:
from puremacro import runtime
from puremacro.var.identify import cholesky_svar

runtime.fit(n_boot=2000)              # -> {'n_boot': 400} on a tablet
svar = runtime.budgeted(cholesky_svar)  # clamps cost arguments of a call

Both are opt-in. No estimator consults the budget, so every default is exactly what it always was and a script that runs on your laptop produces the same numbers after this feature landed. Only parameters that change cost are clamped (n_boot, n_draws, n_grid, n_sim); horizon changes what is being estimated, so it is deliberately left alone.

docs.title: n_jobs falls back to a plain loop
docs.text:
Under Pyodide there are no working OS threads, and ThreadPoolExecutor there either refuses to start or silently runs nothing. Five bootstrap engines take n_jobs — wild_bootstrap, wild_bootstrap_var, block_bootstrap, cum_irf_block_bootstrap and bootstrap_bands — and all five route through one place that decides between the pool and the loop:

  • Each engine draws all of its random material up front with your generator and then maps a pure per-replication function over it. Executor.map preserves input order, so the pool and the loop return identical output; only the wall clock differs.
  • Before an executor is constructed, the engine asks runtime.capabilities().threads. When the answer is no — a Pyodide/WASM kernel, or PUREMACRO_THREADS=0 — it runs the loop and builds no executor at all. Your n_jobs is then simply ignored; nothing raises.
  • If the pool is attempted and cannot start (RuntimeError, OSError or ValueError out of ThreadPoolExecutor), a RuntimeWarning names the engine and says the replications are being evaluated serially instead.
  • n_jobs=0 raises ValueError before anything runs; a negative n_jobs means every CPU core; n_jobs=1 is the loop.
  • An exception raised inside your per-replication function is never swallowed. It propagates unchanged from either path, so a failing refit is reported rather than quietly retried.

PUREMACRO_THREADS is a boolean override, not a thread count. Like the other capability overrides it is true only for 1, true, yes or on; anything else — including PUREMACRO_THREADS=8 — reads as no threads and turns every n_jobs into a serial loop. To pick a worker count, pass n_jobs.

from puremacro import runtime
runtime.capabilities().threads      # the verdict all five engines gate on
runtime.capabilities().overridden   # ('threads',) when the env var set it

docs.title: 5. Offloading Heavy Compute to Google Colab
docs.text:
When a simulation, bootstrap, or MCMC chain exceeds the memory or thermal envelope of an iPad, puremacro.runtime provides a bridge to export self-contained jobs to Google Colab:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from puremacro.runtime import generate_colab_notebook, colab_auth_guide

# Print step-by-step authentication instructions for mobile Safari / iPad
print(colab_auth_guide())

# The data the cloud run needs, embedded losslessly (index and dtypes preserved)
panel_data = pd.DataFrame(np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((200, 6)),
                          columns=[f"x{i}" for i in range(5)] + ["policy_rate"])

# Heavy computation script
heavy_code = """
import numpy as np
from puremacro.var import favar

# Runs 2,000 bootstrap draws on cloud CPUs
result = favar(my_df, my_df["policy_rate"], n_factors=4, p=2, horizon=24, n_boot=2000)
print(result.summary())
"""

# Export a 1-click self-contained Colab notebook with embedded data
generate_colab_notebook(
    heavy_code,
    data_payloads={"my_df": panel_data},
    title="FAVAR Heavy Bootstrap Run",
    save_path="favar_colab_run.ipynb",
    mount_drive=True,
)

docs.title: Why this works seamlessly on iPad:
docs.text:
• Zero File Uploads: data_payloads embeds your DataFrames directly as base64 strings into the notebook cells, so Colab runs without requiring manual CSV uploads.
  • Guided Authentication: Automatically generates cells prompting for Google account login (auth.authenticate_user()) and Drive mounting (drive.mount('/content/drive')).
  • Cloud Acceleration: Colab provides free cloud GPUs, multi-core CPUs, and expansive RAM, returning .pmz cartridges or LaTeX tables back to your Drive.

docs.title: Local models on the iPad
docs.text:
The Juno app's own Python (not the Pyodide kernel of juno.sh) ships MLX and mlx-lm. MLX is selected on the iPad under Juno, where mlx and mlx-lm import; a completion there is not yet verified on a device. Engines are chosen by what can be imported, never by the operating system, which is why MLX is the one picked there, and the narrative LLM features (score_llm, llm_prob_kernel) go through the same puremacro.llm entry point. Three things to know:

  • Keep Juno in front while the model downloads and while a corpus is scored; a suspended app stops both. The completion cache keeps every answer already computed.
  • Models persist in the app's container. The first completion downloads the reference model, qwen3-4b (about 2.3 GB); later sessions find it there.
  • Compute is smaller: 117 GFLOPS for a float32 matrix product on an iPad Pro M4, against 430 on an M3 Pro Mac. A cache built on a Mac and shipped to the iPad answers in cache mode with no model at all, and that is also what the browser can do.

A completion through Juno's mlx-lm build has not yet been verified on a device. Installation, the model ladder, the modes, shipping a cache and troubleshooting are in Local language models.

The micropip steps under Installing on Juno are for the browser kernel of juno.sh (Pyodide). The Juno app's own Python has no pip or micropip: install puremacro there through Juno's package manager.

docs.title: Installing on Juno
docs.text:
Every base dependency ships with Pyodide, so a dependency-resolving install works without reaching PyPI:

# requires: Pyodide (JupyterLite / juno.sh); `await` is only valid there
import micropip
await micropip.install("puremacro")

Add await micropip.install("pyarrow") for the parquet paths if your Pyodide distribution includes it (314.x does; 0.28 does not).

docs.title: What is actually verified
docs.text:
python tools/release_check.py --pyodide (gate 6) boots a real Pyodide kernel, installs the wheel the way the playground does (resolving dependencies, none from PyPI) and runs the pyodide_smoke-marked suite: 31 tests green under Pyodide 0.28.3, including all ten runtime.store frame round-trips, cartridge pack/verify/base64 transport, the longrun invariance property, and dsge.build solving a model to its closed form. test_detection_matches_the_interpreter_it_is_running_on cross-examines the interpreter and confirms on the target that host == "pyodide", sockets is False, js_fetch is True, parquet is False and backends == ("numpy",).

One gap, stated plainly: the synchronous-XMLHttpRequest body of runtime.transport has never executed. Node-hosted Pyodide has no XMLHttpRequest — it is a browser API — so gate 6 cannot reach it either. Its callers, error paths and module patching are tested; the XHR call itself awaits confirmation from a real browser or Juno session.

docs.title: Text as data (corpus, tokenizer, DTM)
docs.text: 🇬🇧 English · 🇪🇸 Español

docs.title: Text as data: corpus, tokenizer and document-term matrices
docs.text:
Two layers turn policy documents into numbers:

  • puremacro.narrative: harvests statements, minutes, speeches, budgets and news from central banks, treasuries and other agencies into a NarrativeCorpus, which can be stored, reloaded and exported.
  • puremacro.text: a tokenizer, sentence and paragraph segmentation, and a sparse document-term matrix (DTM). It works on any list of strings, not only on a harvested corpus, and imports nothing beyond NumPy, SciPy and pandas.

docs.title: Harvesting and storing a corpus
docs.text:
# requires: network
from puremacro.narrative.harvest import harvest_narrative_corpus

corpus = harvest_narrative_corpus(countries=["USA", "MEX"], policy_domains="monetary",
                                  start_date="2020-01-01", db_path="corpus.db")
print(corpus.harvest_report)          # documents and failures per connector

Without db_path=, store= or use_cache=True the corpus stays in memory and nothing is written to disk. With one of them, each harvest upserts into a SQLite CorpusStore that keeps the latest full text of every document, flags documents whose text changed since they were first stored (store.revised()), and logs each harvest run. store.load(...) returns the accumulated corpus.

A connector that fails raises a warning and is listed in corpus.harvest_report (on_error="warn", "raise" or "ignore"). The text connectors are listed in the source registry as unaudited: their terms have not been reviewed one by one, so check a source's own terms before republishing its text, and share the manifest instead.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
• corpus.to_frame(metadata="promote" | "json" | "drop");
  • corpus.to_jsonl(path) / NarrativeCorpus.from_jsonl(path) (no extra dependency) and to_parquet / from_parquet (the io extra);
  • NarrativeCorpus.from_records(records, source=...) builds a corpus from any connector's (date, text, url, metadata) records, including query-driven ones and your own files;
  • every export writes a provenance manifest() next to it (puremacro version, per-source counts, and a content hash per document). A replication package can ship the manifest instead of the text; verify_manifest checks a re-harvest against it.

docs.title: Tokenizer
docs.text:
RegexTokenizer lowercases, keeps numbers and percentages (central-bank text is full of them), and removes the stop words of each document's language (English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Italian).

from puremacro.text import RegexTokenizer

tok = RegexTokenizer()
print(tok("The Committee decided to raise the target range by 25 basis points to 5.25%.", "en"))
# ['committee', 'decided', 'raise', 'target', 'range', '25', 'basis', 'points', '5.25%']
print(tok("subió al 4,2 % en marzo", "es"))       # ['subió', '4,2%', 'marzo']
print(RegexTokenizer(numbers="mask")("cut by 50 basis points to 4.5%"))
# ['cut', '<num>', 'basis', 'points', '<pct>']

Any callable(text, language) -> list[str] can replace it, so a spaCy lemmatizer or an NLTK stemmer plugs in as a plain function.

docs.title: Document-term matrix
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from puremacro.text import build_dtm

texts = [
    "The Committee decided to raise the target range by 25 basis points to 5.25%.",
    "Inflation remains elevated; the Committee will keep policy restrictive.",
    "La Junta de Gobierno decidió mantener la tasa de interés en 11.25%.",
    "La inflación general anual disminuyó y la Junta prevé recortes graduales.",
]
docs = pd.DataFrame({"doc_id": ["fomc-1", "fomc-2", "bx-1", "bx-2"],
                     "country": ["USA", "USA", "MEX", "MEX"],
                     "date": ["2023-07-26", "2023-09-20", "2023-08-10", "2023-09-28"]})

dtm = build_dtm(texts, languages=["en", "en", "es", "es"], docs=docs)
print(dtm)                               # 4 docs x 29 terms, sparse counts
print(dtm.filter(min_df=2).vocab)        # ['committee', 'junta']

weights = dtm.tfidf()                    # scikit-learn's TfidfTransformer definition
panel = dtm.aggregate(by="country", freq="QS")   # one row per country and quarter
print(panel.docs)
tidy = dtm.to_tidy()                     # doc_id, term, value
  • dtm.X is a scipy.sparse.csr_matrix and dtm.docs a row-aligned frame, so memory scales with non-zero cells.
  • filter(min_df, max_df, max_features, terms) prunes the vocabulary, ngram_range=(1, 2) adds bigrams (formed after stop-word removal).
  • aggregate(by=..., freq=...) sums counts into a country-by-month (or quarter, year, week) panel ready for a regression or a VAR; aggregate the counts first, then call tfidf() on the result.
  • transform(new_texts) counts new documents on the same vocabulary.
  • save(directory) writes X.mtx, vocab.txt and docs.csv, which R reads with Matrix::readMM (and from there quanteda or stm).

From a harvested corpus, corpus.dtm(...) and corpus.segment("paragraph" | "sentence" | callable) do the same on the corpus documents, with stop words taken from each document's language.
